100: The collected plays and poems of William Shakespeare, from comedies and histories to great tragedies and sonnets. Rich in language and human insight, it is the essential gathering for anyone who wants the full range of England's greatest dramatist.
10002: A recluse stays in a remote Irish house, where he experiences strange and terrifying visions of other worlds and supernatural creatures. Hodgson's novel is eerie, visionary and full of cosmic horror.
10007: A young woman living in an isolated castle in Styria becomes drawn to a mysterious new friend, and strange events begin to unfold. Le Fanu's Gothic novella is atmospheric, seductive and a foundation of vampire literature.
10055: Lessing's criticism of the theatre, written as a series of reviews for the German National Theatre in Hamburg. The essays are sharp, witty and central to German drama criticism.
10102: A spy story by William Le Queux, full of intrigue, disguise and dangerous secrets in the years before the First World War. It is a fast, old-fashioned thriller.
10148: Howard Pyle's retelling of the Robin Hood legends in Nottinghamshire, woven into a single narrative of outlaw adventure. The tales are lively, colourful and full of archery and fights.
10215: An Italian historical novel set in sixteenth-century Lombardy, with the political rivalries, wars and romance of the period. It is a sweeping and patriotic story.
1023: In the Court of Chancery, a long and tangled lawsuit draws in many characters, from a young orphan to lawyers and poor families. Dickens's novel is intricate, satirical and full of London fog and humanity.
103: The wealthy and punctual Phileas Fogg bets his friends he can circle the globe in eighty days, and his French valet joins him on a race against time. Verne's adventure is brisk, witty and full of exotic places and comic mishaps.
10425: Goethe's verse play follows the Italian poet Torquato Tasso at the court of Ferrara, where love and rivalry press on his fragile mind. The play is reflective, lyrical and full of courtly tension.
10441: A fantasy tale by Robert W. Chambers set in New York, with courtship, magic and a light supernatural touch. It is charming, whimsical and romantic.
105: Anne Elliot, a sensible woman of twenty-seven, is persuaded years earlier to break off her engagement, and now she meets the man again. Austen's last novel is gentle, reflective and tender, with a quiet but emotional mood.
10506: The first part of a trilogy of rough rural comedies set in Galicia, full of brutal passions, feuds and wild country life. Valle-Inclán's play is raw, poetic and striking.
10623: A collection of plays by Susan Glaspell, the American playwright known for her realistic and feminist dramas about ordinary lives. The plays are thoughtful, sharp and emotionally direct.
1063: A man plots an elaborate revenge against a friend he believes has insulted him, during the Carnival season in an Italian city. Poe's short story is chilling, tightly crafted and full of macabre suspense.
10636: Marco Polo's account of his travels through Asia and the court of Kublai Khan, with descriptions of wonders, customs and distant lands. The travelogue is vivid, curious and full of marvels.
1064: Prince Prospero hides with his wealthy courtiers inside an abbey while a deadly plague sweeps the land outside. Poe's short story is haunting, allegorical and full of gothic atmosphere.
10676: A sequel to Rizal's earlier novel, depicting the corrupt and oppressive colonial society of the Philippines under Spanish rule. The novel is political, passionate and full of vivid characters.
10687: Tartarin, a bragging and comic hero of Tarascon, travels to Algeria to hunt lions and his boasts become comic misadventures. Daudet's satire is funny, lively and full of southern French character.
107: Bathsheba Everdene, a proud and independent farm mistress in rural Wessex, is courted by three very different men. Hardy's pastoral novel is warm, earthy and dramatic, full of country life and the rhythms of the seasons.
10746: A group of travellers in a stagecoach during the Franco-Prussian War are forced to share a journey, and their hidden prejudices come to the surface. Maupassant's story is sharp, realistic and full of social satire.
10775: A man keeps a diary in which he describes the growing sense that an invisible presence is living in his house. Maupassant's short horror story is eerie, intimate and deeply unsettling.
1079: Tristram Shandy sets out to tell the story of his life, but his digressions and wayward tangents keep him from ever getting very far. Sterne's comic novel is playful, experimental and very funny.
108: Sherlock Holmes returns in a collection of thirteen puzzling cases, from murders and missing persons to strange robberies, all solved through sharp observation. Doyle's stories are clever, brisk and full of Victorian London atmosphere.
1080: Jonathan Swift's famous essay offers a deliberately shocking solution to poverty in Ireland, written in cool, deadpan style. It is one of the sharpest satires in English, short and unforgettable.
10800: Robert Burton's vast study of melancholy covers its causes, symptoms and cures in learned, witty and digressive prose. It is an encyclopedic classic, full of quotations and curious learning.
1081: Chichikov, a charming swindler, travels through provincial Russia buying up the names of dead serfs on the census rolls. Gogol's satire is funny, grotesque and full of memorable provincial characters.
10822: A Spanish novel by Vicente Blasco Ibáñez with themes of women, engineering and social change, offering a satirical and modern view of its time. It is lively and thoughtful.
10825: A gentle Christmas story set in the mountains, with a warm and sentimental tone. It is a short and simple read.
10841: A scholarly survey of Egyptian archaeology and art by the French Egyptologist Gaston Maspero, covering monuments, sculpture and daily life. It is authoritative and clearly organised.
10909: A verse drama based on the legend of two star-crossed lovers of the Spanish town of Teruel. The play is romantic, tragic and full of old Spanish legend.
10917: A German winter story about a family in the south of Germany, centred on everyday life, school and home. It is warm, gentle and wholesome.
11: A girl tumbles down a rabbit hole into a topsy-turvy land of talking animals, shifting sizes and nonsense logic. Lewis Carroll's classic is playful, witty and dreamlike, and it suits readers of any age who enjoy absurd humour.
110: Tess Durbeyfield, a country girl from a poor family in Wessex, faces hardship and injustice that test her dignity and resilience. Hardy's tragic novel is moving and sympathetic, a powerful critique of social pressures on women.
11070: Benito Pérez Galdós's first novel, set in Madrid during the turbulent years of the Spanish liberal revolution and its aftermath. It is historical, political and full of vivid Spanish society.
11071: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca's account of his years lost in the American wilderness after a failed Spanish expedition. The narrative is gripping, vivid and an important first-hand record of exploration.
11131: Two brothers in Normandy are thrown into rivalry when an unexpected inheritance divides their family. Maupassant's short novel is psychological, realistic and sharp about family tensions.
11197: A novel by Marjorie Benton Cooke about marriage and the theatre, written in the early twentieth century. It is light and romantic in tone.
11231: A copyist in a Wall Street law office begins to refuse his tasks with the quiet phrase 'I would prefer not to', puzzling his employers. Melville's short story is strange, melancholy and deeply thought-provoking.
113: After losing her parents in India, a sour and spoiled orphan is sent to live with an uncle on the bleak Yorkshire moors. Burnett's children's classic is uplifting and charming, centred on friendship, nature and a hidden garden.
11339: A new translation of Aesop's fables, short animal stories with morals that have delighted readers for centuries. The fables are witty, pithy and perfect for all ages.
11529: A satirical novel by Armando Palacio Valdés, portraying Madrid society and its foibles with irony and affection. It is lively and observant.
1153: John Carter returns to Mars in another adventure of sword fights, daring rescues and exotic cities. Burroughs's pulp novel is energetic and colourful, a fine choice for lovers of planetary romance.
1155: Tommy and Tuppence, two young adventurers, set out to uncover a secret conspiracy in post-war England. Christie's thriller is light, playful and full of spy-story twists.
11589: A comic fantasy by Verne about a scientist and his eccentric experiment in a quiet town, with plenty of gentle satire. It is playful and full of imaginative science.
1164: A manuscript written as a historical account recounts how a rising socialist movement in America is crushed by a ruthless oligarchy. London's dystopian novel is political, gripping and bleak.
1170: Xenophon recounts the march of ten thousand Greek mercenaries deep into Persia and their dangerous retreat home. This ancient memoir is vivid, practical and full of adventure and military drama.
11703: A Swiss family is shipwrecked on a tropical island and must use ingenuity and teamwork to build a home and survive. Wyss's family adventure is cheerful, practical and full of inventions.
11714: A collection of Maupassant's stories told within the frame of a hunting party in Normandy, with tales of love, humour and sudden twists. The stories are witty, observant and varied.
11757: A stuffed toy rabbit longs to become real, and his deep attachment to a young boy shapes his journey. Bianco's children's story is tender, gentle and full of heart.
1184: Edmond Dantès, a young sailor falsely imprisoned in a grim island fortress, escapes and rebuilds his life to take revenge on those who betrayed him. Dumas's adventure is thrilling, dramatic and full of disguises.
119: Mark Twain and his companion Harris set off on a walking tour through Germany, Switzerland and Italy, with comic mishaps along the way. This travel book is funny, observant and full of Twain's sharp commentary on European customs.
11987: A collection of legal stories by Arthur Train, a lawyer-writer, with courtroom plots and clever twists. It is brisk and entertaining for readers who enjoy law and crime.
12: Alice steps through a mirror into a world arranged like a game of chess, where everything runs backwards and the characters are strange and funny. Carroll's sequel is clever, wordplay-filled and dreamlike, with a gently satirical edge.
120: The young Jim Hawkins finds a treasure map and joins a voyage to a remote island with a crew of pirates and a suspicious cook. Stevenson's classic adventure is exciting, colourful and full of memorable characters.
1200: The giant Gargantua and his son Pantagruel have comic adventures, feasts and philosophical debates in Rabelais's bawdy masterpiece. This Renaissance satire is boisterous, inventive and full of earthy humour.
12005: A prose poem by the Uruguayan-born French writer Lautréamont, wild, surreal and full of cruelty and dark imagery. It is a challenging and intense work of nineteenth-century French poetry.
12053: A short story by Thomas Mann set in Munich, about religious fanaticism and the clash between faith and art. It is intense, atmospheric and full of Mann's sharp irony.
121: Catherine Morland, a young woman who loves Gothic novels, visits Bath and imagines mysteries in every corner of her new life. Austen's gentle satire is light, funny and warmly observant of young love and imagination.
1210: Lafcadio Hearn collects Japanese ghost stories, legends and strange encounters, each told with a quiet, eerie beauty. The book is haunting, poetic and perfect for readers who enjoy ghostly tales.
12108: A celebrated writer travels to Venice seeking rest and inspiration, and his quiet routine is disturbed by an obsession. Thomas Mann's novella is elegant, psychological and steeped in the atmosphere of the lagoon city.
12116: Ten illustrated cautionary tales in rhyme about naughty children and the grim consequences of their behaviour. The book is funny, grim and a classic of German children's literature.
1212: Austen's youthful burlesque is written as a series of silly, melodramatic letters between foolish and sentimental young people. It is funny and light, showing her early wit and love of parody.
12122: A couple receive a magical monkey's paw that grants three wishes, with a warning that each wish carries a price. Jacobs's short horror story is tense, eerie and a classic of the genre.
12345: A financier plots to manipulate the stock market and spread panic across America, with the risks and tensions of Wall Street at the centre. Lawson's novel is dramatic, topical and full of financial intrigue.
12356: Jacques Cartier's account of his voyages up the St Lawrence River to Canada, with first encounters with the Indigenous peoples and the land. The narrative is direct, curious and an early record of exploration.
12457: A student frees a limping devil from a flask, and the devil takes him flying over Madrid to peek into the lives behind the rooftops. Vélez de Guevara's satirical novel is witty, lively and full of colourful scenes.
1250: In a future society where individuality is forbidden and even the word I is banished, a young man secretly begins to question everything. Rand's novella is short, idealistic and dystopian.
1251: Malory's great prose compilation of the legends of King Arthur, Guinevere, Lancelot, Merlin and the Knights of the Round Table. These tales are romantic, chivalrous and full of noble deeds and tragic loves.
1254: Cyrano de Bergerac is a brilliant swordsman and poet whose enormous nose makes him shy in love, so he helps a rival woo the woman he secretly adores. Rostand's verse play is witty, romantic and bittersweet.
1257: A young Gascon named d'Artagnan arrives in Paris and becomes friends with three musketeers, sharing swordfights and political intrigue. Dumas's swashbuckler is fast-paced, witty and full of loyalty and daring.
1259: d'Artagnan and the musketeers return years later to face new political plots in France, with old friends and old enemies. Dumas's sequel is lively, nostalgic and full of swordplay.
1260: Jane Eyre, an orphaned governess, takes a post at a gloomy country house, where she falls in love with her employer and uncovers a secret. Brontë's novel is passionate, morally serious and a classic of English fiction.
12627: Sketches of mountain life in northern Spain, realistic and affectionate, portraying village characters and their customs. The stories are gentle, descriptive and full of regional colour.
1268: Five prisoners of war escape in a balloon and land on a remote Pacific island, where they must survive and build a new life. Verne's castaway adventure is inventive, practical and full of mysteries.
12758: A broad anthology of detective and mystery stories from many writers, gathered for readers who enjoy clever sleuths, puzzling crimes and the classic whodunit. Each tale brings a different investigator and a different way of solving a crime.
128: A collection of tales from Arabian folklore, told within a frame story of a storyteller who spins tales night after night. Andrew Lang's version is colourful and magical, full of djinns, merchants, princes and clever escapes.
12814: A collection of traditional folk tales from the Philippines, full of the gods, spirits and semi-divine figures of local legend. It suits readers who enjoy myth and folklore from around the world.
12848: A novel by Pío Baroja from his sea series, narrated by an old Basque sailor looking back on a life of voyages and adventure. Reflective and salty, it is steeped in the atmosphere of ships, the sea and the coasts of northern Spain.
12949: A short collection of French stories, the kind of brief, self-contained texts that suit readers building up their French. The catalogue lists it under French fiction and short stories, so it is a straightforward read in the classic French style.
131: Christian, a burdened man, leaves the City of Destruction with his heavy load and makes a long journey toward the Celestial City, facing many obstacles along the way. Bunyan's allegory is vivid, earnest and full of memorable characters.
13187: A political satire written as a dialogue between Machiavelli and Montesquieu in hell, aimed at the regime of Napoleon III. Sharp, witty and pointed, it reads as a debate over power and the methods rulers use to keep it.
13380: A dialogue novel by George Sand set in Renaissance Italy, about a young noblewoman raised as a man so that she can inherit. Passionate and romantic, it explores gender, identity and love.
13415: A short story by Anton Chekhov about a Moscow banker and a young married woman whose affair begins during a holiday in Yalta. Quiet, melancholy and psychologically sharp, it is one of Chekhov's most admired stories.
1342: Elizabeth Bennet, a lively and witty young woman in Regency England, navigates prejudice and social pressure as she meets the proud Mr Darcy. Austen's classic comedy of manners is sparkling, romantic and full of humour.
135: The ex-convict Jean Valjean is hunted by the relentless police inspector Javert as he tries to build a new, honest life and protect a young girl. Hugo's epic novel is sweeping and emotional, set against the revolutionary history of Paris.
13507: Horacio Quiroga's collection of short stories, first published in 1918, in which death and madness drive most of the plots. Set largely in rural and jungle surroundings, the tales are intense, eerie and bleak.
1353: A French officer and his companions are carried off into space on a fragment of Earth torn loose by a passing comet. Verne's voyage is inventive and playful, a sci-fi romp of wonder and comedy.
13594: Literary portraits by Sainte-Beuve, the nineteenth-century French critic, sketching writers of his time and of the past with close, personal judgment. Suited to readers interested in French literature and its critics.
13703: Colette's semi-autobiographical book about her childhood in a small French village, with her mother and the small world of her girlhood. Warm, observant and often wry, it portrays a lively young girl and her family.
13732: A small collection of German children's poems, gentle verses with simple rhymes about home and everyday childhood. It suits young readers, or learners who want easy German poetry.
13765: A locked-room mystery in which the young reporter Joseph Rouletabille investigates a mysterious attack inside a sealed room at a château. Fast-paced and clever, it is a classic French detective story from 1907.
13771: The first volume of Dickens's comic novel about Mr Pickwick and his club of gentlemen, who travel through England and fall into one humorous mishap after another. Light, warm and very funny, it is a classic of episodic comedy.
13789: A history of Britain's neutrality during the American Civil War, looking at how the government and public opinion dealt with the conflict. It covers the cotton shortage, blockade running and the diplomatic tensions, and suits readers interested in nineteenth-century history.
13819: A historical adventure by Dumas about a royalist conspiracy during the turbulent years of the Revolution and the rise of Bonaparte. Full of disguises, daring escapes and political intrigue, it is an exciting read for lovers of swashbuckling history.
13848: A collection of short stories by Barbey d'Aurevilly, each centred on a woman who commits an act of revenge, violence or some other crime. Dark, elegant and psychologically intense, it is a classic of nineteenth-century French gothic fiction.
13856: Dumas and Maquet's historical novel set in sixteenth-century France, around the Valois court and the religious wars between Catholics and Protestants. Intrigue, romance and political danger run through this first volume, set in the years before the St Bartholomew's Day massacre.
139: A journalist joins a professor's expedition to a remote Amazon plateau where dinosaurs and ape-like creatures still survive. Doyle's adventure is energetic and funny, a classic of lost-world fiction full of danger and wonder.
13947: A volume of the later d'Artagnan adventures by Dumas and Maquet, set in the court of Louis XIV with intrigues, rivalries and loyal swordsmen. It is a long, sweeping historical romance for readers who enjoy following a series.
13948: The second volume of Dumas and Maquet's later d'Artagnan adventures, set in the court of Louis XIV. Full of plots, duels and shifting alliances, it continues a long and dramatic historical story.
13950: A later volume of the d'Artagnan series by Dumas and Maquet, set in the reign of Louis XIV, where old friendships and rivalries return. It is a long, dramatic historical novel for readers who want to continue the story.
13951: Dumas and Maquet's famous novel of a young Gascon, d'Artagnan, who comes to Paris and falls in with three musketeers, Athos, Porthos and Aramis. Witty, fast and full of duels and intrigue against the cardinal's men, it is one of the best-loved adventure novels in French.
13952: The sequel to The Three Musketeers, set during the Fronde, when the musketeers are older and the politics of Mazarin and Cromwell stir new intrigues. Lively and adventurous, it introduces new characters, including Raoul, the Vicomte de Bragelonne.
13965: Sainte-Beuve's literary portraits, second volume, sketching French writers with close and personal critical judgment. Best for readers interested in French literature and its history.
1399: Anna Karenina, a married woman in aristocratic Russia, falls in love with a dashing officer, and her choices shape a wide circle of family and society. Tolstoy's great novel is rich, realistic and emotionally deep.
140: Jurgis Rudkus, a Lithuanian immigrant, arrives in Chicago's meatpacking district, hoping for a better life but finding exploitation and despair. Sinclair's novel is grim, angry and socially committed, exposing the hardships of working-class life.
1400: Pip, a poor orphan boy, is taken up by a mysterious benefactor, and he is swept into a new life of ambition and class. Dickens's novel is a moving study of growing up, full of memorable characters.
141: Fanny Price, a poor and shy young cousin, is sent to live with a wealthy family at Mansfield Park, where she observes their rivalries and romances. Austen's quiet novel is subtle, moral and full of sharp social observation.
14156: Flaubert's unfinished satirical dictionary of received ideas, a collection of clichés and fashionable opinions set out as alphabetical entries. Dry, sharp and very funny, it is a short witty read for lovers of French humour.
14157: Flaubert's unfinished satirical novel about two copy clerks who retire to the countryside and try their hand at one science and pursuit after another. Dry, comic and cutting about middle-class ambition and learning, it is a classic of French satire.
14163: Jules Verne's adventure novel in which a Scottish lord and his crew sail across southern oceans to find a missing sea captain. Full of voyages, dangers and geography, it is a classic of nineteenth-century adventure for young and old readers.
14192: Oscar Wilde's Gothic novel about a handsome young man whose portrait ages while he himself stays youthful. Witty, decadent and disturbing, it explores vanity, influence and moral corruption in Victorian London.
14221: A German retelling of Aladdin and the magic lamp, drawn from the Thousand and One Nights and told in an accessible style for young readers. Light and playful, it is full of genies and wishes.
14223: A scholarly study of Goethe's Faust in its earliest form, the Urfaust, written as a university thesis. Academic and detailed, it suits students and specialists rather than casual readers.
14225: A collection of German tales by Arthur Achleitner, short stories told in a gentle, old-fashioned style. It suits intermediate readers and anyone curious about early twentieth-century German storytelling.
14244: A retelling of the medieval love legend of Tristan and Iseult, the knight and the Irish queen whose love is fated and dangerous. Romantic, lyrical and tragic, Joseph Bédier's version is one of the most readable modern tellings of the tale.
14247: A collection of fairy tales by the Comtesse de Ségur, written for very young children with a gentle moral tone. Simple, warm and full of magic and good manners, it is an old-fashioned French storybook.
14285: Homer's epic of the Trojan War in a French translation, following the wrath of Achilles and the long siege of Troy. Grand, dramatic and moving, it is a foundational classic of Western literature.
14287: Jules Verne's adventure novel about five castaways who escape the American Civil War by balloon and land on an uncharted Pacific island. They build a new life with ingenuity and courage while facing strange and unexplained dangers.
1429: Katherine Mansfield's stories capture ordinary life in New Zealand and England, from family gatherings to small moments of change. The stories are delicate, observant and beautifully written.
14417: Aeschylus's Greek tragedy in an English rhyming verse translation, about the homecoming of King Agamemnon from the Trojan War and the grim events that follow. Solemn, poetic and powerful, it is one of the oldest surviving plays in Western drama.
14471: A collection of ghost stories by Algernon Blackwood, full of eerie atmosphere, haunted houses and unexplained presences. Quiet and unsettling, it suits readers who enjoy classic English supernatural fiction.
145: A provincial English town in the 1830s is the stage for the hopes, marriages and disappointments of a range of idealistic and ordinary people. Eliot's large, richly observed novel is thoughtful, wise and deeply humane.
1450: Pollyanna, an orphan girl with an unfailingly cheerful outlook, brings optimism to a grim New England town. Porter's classic is warm, uplifting and charming.
14522: Oscar Wilde's horror comedy about an American family who move into an English castle haunted by an old ghost. Witty and light, it mocks both the ghost and the newcomers in a short story with a sharp satirical edge.
14591: Goethe's tragic verse play in an English translation that keeps the original metres, about the scholar Faust who makes a bargain with the devil Mephistopheles. Passionate, philosophical and full of dark magic, it is one of the great works of German literature.
146: Sara Crewe, the clever and imaginative daughter of a wealthy father, is sent to a London boarding school, and her fortunes change dramatically. Burnett's story is warm, sentimental and full of kindness and hope.
14609: A French translation of the Kama Sutra, the ancient Sanskrit manual on love, desire and the conduct of life. It is a historical and cultural text rather than a novel, read for its frank discussion of sexuality and social manners.
14688: George Sand's travel account of a winter spent on the island of Majorca with her children and the composer Chopin, who was ill. Reflective and observant, it blends travel writing, personal memoir and descriptions of nature.
14692: Sainte-Beuve's literary portraits, third volume, sketching French writers with close and personal critical judgment. Best for readers interested in French literature and its history.
14790: A collection of short stories by Guy de Maupassant, written in a clear, sharp style about ordinary people in Paris and the countryside. Some tales are light and comic, others eerie and unsettling.
14795: A Spanish-language drama by the Filipino writer José Rizal, a short work from his youth. Its themes reflect the education and ideas of its time, and it suits readers of Spanish drama and Filipino literature.
14796: A short play by José Rizal, written when he was nineteen, set in a council of the gods. It shows the humanist learning of its time and is a good introduction to Rizal's early work.
14818: A novel by George Barr McCutcheon about a foundling girl in New York and the people who shape her life. A light, sentimental story of city life, it suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century American fiction.
14860: Walter Scott's diary from 1825 to 1832, written as he faced financial ruin and worked to repay his debts through his writing. Candid, reflective and often moving, it is counted among the finest diaries in English.
149: An early twentieth-century science fiction adventure by Edgar Rice Burroughs, set partly in England and involving a lost land. Its subjects point to imaginative, fast-moving pulp storytelling in the style of his Mars and Tarzan books.
14913: La Rochefoucauld's collection of short moral maxims, sharp reflections on self-love, vanity and human motives. Brief and witty, it is best read a few at a time.
14915: The medieval German epic of Siegfried, the Burgundian court and the terrible feuds that follow. Heroic, dramatic and tragic, it is a foundational work of German literature.
14944: Blasco Ibáñez's novel about tenant farmers in the Valencian countryside, working land owned by a landlord who lives far away. Realistic and dramatic, it portrays rural life and social conflict in the marshes around Valencia.
1497: Socrates and his companions discuss justice, the ideal city and the just person in Plato's most famous dialogue. It is philosophical, imaginative and still widely read as a classic of political thought.
14975: Ida B. Wells-Barnett's pamphlet exposing lynching in the American South in the 1890s and examining the excuses given for mob violence. Direct, powerful and carefully argued, it is an important work of journalism and civil rights history.
14977: Ida B. Wells-Barnett's statistical record of lynchings in the United States, with analysis of the reasons given for them. Factual, sober and angry, it is an essential source for the history of racial violence.
14988: Cicero's philosophical dialogues on death, pain, virtue and happiness, together with works on the nature of the gods and the state. Clear and reflective, they are classics of Roman thought for readers interested in philosophy.
14995: A Spanish novel by José María de Pereda, a realist writer known for portraying provincial life in northern Spain. It suits readers who enjoy detailed social fiction of the nineteenth century.
15027: A study of the Spanish picaresque novel, the genre of rogues' tales that emerged in Spain's Golden Age. It explains the form, its anti-hero and its influence across European literature, and suits students of Spanish literature.
15058: Ségur's children's novel about Sophie, a mischievous girl whose misbehaviour leads her into trouble on a French country estate. Warm and moralising, it is the first book of a trilogy and a classic of French children's literature.
1510: The King of Navarre and his three companions swear to study for three years without the company of women, and a visiting princess soon changes their plans. Shakespeare's early comedy is witty, playful and full of wordplay.
15115: Cervantes's novellas and plays, including works beyond Don Quixote. Witty, inventive and full of Spanish Golden Age character, this volume offers a broad sample of his storytelling and drama.
1513: The young lovers Romeo and Juliet, from feuding families in Verona, fall in love in secret and face fate and violence. Shakespeare's tragedy is passionate, poetic and heartbreaking.
1514: Lovers, fairies and a group of amateur actors tangle in an enchanted wood outside Athens. Shakespeare's comedy is magical, playful and full of lively mischief.
1519: Two pairs of lovers in Messina are caught up in wit, schemes and misunderstandings. Shakespeare's sparkling comedy is witty, romantic and full of delightful banter.
15206: Benito Pérez Galdós's novel about Francisco Torquemada, a grasping moneylender in nineteenth-century Madrid. Realist, sharp and sometimes sad, it follows his obsession with money and his disappointments.
15208: A collection of ghost and supernatural stories by Alexandre Dumas, written with Paul Lacroix and Paul Bocage. Eerie and varied, the tales offer atmospheric accounts of the uncanny for readers who like classic French horror.
1522: The Roman conspirators plot to kill Julius Caesar, and their decision leads to political turmoil and the struggle for power. Shakespeare's tragedy is dramatic, political and full of famous speeches.
1523: Rosalind flees her uncle's court with her cousin Celia and finds refuge in the Forest of Arden, where love and disguise abound. Shakespeare's pastoral comedy is cheerful, witty and full of songs.
1524: Prince Hamlet is haunted by his father's ghost and sets out to take revenge on his uncle, who has seized the throne. Shakespeare's great tragedy is philosophical, dark and full of memorable soliloquies.
15272: The first book of Spenser's allegorical epic, following the Redcrosse Knight and Una on a quest through a magical land. Rich in symbolism and in the music of its archaic verse, it is a foundation of English poetry.
15288: The fourth volume of Proust's In Search of Lost Time, in which the narrator's view of Paris high society opens onto hidden desires. Introspective and elegant, it is written in long, observant sentences.
1533: The Scottish general Macbeth, urged on by ambition and a prophecy, is drawn into murder and a ruthless grip on power. Shakespeare's tragedy is dark, intense and full of psychological horror.
15381: An anthology of short Victorian stories about courtship, romance and the social rules of love. Gentle, period-flavoured and varied, it offers a glimpse of how love and marriage were pictured in English fiction of the era.
15384: A novel about a married couple and the restless questions that marriage raises. Written in the early twentieth century, it is a light, reflective domestic drama from American fiction.
15474: The first three books of the Mahabharata, the great Sanskrit epic of India. It tells of the rivalry between the Pandavas and the Kauravas, with gods, sages and heroes. Vast, dramatic and full of moral dilemmas, it is one of the world's longest poems.
155: A valuable diamond goes missing from an English country house, and a series of witness letters reveal the secrets of the household. Collins's novel is a clever, twisting mystery and one of the earliest modern detective stories.
15554: Another mystery featuring the young reporter Joseph Rouletabille, who investigates crimes with curiosity and daring. Fast-paced and atmospheric, it is a classic French detective novel from the early twentieth century.
15556: Arthur Young's travel diary of his journeys through France from 1787 to 1789, recording its farming, roads and society on the eve of the Revolution. Observant and opinionated, it is valuable both as history and as travel writing.
1564: James Boswell's classic biography follows the life of the great eighteenth-century writer Samuel Johnson, with his wit, conversation and quirks. This abridged edition is warm, lively and full of anecdotes.
15711: Flaubert's Madame Bovary: Emma, a bored doctor's wife in a provincial Normandy town, seeks romance and escape. Realistic, ironic and tragic, it is a landmark of the European novel.
15721: A romantic adventure novel set in Egypt, full of desert scenes, mystery and danger. It is an escapist read in the style of early twentieth-century British adventure fiction.
158: Emma Woodhouse, a clever and confident young woman in a Surrey village, enjoys matchmaking for her friends and learns hard lessons about herself. Austen's witty comedy is lively, observant and full of delightful social manoeuvring.
15898: Christian Morgenstern's collection of aphorisms and diary notes, tracing his development as a writer and thinker. Brief, playful and reflective, it reads like a personal journal of ideas.
159: A shipwrecked man is left on a remote island, where a scientist conducts disturbing experiments that blur the line between animal and human. Wells's short novel is a chilling horror story with sharp ideas about science and ethics.
1597: Andersen's first collection of fairy tales includes classic stories written for children, full of magic, emotion and folk wonder. These tales are charming, moving and timeless.
16: Peter Pan, the boy who never grows up, takes the Darling children flying to Neverland, home of fairies, pirates and the Lost Boys. J. M. Barrie's story is whimsical and bittersweet, a mix of adventure and wistful reflection on childhood.
160: Edna Pontellier, a married woman in late nineteenth-century New Orleans, begins to question the roles society expects of her. Chopin's short novel is subtle, lyrical and sensitive, a pioneering portrait of female independence.
1608: In Paris, a young man falls in love with a courtesan named Marguerite, whose fragile health and past shape their romance. Dumas's novel is romantic, sentimental and tender.
16082: Rafael Delgado's Mexican novel of love and feeling, first published in serial form in 1894. Sentimental and tender, it follows a romance set against the social life of its time, and is often compared with Jorge Isaacs's María.
161: The Dashwood sisters, the sensible Elinor and the passionate Marianne, must adapt to a reduced fortune and to romantic disappointments. Austen's first novel is witty, humane and gently satirical, full of social comedy.
16110: Cervantes's Viaje al Parnaso, a long verse journey to the mountain of the poets, printed with two plays: the tragedy La Numancia and the comedy El trato de Argel. Playful and reflective, it shows Cervantes as a poet and dramatist.
1619: A young lover, Calisto, enlists the help of a clever go-between, Celestina, to win the heart of Melibea. This Spanish dialogue work is witty, bawdy and full of vivid street characters.
16199: William Godwin's memoir of his wife Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. Candid, personal and frank for its time, it is a key source on her life and on feminist thought in the 1790s.
16235: Charlotte Brontë's novel of Jane Eyre, an orphan who becomes a governess at Thornfield and falls in love with her employer, Mr Rochester. A story of independence, moral courage and romance, it is read here in French translation.
16302: Lily Braun's memoir of her years as a socialist activist and writer in Germany. Personal and political, it describes the struggles of women and the labour movement in the late nineteenth century.
16304: Franz Kafka's short story, the first chapter of his unfinished novel Amerika. A young man sent away from home finds himself a stoker on a ship, in a strange and unsettling world. Dreamlike and precise, it is a good entry point into Kafka's German prose.
16328: The Old English epic of Beowulf, in which a hero battles the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother and a dragon. Heroic and atmospheric, it is one of the foundational works of English literature.
16372: A Spanish novel from the late nineteenth century in which a dog plays a central part in the story. Sentimental and simple, it suits readers who like animal-centred tales.
16389: Four very different English women rent a castle in Italy for a month, and the warm sunshine begins to change them. A witty, gentle comedy about friendship, freedom and romance, it is one of the most charming novels of the 1920s.
164: A French professor and his companions are taken aboard a mysterious submarine captained by an enigmatic man, and they explore the wonders of the deep ocean. Verne's underwater adventure is inventive, detailed and full of marine wonder.
16413: Blasco Ibáñez's novel of customs set in Valencia, with its local characters, rural life and daily habits. Vivid and colourful, it is a good introduction to his regional writing.
16433: A collection of short stories by Temple Bailey, light tales of American life in the early twentieth century. Sentimental and easy to read, they suit readers who want a gentle, uncomplicated story.
16464: The Irish epic Táin Bó Cúailnge, in which Queen Medb of Connacht leads an army to seize a great bull from Ulster. The hero Cú Chulainn stands alone against the invaders in a fierce tale of Irish myth.
16484: Juan Valera's novel set in Andalusia, about a woman whose life and reputation are shaped by the judgment of her community. Witty, realist and lightly ironic, it is a classic of nineteenth-century Spanish fiction.
1661: Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson solve a series of cases in Victorian London, from missing persons to strange thefts, with sharp deduction and wit. This collection is brisk, clever and an ideal introduction to the detective.
16643: Ralph Waldo Emerson's essays on self-reliance, nature, the individual and the spirit. Aphoristic and inspiring, they are a central text of American thought for thoughtful readers.
16653: A retelling of the myths of ancient Babylonia and Assyria, including creation stories and the epic of Gilgamesh. Clear and accessible, it sets Mesopotamian beliefs alongside comparisons with other traditions.
1680: A short novel by Balzac of nineteenth-century French life, offering a stylish portrait of Paris and its ordinary people. The work is witty and observant of everyday society.
16820: Octave Mirbeau's novel in diary form, told by a chambermaid who comes to work in a bourgeois country house. Sharp, satirical and dark, it exposes the cruelty and hypocrisy of the wealthy through a servant's eyes.
1685: A young reporter, Rouletabille, investigates a bizarre crime in a room locked from the inside at a château. Leroux's mystery is clever, playful and one of the first locked-room puzzles.
16852: Zola's novel about a young woman who arrives in Paris and takes a job in a great department store, the Ladies' Paradise. Lively and vivid, it portrays the rise of modern retail and the rivalries among its staff.
1686: Rouletabille travels to Russia, where a plot against the Tsar brings him into danger and intrigue. Leroux's mystery is fast-paced, witty and full of adventure.
16884: Alfred Jarry's absurdist farce about Père Ubu, a greedy, cowardly and outrageous figure who seizes power in Poland. Crude, anarchic and very funny, it shocked its first audience and remains a landmark of modern theatre.
16921: A science fiction adventure set aboard a spaceship, the second volume of Andre Norton's Solar Queen series. Full of space travel and strange alien worlds, it is a fast-paced classic of 1950s science fiction.
1695: A poet joins a secret police force in London, where he meets a group of anarchists and a series of strange, dreamlike events unfold. Chesterton's metaphysical thriller is witty, surreal and full of philosophy.
16952: An Italian novel by Antonio Ghislanzoni, the writer best known as librettist of Verdi's Aida. Written in a late nineteenth-century literary style, it suits readers of Italian fiction of the period.
16961: The opening novel of Galdós's Episodios nacionales, set around the Battle of Trafalgar during the Napoleonic Wars. Seen through the eyes of a young man at sea, it is a vivid historical novel full of naval battles and national feeling.
16980: An Italian novel by Memini, the pen name of a Piedmontese countess, from the late nineteenth century. Written in Italian, it offers a literary glimpse of the society of its period.
17013: Galdós's novel of two married women in Madrid, Fortunata and Jacinta, whose lives are shaped by love and social expectation. Realistic and richly detailed, it is a major work of Spanish literary realism.
17073: Clarín's realist novel set in the provincial town of Vetusta, following Ana Ozores, a married woman, and the clergy and society who watch her. Ironic, detailed and psychologically sharp, it is a masterpiece of Spanish realism.
17157: Swift's satire of voyages to lands such as Lilliput and Brobdingnag, narrated by the surgeon Lemuel Gulliver. Witty, bizarre and biting, it is a classic of satirical fiction that works for both children and adults.
17161: Wilhelm Busch's illustrated rhyming story of two mischievous boys whose pranks keep getting them into trouble. Funny and sharp, with a moral edge, it is a classic of German children's verse.
1719: Chesterton's ballad celebrates King Alfred the Great and his defeat of the invading Danes, told in the style of a traditional heroic epic. The poem is stirring, patriotic and vivid.
17199: A children's periodical from 1891 with stories, poems and articles for boys and girls. It offers a snapshot of late nineteenth-century children's publishing, lively and varied.
172: A bookseller in Brooklyn and his colourful friends become involved in a series of mysterious events. Morley's bibliomystery is charming and warm, full of love for books and the people who sell them.
17223: Juan Valera's novel of a young widow, Pepita, and the seminarian who falls in love with her, set in Andalusia. Lyrical, ironic and romantic, it explores desire set against religious duty.
1727: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, struggles home from the Trojan War, facing monsters, gods, temptations and a household overrun by suitors. Homer's epic is adventurous, moving and full of memorable scenes.
1728: This translation of Homer's epic tells how the wily Odysseus wanders the sea for ten years, meeting monsters, goddesses and a long-lost home. It is a rich, lyrical version of one of the world's oldest stories of return.
173: Dr Fu Manchu, a brilliant and sinister criminal mastermind, plots to bring down the British Empire, and detectives race to stop him. Rohmer's pulpy thriller is melodramatic, exotic and full of fast-paced villainy.
17335: The second part of an adventure story about Captain Corcoran, who recounts marvellous and supposedly authentic voyages. Lively and imaginative, it suits readers who enjoy nineteenth-century French adventure stories.
17340: Galdós's novel about Marianela, a poor and plain orphan girl who guides a blind young man through a small Spanish town. Tender, sad and sharply observant of social inequality, it is an early classic of Spanish realism.
17341: Clarín's second novel, a provincial story of a marriage and an adultery. Less celebrated than La Regenta, it still offers a sharp portrait of provincial Spanish society.
17362: E. T. A. Hoffmann's fairy tale of a young student, Anselmus, who is drawn into a world of magic, spirits and a golden snake maiden. Playful and imaginative, it is Hoffmann's most successful work.
17383: A non-fiction account of expeditions across Borneo, combining travel description with observations on the peoples and cultures of the island. Factual and detailed, it suits readers interested in exploration and early ethnography.
174: A beautiful young man in Victorian London remains youthful while a portrait of him ages and grows monstrous. Wilde's Gothic novel is witty, decadent and philosophical, exploring beauty, vanity and moral corruption.
17406: A novel by Emilia Pardo Bazán about a newly married couple travelling through Europe on their honeymoon. Observant and witty, it mixes travel description with a gentle look at manners, marriage and social life.
17443: The last novel of Galdós's second series of Episodios nacionales, set during the Carlist conflicts over the Spanish throne and the role of the clergy. Historical, lively and full of political intrigue, it suits readers of Spanish history in fiction.
17457: Maupassant's first novel, following a young woman from convent-school hopes into marriage and family life in Normandy. Realistic and melancholy, it looks closely at how dreams of happiness fare against everyday disappointment.
17460: A historical romance set on Exmoor in the late seventeenth century, with a young farmer, a feud with a lawless family and the turmoil of Monmouth's rebellion. Adventurous and tender, it is a classic of Victorian romance.
1747: A mystery novel by Natalie Sumner Lincoln, published in the early twentieth century, full of intrigue and suspense. It is a light, traditional detective story for readers who enjoy old-fashioned mysteries.
17489: Victor Hugo's sweeping social epic, following the former convict Jean Valjean and the poor, the outcast and the idealists whose lives cross his in nineteenth-century France. This first volume centres on Fantine, a poor mother, and the injustice she suffers. Long, moving and deeply humane.
17491: A realist novel by Pardo Bazán set among the workers of a tobacco factory in Spain, with the political passions and rivalries of its people. Vivid and critical of social conditions, it suits readers of Spanish realism.
17493: The second volume of Hugo's Les Misérables, following Cosette's childhood and her life with Jean Valjean. Tender, dramatic and rich in social detail, it deepens the novel's long moral story.
17494: The third volume of Les Misérables, which introduces Marius, an idealistic young student in Paris, and the revolutionary movement that stirs the city. Passionate and sweeping, it widens Hugo's canvas of social life.
175: At the Paris Opera, a mysterious masked figure haunts the theatre and terrorises its performers, while a young singer is caught between him and a young nobleman. Leroux's Gothic romance is dramatic, atmospheric and full of suspense.
17517: Zola's novel about a painter, Claude Lantier, and his circle of Impressionist friends in Paris, struggling with ambition and the pressure to create a masterpiece. Intense and bitter, it is a vivid study of artistic life and rivalry.
17518: The fourth volume of Hugo's Les Misérables, which alternates a quiet Paris romance with the epic of the city's streets in revolt. Dramatic and emotional, it carries the novel's story deeper into the turmoil of 1832.
17519: The final volume of Hugo's Les Misérables, returning to Jean Valjean, the fugitive whose choices drive the whole novel. It brings the long moral story of his life to its close.
1754: At a country estate, a young writer and an actress, along with a literary celebrity, meet and misunderstand each other as their dreams collide. Chekhov's play is subtle, melancholy and full of quiet humour.
17565: Dickens's first-person novel of Pip, a poor orphan who is suddenly given money and expectations in London. Mysterious, funny and moving, it explores snobbery, guilt and what it means to grow up.
17622: Three linked tales by Hermann Hesse about Knulp, a carefree vagabond who wanders the Black Forest and the towns of his youth. Gentle, reflective and wistful, the stories explore freedom, friendship and an unsettled life.
17691: A novelised account of an imagined journey around France by aeroplane, from the early days of flight. Light, enthusiastic and full of the excitement of travel and invention.
17805: A school reader for Italian children, combining short lessons with moral stories and tales. Simple and didactic, it offers a window onto the reading of Italian children in the late nineteenth century.
17837: Guerrazzi's historical novel about Beatrice Cenci, a noblewoman of sixteenth-century Rome caught up in her father's cruelty and the legal drama that followed. Dark and dramatic, it reflects the Italian romantic taste for history.
17851: The autobiography of Mary Prince, born enslaved in Bermuda, who was sold around the Caribbean and later came to England. Direct, painful and important, it is one of the first slave narratives published in Britain by a Black woman.
17930: A French version of Shakespeare's comedy of lovers, fairies and mischief in an enchanted wood outside Athens. Playful, romantic and magical, it is a light comedy about love, confusion and the power of illusion.
17941: Jean de La Fontaine's verse fables, in which animals stand for human vices and follies. Witty, wise and concise, they are a cornerstone of French literature and a favourite way to learn the language.
17949: The first volume of Tolstoy's epic of Russian aristocrats and the Napoleonic invasion, following Pierre, Andrei and Natasha. Vast, humane and absorbing, it moves between the drawing rooms of Moscow and the battlefield.
17950: The second volume of Tolstoy's epic of Russian aristocrats and the Napoleonic wars, following Pierre, Andrei and Natasha through war and society. Vast, humane and absorbing, it continues the great canvas of the novel.
17980: La Bruyère's satirical character sketches of French society in the late seventeenth century, portraits of courtiers, townspeople and types. Witty, sharp and aphoristic, it is a classic of French moral observation.
17989: The first volume of Dumas and Maquet's novel of Edmond Dantès, a young sailor wrongly imprisoned, and his escape and rise to wealth. Gripping and dramatic, it is one of the great adventure novels of French literature.
17990: The second volume of Dumas and Maquet's Monte-Cristo, following Edmond Dantès as he builds a new identity in Paris society and sets his plans in motion. Gripping and dramatic, it sustains the story's suspense.
17991: The third volume of Dumas and Maquet's Monte-Cristo, in which the count's elaborate schemes against his enemies unfold in Paris. Intricate, dramatic and suspenseful, it continues the story of revenge and disguise.
17992: The fourth volume of Dumas and Maquet's Monte-Cristo, continuing the count's elaborate campaign of revenge across Paris society. Gripping and intricate, it is a long, suspenseful adventure.
18005: A naturalist novel by Pardo Bazán set in a decaying manor house in rural Galicia, where a young priest arrives to serve an aristocratic family. Dark, sensual and sharply observed, it portrays rural decline, pride and religious conflict.
18112: Defoe's picaresque memoir of a London woman who survives poverty, several marriages and crime by her wits. Frank, lively and morally complex, it follows her career through the eighteenth-century underworld.
18143: A French translation of Shakespeare's tragedy of two young lovers from feuding families in Verona. Passionate, lyrical and tragic, it is one of the most famous love stories in world literature.
18151: A science fiction story by H. Beam Piper in which time travel and its crimes drive the plot. Inventive and fast, it suits readers who enjoy classic science fiction of the mid-twentieth century.
18166: A short novel by the Cuban writer José Martí, showing his talent for fiction alongside his better-known political and poetic work. It suits readers interested in Martí's literary writing.
18199: The first volume of Dumas's novel about the Diamond Necklace affair, a scandal at the court of Louis XVI that engulfed Marie Antoinette. Intrigue, swindles and court life drive a richly detailed historical romance.
18244: Hans Christian Andersen's famous fairy tales in a French translation, many of them well known to children and adults alike. Magical, tender and sometimes sad, they are classics of the genre.
18245: The second volume of Andersen's fairy tales in French translation, continuing the mix of magic, moral feeling and bittersweet endings. Classic storytelling for readers of all ages.
18258: Jakob Wassermann's historical sketches of German figures, from alchemists to princes, told as vivid narratives. Dramatic and readable, they blend history with biography.
18367: Fairy tales by Madame d'Aulnoy, the seventeenth-century writer who helped popularise the literary fairy tale in France. Ornate, witty and full of princesses, enchantments and marvels.
1837: A poor London boy and a young prince of England, who look alike, swap places and discover how the other half lives. Twain's historical novel is charming, witty and full of Tudor adventure.
18446: Henri Murger's episodic sketches of poor artists, writers and their lovers in the Latin Quarter of Paris. Warm, witty and bittersweet, the stories capture the bohemian life of struggling young creators.
18456: Pirandello's three-act drama about a man who believes himself to be a medieval emperor, and the people around him who try to understand his madness. Psychological and unsettling, it probes the line between madness and reality.
18457: Pirandello's play in which six unfinished characters arrive during a rehearsal and demand that their drama be staged. Witty, self-reflective and provocative, it is one of the most influential plays of the twentieth century.
18459: A dream allegory attributed to the fifteenth-century monk Francesco Colonna, in which a young lover searches for his beloved through a strange landscape of ruins, gardens and architecture. Richly illustrated in its original and dense with learning, it is a strange and beautiful curiosity.
18475: A popular German novel about emigrants leaving northern Germany for America, following their hopes, hardships and adventures. Folksy and vivid, it belongs to the nineteenth-century German emigrant tradition.
1849: A mystery and detective story by E. Phillips Oppenheim, one of the popular thriller writers of the early twentieth century. It is a fast, traditional tale of crime and suspense.
1872: A country-house murder mystery by A. A. Milne, better known for Winnie-the-Pooh, with a cast of suspects and a neatly puzzling plot. It is light, witty and suited to fans of classic English whodunnits.
18731: A German-language history of English language and literature from its earliest times, written for students and readers of English. Scholarly and informative, it suits those studying the history of the language.
1874: Three children whose comfortable life collapses move with their mother to a country village near a railway line, where they make friends and help their neighbours. Nesbit's children's classic is warm, funny and full of cheerful adventure.
18812: Arnauld d'Abbadie's account of twelve years spent in highland Ethiopia, recording its landscapes, peoples and rulers. A factual travel memoir, it is valuable as an eyewitness record of nineteenth-century Abyssinia.
1883: A collection of Chekhov's short stories about ordinary Russian lives, marked by quiet humour, sadness and sharp observation. Each story is short and easy to dip into.
18857: Jules Verne's classic adventure in which a German professor, his nephew and a guide descend into an Icelandic volcano in search of the centre of the Earth. Inventive, suspenseful and full of scientific wonder, it is a foundation of science fiction.
18875: A novel set on the Canadian prairies that follows the life of a frontier wife and the hardships of pioneer life. Grounded and earthy, it captures the isolation and endurance of settlers.
18897: Stephen Langdon's translation of a fragment of the Gilgamesh epic in Old Babylonian cuneiform, with scholarly commentary. Specialised and historically important, it suits readers interested in ancient Mesopotamian literature.
18921: Eugène Sue's sensational serial novel of Paris's underworld, in which a mysterious prince moves among the poor, criminals and the wealthy. Melodramatic, sweeping and socially conscious, it was a huge bestseller in the 1840s.
18947: Snorri Sturluson's thirteenth-century guide to Norse myth, with stories of the gods Odin, Thor and Loki and rules of Old Norse poetry. Vivid and witty, it is the main source for much of what we know of Norse mythology.
19: Longfellow's 1855 epic poem retells the legendary story of Hiawatha, an Ojibwe hero, and his love for Minnehaha, set around the shores of Lake Superior. Written in a rhythmic, chant-like verse, it is a lyrical and melancholy read.
19024: Guerrazzi's Italian historical novel about the Battle of Benevento in 1266, when a French army confronted the last Hohenstaufen king of Sicily. Patriotic and dramatic, it reflects the nineteenth-century Italian love of history.
19027: A juvenile science fiction adventure of space travel to Venus, with young space cadets and a revolt. Fast and wholesome, it is typical of the space-adventure books for young readers of the 1950s.
19048: The autobiography of Ambrogio Bazzero, a nineteenth-century Italian writer, offering a personal and introspective account of his life. It suits readers of Italian autobiography and the inner lives of ordinary people.
1906: A young Englishman travels to a remote country where illness is treated as a crime and crime as an illness. Butler's utopian satire is witty, thoughtful and a sharp mirror held up to Victorian society.
19146: A historical novel set on Maryland's Eastern Shore, drawing on the true story of the notorious kidnapper Patty Cannon. Set in a region of rural secrets and crime, it mixes romance with dark events.
19163: Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales in German, familiar, gently moral and often bittersweet. A classic of childhood reading, they suit German learners and young readers alike.
1931: A First World War adventure by E. Phillips Oppenheim, a popular thriller writer of his day, full of wartime intrigue and suspense. It is a fast, old-fashioned read for fans of spy stories.
19412: A light romance told in letters, following a relationship that unfolds across a sea voyage and changing circumstances. Typical of early twentieth-century popular fiction, it suits readers who enjoy romance and travel.
19476: A scientific romance in which a honeymooning couple tour the planets of the Solar System in a spaceship. Adventurous and imaginative, it reflects the early science fiction of the turn of the twentieth century.
1952: A woman, confined to a room by her husband for a supposed rest cure, writes a secret journal that reveals her growing unease. Gilman's short story is claustrophobic and unsettling, a classic of feminist literature.
19584: Jacob Bryant's eighteenth-century scholarly analysis of ancient mythology, arguing for connections between the myths of many nations. Dense and speculative, it is a historical document of early comparative mythology.
19707: A romantic novel set in New York, in which a single night brings unexpected adventure and love. Light and entertaining, it belongs to the popular fiction of the early twentieth century.
19738: The first part of a French science fiction adventure in which a Russian scientist travels to the Moon. Imaginative and fast-moving, it belongs to the early days of the scientific romance.
19742: A romance between a young woman and a man in Britain, with the love and social complications typical of early twentieth-century popular fiction. Light and sentimental, it suits readers who enjoy classic romance.
19771: A love story set in London society of the 1830s, following a young man whose hopes of marriage are complicated by debts and social pressure. Witty and romantic, it is one of Disraeli's early novels.
19778: Lewis Carroll's classic about Alice, who tumbles down a rabbit hole into a strange world of nonsense, here in a German translation. Playful, surreal and quotable, it is one of the most beloved children's books ever written.
19847: A four-act Spanish drama about the poet and satirist Francisco de Quevedo, presenting him as a figure of wit and courtly intrigue. It suits readers of nineteenth-century Spanish theatre.
19898: José Martí's monthly magazine for children, written with warmth, humour and a love of America. Its stories, poems and essays introduce young readers to history, nature and culture in clear, lyrical Spanish.
19919: The fifth volume of Féval's serial novels about the Habits Noirs, a secret criminal organisation in Paris. Melodramatic, twisty and full of crime, it belongs to the nineteenth-century French serial tradition.
19942: Voltaire's satirical tale of the naive young Candide, who is taught that all is for the best and then tossed across the world. Brisk, witty and savagely funny, it is a classic of Enlightenment satire.
19994: Aesop's fables retold for children, with bright illustrations by Milo Winter. Short, moral and memorable, the animal stories are a good first introduction to classic folk wisdom.
2000: The hidalgo Alonso Quijano reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out as a knight-errant with his squire Sancho Panza. Cervantes's comic masterpiece is witty, wise and full of memorable adventures.
20011: A moral novel by the Jesuit priest Luis Coloma about the vanities and moral failings of Spain's aristocracy. Melodramatic and cautionary, it was a huge bestseller in its day.
20094: Giovanni Berchet's critical and literary writings, the essays of a leading Italian Romantic poet and critic. Best for readers interested in Italian Romanticism and literary debate.
201: A square living in the two-dimensional land of Flatland describes his society and his encounters with a sphere from three-dimensional space. Abbott's satirical novella is witty, mathematical and playful, a classic introduction to higher dimensions.
20121: A science fiction novel by H. Beam Piper and John J. McGuire about Texans who settle on a distant planet. Brisk and good-humoured, it reflects the frontier optimism of 1950s American science fiction.
20211: A selection of the best-loved stories of Selma Lagerlöf, the Swedish writer who won the Nobel Prize, drawing on folklore, legend and the landscapes of Sweden. Warm, imaginative and full of wonder, it suits readers new to her work.
20262: Madame de La Fayette's classic of French psychological fiction, about a young princess at the court of Henri II who is caught between her feelings and her sense of duty. Restrained, elegant and morally intense, it is a foundation of the French novel.
203: Uncle Tom, a kind and devout enslaved man, is sold away from his family, and his story unfolds alongside other enslaved and free characters. Stowe's famous anti-slavery novel is emotional, dramatic and full of moral urgency.
2038: A collection of classic English detective and mystery short stories, offering a varied selection of puzzles and twists. It is a good sampler for readers who enjoy the golden age of the genre.
204: Father Brown, a small and unassuming Catholic priest, uses his keen insight into human nature to solve a series of puzzling crimes. Chesterton's short stories are witty, gentle and full of paradox and moral reflection.
2040: De Quincey's memoir describes his years of addiction to laudanum, with vivid dreams, sharp self-analysis and reflections on the drug. It is lyrical, candid and haunting.
205: Thoreau describes his two years living simply in a small cabin by Walden Pond, reflecting on nature, solitude and self-reliance. Alongside it is his essay urging individuals to follow conscience over unjust laws. The mood is contemplative and inspiring.
2054: Iphigenia, a priestess marooned on a distant shore, faces a moral choice when a stranger arrives and a deception is proposed. Goethe's verse drama is calm, dignified and full of thoughtful speeches.
20546: A detective mystery by Arthur J. Rees with a suspenseful crime at its centre. Brisk and atmospheric, it belongs to English detective fiction of the early twentieth century.
20577: Beaumarchais's comedy in which the clever servant Figaro outwits his master, the Count, on the eve of his own wedding. Witty, fast and sharply satirical, it is a landmark of French comic theatre.
20628: Light humorous stories of two working women in New York, a typist and a secretary, and their adventures in city offices. Brisk and cheerful, they belong to early twentieth-century American popular humour.
20717: A light comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse, full of mischief, romance and the chaos of well-off young people. Witty, playful and delightfully silly, it is classic Wodehouse, with plenty of golf.
20761: Edgar Allan Poe's tales of mystery and horror, translated into French by Baudelaire. Dark, precise and macabre, the stories are a masterclass in the Gothic and the detective tale.
20780: Johanna Spyri's stories for children, and for adults who love children, set in the mountains of Switzerland. Warm, simple and sentimental, they show her gift for tender tales of mountain life.
20782: E. E. Smith's space opera, first serialised in 1934, which spans the Solar System and a struggle against alien threats. Bold, fast and full of grand battles, it is the opening novel of the Lensman saga.
20790: A second collection of Edgar Allan Poe's tales of mystery and horror, translated into French by Baudelaire. Dark and precise, the stories range from the Gothic to the detective tale.
20796: A 1963 science fiction novel by Marion Zimmer Bradley, written in the imaginative style of the period's space fiction. It suits readers who enjoy classic science fiction of the 1960s.
208: Daisy Miller, a lively young American woman travelling in Europe, is watched with disapproval by her compatriots as she flirts with an admirer. James's short novella is subtle and ironic, a study of manners and social judgement.
20864: The second volume of Thackeray's satirical novel of English society, following Becky Sharp and her social climbing. Witty, ironic and full of memorable characters, it is a masterpiece of Victorian fiction.
209: A young governess is hired to care for two orphaned children at a lonely English country house, and she becomes convinced that something is wrong. James's novella is ambiguous and chilling, a masterpiece of psychological suspense.
20944: The second volume of Gerstäcker's popular German emigrant novel, following emigrants on their journey and their new lives in America. Adventurous and folksy, it belongs to nineteenth-century German emigrant literature.
2097: Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson take on a case involving a stolen treasure and a sinister, one-legged figure. Doyle's second Holmes novel is brisk, exotic and full of clever deduction.
21: A collection of short animal fables from ancient Greece, in which foxes, lions, crows and tortoises teach lessons about pride, greed and cleverness. Each tale ends with a moral, making it brief, witty and easy to dip into.
21001: A travel account of Newfoundland, with descriptions of its landscape, its fishing life and its people. Non-fiction, written in the style of late nineteenth-century travel writing.
21021: A German children's novel about the little bee Maja and her friends, who explore the meadow and meet its dangers. Warm, gentle and full of wonder, it became a worldwide bestseller.
21115: A short German work of love, presented as a fragment, about the feelings and hopes of a relationship. Intimate and lyrical, it suits readers interested in early twentieth-century German writing.
21279: A short science fiction story by Kurt Vonnegut, a sharp and bleakly funny look at a future society that has solved the problem of death. Brief and provocative, it is a classic of the genre.
21282: Ricardo Palma's Peruvian Traditions: short, witty historical tales from Peru's colonial and early republican past. Playful, anecdotal and full of local colour, they are a classic of Latin American storytelling.
2130: A traveller who has visited a remote island called Utopia describes its peaceful, communal society to a group of visitors. More's classic is witty, political and full of ideas about how a good society might work.
21300: A collection of cowboy songs and frontier ballads from the American West, gathered by John A. Lomax. Lively and nostalgic, it preserves the songs of range life for readers and singers.
21349: A German critical essay on Goethe's idyll Hermann and Dorothea, examining its themes, style and place in Goethe's work. Scholarly and reflective, it suits readers of German literature.
21415: A comic novel written by a child, following the grand social adventures and love affairs of Mr Salteena. Naive, funny and full of charmingly grand manners, it is a delight for adult readers.
21420: A melodrama by Carolina Invernizio, the popular Italian novelist, about a foundling in Milan. Sentimental and dramatic, it reflects the popular fiction that thrilled Italian readers in the late nineteenth century.
21422: A collection of short stories set in Lombardy, portraying the people and customs of the region. Realistic and local in feel, they suit readers of Italian regional fiction.
21423: A novel by Matilde Serao, the Neapolitan writer, about love, betrayal and social life. Realistic and emotionally intense, it reflects the psychological fiction of late nineteenth-century Italy.
21424: Boccaccio's commentary on Dante's Divine Comedy, with lectures and essays on Dante's life and work. Scholarly and admiring, it shows how Dante was read in the fourteenth century.
21425: A historical novel by Giuseppe Cesare Abba set in 1794 along the Bormida river, during the wars that followed the French Revolution. Patriotic and vivid, it portrays military life and the hopes of its young soldiers.
2148: A collection of Edgar Allan Poe's fantasy and horror stories, with eerie narrators, macabre plots and gothic atmosphere. It is ideal for readers who enjoy shivers and psychological dread.
215: Buck, a strong and loyal dog, is stolen from a comfortable California home and sold into the harsh world of Klondike sled teams. London's short adventure novel is vivid, powerful and full of wild landscapes and the call of nature.
21535: Three novellas by Jakob Wassermann, with historical figures including the Spanish queen Joanna of Castile. Dramatic and psychologically intense, they suit readers of German historical fiction.
21593: Kafka's short story of a young merchant who is drawn into a bitter confrontation with his father. Intense, strange and unsettling, it is one of Kafka's most powerful early works.
2160: A family travels through England and Scotland, and their letters reveal their humorous and often irritable views of the people and places they encounter. Smollett's comic novel is lively and full of eccentric characters.
21638: A pulpy science fiction adventure by Ray Cummings, the kind of fast-moving space story published in early magazines. Bold and simple, it suits readers who like classic adventure science fiction.
21658: A collection of Estonian folk tales, gathered and retold in German by Kreutzwald, who also wrote the national epic Kalevipoeg. Simple, imaginative and rooted in rural tradition, they offer a window onto Estonia's oral storytelling.
2166: Allan Quatermain leads an expedition into unexplored Africa to search for a missing brother, following an ancient map to a legendary treasure. Haggard's adventure is brisk, romantic and full of exotic dangers.
21683: A comedy by Giambattista della Porta about rival brothers and the mix-ups that follow, in the lively style of Renaissance Italian comic theatre. Witty and fast, it suits readers who enjoy stage comedy of the period.
21765: Ovid's epic of transformations, from the creation of the world towards the age of Augustus, in which gods and mortals change into trees, stones and birds. Vivid, witty and endlessly inventive, these first seven books retell some of the best-known myths of antiquity.
21801: Wilhelm von Humboldt's letters to his female friend Charlotte Diede, offering reflections on love, friendship, nature and learning. Intimate and thoughtful, they show the mind of a German Enlightenment scholar at ease with a friend.
21804: The memoir of a Breton adventurer who spent years in the Philippines in the early nineteenth century, recounting his life among the islands and their peoples. Vivid and first-person, it is of interest both as adventure and as a historical account.
21831: Galdós's novel about Benina, a faithful former servant who begs in the streets of Madrid to support the poor household she serves. Tender, funny and deeply humane, it portrays urban poverty, charity and loyalty.
2188: A young poet in Paris records his lonely impressions of the city, its poverty and its memories in fragmentary notebook entries. Rilke's novel is introspective, lyrical and intense.
219: The sailor Marlow recounts his journey up an African river as a steamboat captain for a Belgian trading company, where he encounters the enigmatic ivory trader Kurtz. Conrad's novella is dark, atmospheric and deeply critical of colonialism.
21989: Kafka's collection of short prose pieces, including the strange title story about a country doctor called out on a snowy night. Dreamlike, precise and unsettling, the stories are a good introduction to his German prose.
22020: A psychological novel by Neera, one of the leading women novelists of late nineteenth-century Italy, centred on the inner life of its heroine. Subtle and introspective, it suits readers of Italian realism.
22024: An Italian novel by Anton Giulio Barrili, set in the everyday social world of its time. Realistic and readable, it suits readers of nineteenth-century Italian fiction.
22026: A mystery novel set in the port city of Livorno, with political agitation and hidden secrets. Melodramatic and lurid, it reflects the popular Italian serial fiction of the nineteenth century.
22049: J. J. Jusserand's history of English literature from its origins to the Renaissance, written by a French scholar. Scholarly yet accessible, it traces the making of English literature through its early poets, chroniclers and ballads.
22065: A graded reader in Spanish for learners, with short passages and exercises that build vocabulary and reading ability. Practical and clear, it suits students at an early stage.
22091: An annual anthology of the best American short stories of 1920, selected by the editor Edward O'Brien. A varied collection of realist and experimental tales, it offers a snapshot of American fiction of the period.
22113: A girls' school story set around the United States Naval Academy, following a young woman's education and friendships. Wholesome and old-fashioned, it suits readers of early twentieth-century juvenile fiction.
22123: Raabe's novella of a middle-class friendship between two men that begins to break apart, set in a German town of the nineteenth century. Quiet, ironic and psychologically observant, it belongs to his Krähenfeld tales.
22159: Ibsen's social drama of a widow who confronts the secrets of her husband's past and the illness that threatens her son. Intense and unflinching, it attacked the hypocrisy of respectable society.
22160: A German textbook of composition and conversation exercises for learners, with short texts on everyday topics. Practical and educational, it is written for students of German.
22163: A juvenile adventure story in the Rover Boys series, following the brothers through their last days at a military school and their life on a farm. Wholesome and fast-paced, it is classic early twentieth-century boys' fiction.
22188: Terence's six Latin comedies in a literal English prose translation with notes. Witty and worldly, they portray young lovers, scheming slaves and stern fathers in Roman city life.
22209: A German retelling of the Siegfried legend, the hero who slays a dragon and wins a great treasure, in the style of a popular novel of heroic myth. Adventurous and grand, it suits readers of German folklore.
22235: Strindberg's naturalist tragedy set on a Midsummer Eve in a Swedish count's kitchen, where the count's daughter is drawn into a charged relationship with a servant. Tense, psychological and claustrophobic, it is a landmark of modern theatre.
2228: A comic animal epic in which the cunning fox Reineke outwits the other beasts of the kingdom, mocking courtly life and human vanity. Goethe's verse satire is witty, lively and full of sly humour.
2229: The learned scholar Faust makes a bargain with Mephistopheles, and his pursuit of knowledge and pleasure leads him into love and tragedy. Goethe's great verse drama is philosophical, poetic and deeply human.
22298: A practical handbook for boys, explaining the tools and simple mechanical projects that let young readers build and mend things. Hands-on and instructive, it reflects early twentieth-century ideas of self-reliance.
223: Father Brown, the modest Catholic priest, returns in more stories where he uses his shrewd understanding of people to solve puzzling crimes. Chesterton's collection is witty, humane and full of clever reasoning.
