345: Young English solicitor Jonathan Harker travels to a remote Transylvanian castle, where his mysterious host Count Dracula reveals a sinister secret. Stoker's Gothic horror is told through letters and diaries, and it builds tension steadily.
34717: Robert Musil's first novel, about a sensitive boy at a strict military boarding school in Austria who becomes entangled in cruelty and bullying. Psychological, tense and disturbing, it is a key early modernist work.
34735: A futurist African drama by F. T. Marinetti, built on heat, colour, noise and smell and meant to overwhelm the senses. Experimental, loud and dramatic, it is an important text of Italian futurist theatre.
34782: A German novel by Max Brod about the fate of a Jewish man in early twentieth-century German-speaking Europe. Serious and socially observant, it deals with Jewish life, identity and assimilation.
348: A collection of early Greek epic poems, including Hesiod's Theogony and Works and Days, the Homeric Hymns and other fragments. These poems describe the gods, the origins of the world and everyday rural life, in a solemn and lyrical voice.
34811: Thomas Mann's first great novel, chronicling the decline of a wealthy merchant family in a north German city over four generations. Richly detailed, ironic and melancholy, it portrays the manners and social world of the Hanseatic middle class.
34983: An Italian novel by Annie Vivanti, a writer of the early twentieth century, exploring the strained relationship between mothers and daughters. Emotional and introspective, it considers women's lives and desires.
35: A Victorian inventor builds a machine that carries him far into the future, to a world divided between gentle surface dwellers and dangerous underground beings. H. G. Wells's novella is a thought-provoking, eerie early science fiction classic.
35048: An Italian drama in four acts by Roberto Bracco, a playwright of the early twentieth century. Its title, The Madmen, promises an intense psychological stage work about the fragility of the mind.
35065: An Italian novel by Antonio Caccianiga, a nineteenth-century writer of romance and society fiction. Its title, The Kiss of Countess Savina, hints at romance and intrigue among the aristocracy.
35103: A science fiction novel by the French artist and writer Albert Robida, which imagines life in France in 1955. Its electric city, inventions and scientific wonders are presented with playful satire and vivid illustrations.
35181: A German version of Cervantes's novella La gitanilla, about a young Romani girl in Spain who sings and tells fortunes, and the romance that surrounds her. Lively, colourful and told with Cervantes's wit.
35264: Heinrich Mann's satirical novel about Professor Unrat, a strict and tyrannical schoolteacher in a provincial German town, whose rigid world is upset when he becomes entangled with a cabaret singer. Biting and dramatic, it became the basis of the film The Blue Angel.
35312: A short novella by Joseph von Eichendorff about a young wanderer who sets out into the world, full of songs, nature and chance encounters. Light, romantic and musical, it is a high point of German late Romanticism.
35321: An Italian historical novel by Giuseppe Tigri in the nineteenth-century manner, named after its heroine, Selvaggia de' Vergiolesi. Romantic and sentimental in tone.
35328: A novel by Thomas Mann about a German prince and his struggles with duty, love and the formal life of a small princely court. Witty, ironic and sometimes fairy-tale-like, it examines royalty against personal freedom.
35339: A German volume of Dostoyevsky's early novels, Poor Folk and The Double. Poor Folk is a tender story told in letters between a poor clerk and a young woman, while The Double is a psychological tale of a man confronted by his own double. Intense and psychologically sharp.
35404: A children's novel by the Comtesse de Segur, the second part of a trilogy about Sophie de Rean. Its model girls are lively and well-meaning, and the book gives a moral, gently humorous picture of childhood in nineteenth-century France.
35435: A collection of short stories by the German writer Gottfried Benn, who was also a physician. Stark, modernist and unsettling, these stories are fascinated by the mind and the body.
35451: Euripides's ancient Greek tragedy about Medea, a foreign woman abandoned by her husband Jason in Corinth. Her fury at this betrayal drives a passionate and harrowing drama, one of the most powerful plays of antiquity.
35548: A Victorian romance by Rhoda Broughton, a popular writer of romantic fiction, about love, marriage and social manners in England. Witty, lively and typical of its period.
35549: Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic study of Wilhelm Jensen's novella Gradiva, reading the hero's dreams and delusions as a case study in the mind. Analytic and literary, it is a key text for readers of psychoanalysis and literature.
35569: A satirical novel of the near future by Hugo Bettauer, set in an Austrian city that expels all its Jewish residents. Written in the 1920s, it is a dark, alarmed warning about antisemitism and demagoguery, later adapted into a silent film.
35605: A collection of short stories by Karl Heinrich Ulrichs, the nineteenth-century writer and early campaigner for gay rights, with a vampire theme among its tales. Unusual and provocative for its time, it deals with desire and hidden identity.
35635: A collection of aphorisms and witty sayings by Alexander Engel about men, women and their relationships. Short, pointed and humorous, the maxims are easy to dip into.
35660: An Italian novel by Anton Giulio Barrili, with the subtitle Colombian novel. Its title, Virgin Land, suggests a story of exploration and the New World.
35794: A German reader for beginners, offering simple fairy tales and stories in easy German for learners. Short, familiar and warm, the texts are built for practice.
35797: A German textbook of composition and conversation by Sigmon and Menco Stern, with stories and exercises about German life. A practical study aid for students of German.
35800: A one-act Italian drama by Salvatore Di Giacomo, the Neapolitan writer known for vivid scenes of life in Naples. Short, emotional and rooted in the city's streets.
35801: A Neapolitan popular drama in three acts by Salvatore Di Giacomo, in which a vow and the everyday life of the city's people take centre stage. Vivid and emotional, it was later filmed as Miracolo a Piedigrotta.
35802: A collection of Portuguese folk songs and ballads in Italian translation. Simple, lyrical and emotional, the songs express love, longing and everyday life.
35804: A Sicilian-dialect play, Cappiddazzu Pays for Everything, by Nino Martoglio and Luigi Pirandello from the early twentieth century. A comic and social look at Sicilian life, in the earthy dialect theatre of the island.
35825: A collection of satirical and humorous articles by Hector Berlioz about music, musicians and concert life, first written for newspapers. Witty, sharp and full of anecdotes, the book pokes fun at composers and performers.
35969: A French selection of tales from The Thousand and One Nights, in which Scheherazade keeps her life by telling stories each night. Enchanting, varied and full of djinns, merchants and magic.
35999: A German novel about the fate of a German-American woman, told in the sentimental manner of its period. It suits readers who enjoy emotional stories of emigration and family life.
36: Martians invade southern England with towering war machines and deadly heat rays, and the narrator tries to survive and find his family. H. G. Wells's classic invasion novel is tense, vivid and unsettling, with a sharp view of human arrogance.
3600: Montaigne's personal essays explore his thoughts on everything from death and friendship to cannibals and cruelty. They are wise, digressive and full of human warmth.
36011: The third volume of Pierre Corneille's collected plays, the tragedies and dramatic works of the French classical stage. Heroic, verse-based drama on honour, love and power.
36034: A collection of Dostoyevsky's shorter fiction, including White Nights, the tale of a lonely dreamer in St Petersburg who falls in love over a few summer nights. Tender, melancholy and psychologically intense.
36164: A long, rambling German novel by Jean Paul, translated into English, full of comic digressions and philosophical musings on marriage, death and the imagination. Playful and eccentric, it suits readers of Romantic experimental fiction.
36165: Short stories by Giuseppe Giacosa set in the Aosta Valley of northern Italy, portraying mountain villages and their people. Quiet, scenic and humane, the tales are rooted in the landscape.
36172: Robert Walser's first novel, written quickly in 1906 in Berlin, about a family of siblings and their different paths in life. Wry, playful and gently ironic, it has the observant lightness of Walser's prose.
36223: A romantic novel by Berta Ruck, a popular British writer of love stories, set in England during the First World War. Sentimental and emotional, it deals with love and loss at home during the war.
36227: A short German allegorical story by Hans von Kahlenberg, built around a mysterious stranger who arrives among ordinary people. Reflective and symbolic, it suits readers of parable-like fiction.
3623: James Frazer's wide-ranging study compares magic, religion and myth across the world, from ancient rites to folk custom. It is scholarly, sweeping and full of fascinating anthropological detail.
36253: The third volume of Adolf Friedrich von Schack's history of Spanish drama and theatre, a scholarly work for readers of Spanish literary history.
36275: A short German novella by Wilhelm Jensen set in Pompeii, about an archaeologist obsessed with a Roman relief of a woman walking. Dreamlike and romantic, it blends archaeology, desire and the power of the past.
36326: An Italian novel by Guido da Verona, a popular early twentieth-century writer known for sensual society fiction. Its provocative title, Unbraid Your Hair, Mary Magdalene, signals a bold and sensual story.
36349: A collection of fantastic and supernatural tales by Ivan Turgenev, in German translation. Dreamlike and eerie, the stories explore visions and mysterious encounters, with a quietly ironic tone.
36379: A short Italian tale by Antonio Caccianiga, set in a family circle of the nineteenth century. It suits readers of quiet domestic fiction from that period.
36453: A historical adventure novel by Arthur Conan Doyle, set in fourteenth-century England and France during the Hundred Years' War. It follows a band of archers and knights through battle, chivalry and adventure.
36462: A children's retelling of the Arthurian legends by Roger Lancelyn Green, drawing mainly on Malory. King Arthur, Camelot, Merlin, Lancelot and the quest for the Holy Grail are told in a clear, lively style for young readers.
36488: Jewish folk stories and tales by the Yiddish writer I. L. Peretz, in German translation. Warm, humorous and poignant, they portray the life and faith of Eastern European Jewish communities.
36528: A controversial novel by the French symbolist writer Rachilde, first published in 1884. It explores gender, desire and social class in a provocative, erotic story that caused a public scandal. Strictly for adult readers.
36546: An adventure novel by Emilio Salgari, set among the seas and islands of Oceania. A tale of fishermen, danger and exotic places, in Salgari's swashbuckling style.
36558: A children's tale by Luis Coloma about Raton Perez, the little mouse of Spanish folklore who collects children's lost milk teeth. Gentle, whimsical and affectionate, it is a classic for young readers.
36635: A French novel by Hermine Lecomte du Nouy, whose title, Loving Friendship, points to an intimate bond between two people. Told in the sentimental style of nineteenth-century French fiction, it suits readers who enjoy emotional stories.
36725: A romance by Wilhelmine von Hillern set around the Oberammergau Passion Play in Bavaria, which the village performs every ten years. Melodramatic and devout, it blends a love story with the drama of the Passion.
36766: A story collection by Thomas Mann, whose title tale is about a small, lonely man, Herr Friedemann, and his isolation from the world. Melancholy, ironic and psychologically precise, it shows Mann's early style.
36780: Alphonse Daudet's classic collection of tales and sketches, set in Provence near a windmill. Charming, sunny and sometimes wistful, the stories portray village life and its characters.
36805: A graded reader of short Spanish tales for beginners, with simple language and notes. Easy, varied stories built for learners, useful for growing reading confidence.
36826: Beaumarchais's comic play about Figaro, the barber and go-between, who helps Count Almaviva win the hand of Rosine from her guardian. Quick, witty and scheming, it is the first part of his Figaro trilogy and the basis of Rossini's opera.
36901: A fantastic novel by Leo Perutz, first published in 1918 and set in Vienna. It turns on questions of identity and a strange, dreamlike mystery, blending the uncanny with city life.
36905: A novella by Theodor Fontane set in Berlin during the Napoleonic era, about a young officer's engagement and a crisis of honour. Restrained, psychologically subtle and ironic, it is a classic of German realism.
36940: A Spanish novel by Armando Palacio Valdes, a realist work of the late nineteenth century about a young gentleman in Spanish society. It shows the author's close eye for character and manners.
36965: A short biography of Harriet Martineau, the nineteenth-century English writer and social thinker, by Florence Fenwick Miller. It covers Martineau's life, writing and campaigns for social reform.
36990: Hawthorne's classic novel about Hester Prynne, a woman in seventeenth-century New England publicly shamed for adultery and forced to wear a scarlet letter. A dark, moral and psychological study of guilt, sin and society.
36997: Ibsen's 1886 play about Johannes Rosmer, a former clergyman living at a Norwegian manor, haunted by a tragic past and by his ideals for social reform. Psychological and tense, it explores guilt, idealism and the pressures of a small community.
37054: A collection of humorous sketches and short stories by the Italian writer and journalist Luigi Arnaldo Vassallo. Light, witty and observant, the pieces are full of the small follies and characters of Italian society.
37067: The fourth volume of Adolf Friedrich von Schack's history of Spanish drama and theatre, a scholarly work for readers of Spanish literature and the stage.
3707: O. Henry's stories follow working New Yorkers through humour and romance, with sharp characters and a sudden twist. The collection is warm, witty and full of city life.
37096: A scholarly bibliography of Pierre Corneille's works by Emile Picot, describing every edition of the French playwright's plays and writings in detail. Of interest chiefly to specialists in French literature and book history.
37106: Louisa May Alcott's beloved novel about four sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy March, growing up with their mother during and after the American Civil War. Warm, funny and bittersweet, it follows their passage from childhood to womanhood.
37123: A collection of short stories by Gabriele D'Annunzio, set in his native Abruzzo and part of a cycle of tales of that region. Sensual, lyrical and rooted in rural life, the stories show the young writer's early style.
37128: A collection of small prose pieces by Robert Walser, slight sketches and fragments with a dreamy, playful tone. Each brief text is a little world of observation, wit and gentle melancholy.
37139: A Spanish novel by Vicente Blasco Ibanez, whose title, The Enemies of Women, suggests a dramatic study of men, women and social attitudes of its time.
37266: Ten dialogues by Arthur Schnitzler, linked in a chain of encounters between characters in Vienna, each passing on to the next. Witty, frank and sharply observed, this cycle portrays love and desire across the social classes of fin-de-siecle Vienna.
37382: A one-act comedy by the French writer Pierre Veber, here in Spanish. Short and light, it is a stage piece built on wit and social comedy.
37484: An issue of The Strand Magazine from April 1904, the popular British illustrated monthly of short stories, articles and pictures in the Edwardian age. A window onto the reading of its time.
37491: Diderot's first novel, a bawdy libertine satire published anonymously in 1748. A magic ring makes women's private parts speak, and the device is used to mock King Louis XV and his court. Explicit and playful, for adult readers.
375: A Confederate sympathiser is condemned to hang from a bridge during the American Civil War, and his final moments unfold in a dreamlike sequence. Bierce's short story is haunting and tightly crafted, a classic of suspense and surprise.
37579: A collection of essays and short prose by Robert Walser, witty and digressive pieces on everyday things, writers and small events. Light, sharp and playfully observant.
37819: Essays on Italian literature by Adolfo Albertazzi, with a study of a countess among its subjects. Written for readers of Italian literary history.
37849: A stage drama by Gabriele D'Annunzio, the poet and playwright whose work is marked by intense passion and lyrical language. Its title, Iron, points to a hard, unyielding theme.
37931: A one-act Italian drama by Roberto Bracco, the Neapolitan playwright of the early twentieth century. Its title, A Travel Adventure, suggests a light, incident-driven stage piece.
37932: An Italian play by Roberto Bracco, whose title, The Disillusioned Women, points to a serious drama about disappointment in love and in society.
37933: An Italian play by Roberto Bracco, whose title, He, She, He, suggests a tangle of relationships on the stage. Realist and psychological, in the playwright's typical manner.
37934: An Italian play by Roberto Bracco, whose title echoes the old proverb about treating others as you would be treated. A drama of social morality in the playwright's realist style.
37935: A short Italian play by Roberto Bracco, titled A Woman, which focuses on the situation and inner life of its central female character. Serious and psychological, in the playwright's realist manner.
37940: A collection of folk tales and legends of Rubezahl, the mountain spirit of the Riesengebirge in Silesia. Playful and sometimes mischievous, the stories of this shape-shifting giant are part of German folklore.
37989: A series of fictional letters by George Sand, written from the point of view of a male traveller, with frequently autobiographical musings on love, art and travel. Reflective, lively and intimate.
38049: A biography of Louisa May Alcott, the author of Little Women, drawn from her own letters and journals. It shows the life of the New England writer, her family and her literary career, in an intimate and reflective way.
38082: A historical novel by the Italian writer Anton Giulio Barrili. Its title, The Black Book, hints at secret records and political scheming.
38126: Heinrich Mann's satirical novel about Diederich Hessling, an ambitious and servile man in imperial Germany who worships authority and power. Biting and funny, it is a classic satire of German nationalism and the subservient mentality.
38177: A light romantic novel by Compton Mackenzie, set in eighteenth-century England at a fashionable health resort. Witty and full of period high spirits, it is built around a romantic elopement.
38216: An Italian play by Roberto Bracco, whose title, Orange Blossoms, evokes weddings and romance. A drama of marriage and love in the playwright's realist style.
38217: An Italian play by Roberto Bracco, named after its central character, Don Pietro Caruso. A realist drama of character and social life.
38218: An Italian play by Roberto Bracco, whose title, The End of Love, points to a serious drama about the fading of passion and the strains on a relationship.
38239: A medieval German romance of Magelone and her knight Peter of Provence, a love story full of adventure, sea voyages and chivalry. Charming, lively and full of courtly romance.
3825: Professor Higgins bets he can transform a flower-seller from the London streets into a lady, and the wager raises questions about class and identity. Shaw's comedy is witty, sharp and full of wordplay.
38259: A novel by Annie Vivanti, published in 1917. Its title, Vae Victis (woe to the conquered), suggests a story of defeat, suffering and survival, told in an emotional and dramatic style.
38281: A three-act play by Andre Gide, based on the ancient story of King Candaules of Lydia. Psychological, sensual and tense, it treats power and desire at the royal court.
38298: An Italian historical novel by Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi about Isabella Orsini, a Renaissance noblewoman in the Medici world of Florence. Dramatic and passionate, it portrays court intrigue.
38311: A novel by the American writer Rupert Hughes about love, reputation and social expectations among New York society. Light and romantic, it shows how public opinion shapes private choices.
38336: The Grand Inquisitor is a chapter from Dostoyevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, in which Ivan tells a story of Christ returning to Seville in the age of the Spanish Inquisition. A philosophical, intense dialogue on faith, freedom and power.
38338: A collection of short stories by Adolfo Albertazzi, an Italian writer of the early twentieth century. Brief and observant, the tales suit readers of short Italian fiction.
38360: A short Italian tale by Anton Giulio Barrili, whose title, The Bridge of Paradise, suggests a romantic or spiritual setting. A late nineteenth-century work of Italian fiction.
38385: A charming book by the French writer Alphonse Karr about his garden, from flowers and vegetables to the small everyday pleasures of cultivation. Gently witty, personal and calm, it is a classic for garden lovers.
38402: A collection of short stories by Rainer Maria Rilke about God, angels and ordinary people, told as simple, fairy-tale-like parables. Tender, lyrical and devout in tone.
38547: Two Italian novellas by Stendhal, featuring Roman women in Italian settings. Romantic, passionate and psychologically sharp, they show Stendhal's interest in love and Italian society.
38578: A critical study by Vittorio Imbriani of literary fame and of false reputations among writers, with a section on Goethe's Faust. Polemical and witty, it suits readers of nineteenth-century Italian criticism.
38628: A collection of old love stories by the Italian writer Adolfo Albertazzi, short tales of romance written in the early twentieth century. Gentle, nostalgic and sentimental.
38637: A collection of short stories by Adolfo Albertazzi, whose title, The Devil in the Bottle, suggests fantasy and the uncanny. Brief, playful tales of Italian life.
38674: Jules Verne's science fiction classic about a club of American artillery enthusiasts who build a giant cannon to fire a capsule with three men towards the Moon. Witty, ambitious and full of scientific speculation, it is a foundational space adventure.
38686: A collection of early novellas by Stefan Zweig, the title story being about the love of a young woman, Erika Ewald. Lyrical, emotional and finely observed, these early works show Zweig's gift for the inner life.
38698: Essays of polemic and criticism on Italian literature, by the writer known as Jolanda. Pointed and combative, the pieces reflect the literary debates of their era.
38705: Daniel Defoe's classic adventure of a sailor shipwrecked on a remote island, who survives for many years by his own resourcefulness. A foundational adventure novel, full of practical detail and self-reliance. This French edition is the first part of two.
38720: An Italian novel by Guido da Verona, a popular early twentieth-century writer of sensual romance. Its title, Love That Returns, promises a story of passion and second chances.
38780: E. T. A. Hoffmann's satirical novel about Murr, a witty and self-important tomcat who writes his memoirs on the back of pages from the biography of the composer Kreisler. Playful, ironic and full of Romantic wit, it is an unusual experiment in fiction.
38814: A novel by Armando Palacio Valdes about a writer, following the literary life and the world of creating fiction. Reflective and urbane, it shows the author's realist eye.
389: A scientist's strange experiment to reveal a hidden world has terrible consequences that ripple through the years, unsettling those who learn the secret. Machen's novella is an eerie, decadent horror story with occult overtones.
38972: A German collection of Inuit folk tales from the Arctic, passing on stories of animals, spirits and northern life. Simple, vivid and full of the wonder of folklore.
38983: A juvenile mystery story by Hildegard G. Frey, in which a group of Camp Fire Girls investigate a puzzle during the Christmas holidays at an old house. Friendly, wholesome and gently suspenseful, it suits young readers.
39101: George Sand's autobiography, written between 1847 and 1854, recounting half a century of her life from childhood through to her career as a writer and her many loves. Candid, reflective and lively.
3913: Rousseau's frank autobiography recounts his youth and early adult life, with candid confessions and sharp reflections on his character. It is intimate, reflective and provocative.
39247: A short prose work by Robert Walser, a walk narrated with his characteristic lightness, wit and eye for small things. Relaxed, gently humorous and reflective, it reads like a stroll in the company of an intelligent companion.
39289: A collection of short stories by Federico De Roberto, the Sicilian writer known for realist and psychological fiction. Its title, Loves, brings together tales of passion in the author's clear, unsentimental style.
393: Two children are shipwrecked on a tropical island, where they grow up together in innocence and love. Stacpoole's romance is idyllic and adventurous, a coming-of-age story about nature and youthful innocence.
39337: An Italian novel by Guido da Verona, a popular writer of his time. Its title, Life Begins Tomorrow, suggests an optimistic story about new beginnings in the style of early twentieth-century popular fiction.
39389: A novel by the Italian writer Alfredo Panzini, whose title, The World Is Round, suggests a light, travelling and humorous story of Italian life. Panzini wrote with an ironic affection for ordinary people.
394: The genteel, gossipy ladies of a small English country town are portrayed with gentle humour and affection. Gaskell's episodic novel is warm, witty and nostalgic, full of small domestic events and quiet charm.
39444: A selection of pages from the work of the Spanish writer Armando Palacio Valdes, offering a sampler of his realist novels and sketches. Good for readers new to his style.
39506: A humorous Italian novel by Alfredo Panzini about a man looking for a wife, a comic story about marriage, wealth and social pretension in Italy. Light, funny and satirical in spirit.
39541: A collection of short stories by Matilde Serao, the Neapolitan writer known for portraying the life and passions of Naples and its people. Emotional and vivid, the stories reflect her sharp eye for women's lives.
39613: A novel by Armando Palacio Valdes, whose title, The Papers of Doctor Angelico, suggests a story told through documents and the life of a physician. Realist and reflective.
39619: A German family novel by Suze La Chapelle-Roobol. Its title, Trotzkopf as a Grandmother, links it to the popular Trotzkopf series of girls' stories, with a grandmother at its centre.
39658: A collection of short stories by Cesare Balbo, the Piedmontese writer and statesman of the Italian Risorgimento. Earnest, historical and moral in the manner of nineteenth-century Italian fiction.
39667: A 1922 study by the German statistician and political writer Emil Julius Gumbel, documenting political murders in Germany between 1918 and 1922. Factual, angry and carefully argued, it is an important record of the violence of the early Weimar years.
39738: A philosophical and lyrical novel by George Sand, whose heroine Lelia is a woman worn down by life and troubled by doubt. Dark, passionate and symbolic, it is one of Sand's bold early novels on women's freedom.
39774: A French war idyll by Paul Gsell, a drama of the First World War in which children and civilians live among ruins. Sentimental and moving, it reflects the suffering of ordinary people in wartime France.
398: A retelling of the story of Adam and Eve, drawing on apocryphal Old Testament traditions about their lives after leaving Eden. The book is reflective and imaginative, appealing to readers interested in biblical legend.
39902: A three-act Italian comedy by Marco Praga, first staged in Turin in 1890 with the company of the great actress Eleonora Duse. A light social comedy about marriage and family life.
39976: Diderot's playful, digressive novel about Jacques the fatalist and his master, who travel and tell each other stories. Witty and philosophical, it plays with fate, free will and the art of storytelling itself.
39988: A scholarly study by Angelo De Gubernatis comparing wedding customs and marriage rites in Italy and among other Indo-European peoples. Erudite, detailed and anthropological, it suits readers of folklore and comparative history.
40052: A series of satirical essays by Alphonse Karr, first published as a periodical called The Wasps. Witty and pointed, the pieces mock the follies of Parisian society and politics.
40059: A romantic adventure novel by Cynthia Stockley, a popular early twentieth-century writer of romance and exotic settings. Its title, The Dream Ship, suggests a voyage of longing and wonder.
40086: The first volume of Moliere's complete works, the comic masterpieces of the great French playwright of the seventeenth century. Sharp and sparkling comedies about hypocrisy, vanity and society, they remain staples of world theatre.
4018: A collection of Japanese folk tales, retold for English readers with charm and gentle wonder. The stories feature magical animals, clever commoners and everyday enchantment.
40284: A science fiction novel by M. E. Knerr about alien beings and the gods. Its provocative title promises a short, irreverent and pulpy tone.
40326: An Italian translation by Elia Morpurgo of Naphtali Herz Wessely's Hebrew discourses on tolerance and happiness, written in support of Emperor Joseph II's reforms for Jewish people. Historical and political, it is a document of the Jewish Enlightenment.
40361: A science fiction adventure by Guy Thorne about pirates who take to the skies in airships over England. Fast, inventive and pulpy, it imagines aerial piracy and the new technology of flight.
40377: A three-act Italian comedy by Roberto Bracco, whose title, Unfaithful, points to a drama of marital betrayal and social manners.
40378: A four-act Italian drama by Roberto Bracco, whose title, The Triumph, suggests a play about ambition, success and the cost of winning. Serious and psychological, in the playwright's realist style.
40496: The satirical roman a clef of Bussy-Rabutin, a gossipy account of love affairs at the court of Louis XIV, first published in 1665. Witty, racy and pointed, it caused a scandal in its day.
40564: A dramatic poem by Stefan Zweig in nine scenes, about the Hebrew prophet Jeremiah, who warns of the fall of Jerusalem and is rejected by his people. Solemn, poetic and sombre, it reflects on conscience and prophecy.
40580: A famous early history of pirates, published in two volumes in 1724 under the name Captain Charles Johnson. It collects lively biographies of real and legendary sea robbers, and shaped the popular image of pirates for centuries.
40595: A humorous Spanish cookbook by Juan Perez Zuniga, with recipes for stews and desserts alongside culinary poems and comic writing. Light, witty and full of playful excess.
40827: A volume of the best short novels and tales by Spanish writers, gathered as an anthology with contributions by Pio Baroja and Jacinto Benavente. A varied sampler of early twentieth-century Spanish fiction.
4085: Roderick Random, a young Scottish orphan, is cheated and bullied as he makes his way through the British navy and society. Smollett's picaresque novel is rowdy, satirical and full of colourful rogues.
40917: A collection of short stories by Ercole Luigi Morselli, whose title, Stories to Laugh and Weep At, promises a mix of comedy and pathos. Vivid, emotional and varied, the tales show the Italian writer's gift for mood.
4093: Hedda Gabler, a restless and proud woman, feels trapped by her marriage and the stifling respectability of her life in Christiania. Ibsen's play is tense, psychological and full of sharp social observation.
41: A schoolmaster named Ichabod Crane courts a wealthy farmer's daughter in a Dutch-settled Hudson Valley village, where local ghost stories feed his fears. Irving's tale is atmospheric, witty and spooky, perfect for a moody autumn read.
41006: A classic survey of fairy belief and folklore from many countries, gathered by Thomas Keightley in the nineteenth century. Full of tales of fairies, elves and spirits, it is a rich source for readers of folklore.
41051: Hermann Hesse's first novel, about a young man from a Swiss mountain village who seeks meaning through art, nature and wandering. Lyrical, introspective and romantic, it explores the search for identity amid nature and modern life.
41087: The second volume of Hippolyte Taine's history of English literature, a critical study of English writers interpreted through race, environment and historical moment. Scholarly and vivid, for readers of literary history.
41106: The second volume of an anthology of the best Spanish short novels and tales, with contributions by the Alvarez Quintero brothers, popular playwrights of Andalusian life. Charming, varied and rooted in Spanish popular culture.
41112: The fourth volume of Hippolyte Taine's history of English literature, a critical study of English writers, bold in its interpretations and written for readers of literary history.
41113: A French novel by Paul Feval about an actress who becomes entangled with the French nobility. Romantic and dramatic, it is full of intrigue and melodrama.
41114: The final volume of Hippolyte Taine's history of English literature, covering later English writers in his distinctive critical manner. Scholarly and vivid, for readers of literary history.
41157: Marinetti's political manifesto for a futurist democracy, setting out the programme of the Futurist party he founded in 1918. Bold, polemical and energetic, it is an important text in the history of Italian Futurism and politics.
41161: A collection of short novels by Giovanni Verga, in Spanish, depicting peasant and rural life in Sicily and across Italy. Realist, austere and deeply human, the stories show the harsh world of the countryside.
41211: The first volume of Balzac's great cycle of novels portraying French society in the nineteenth century, from Paris to the provinces. Richly detailed and sweeping, it is a panorama of ambition, money and class.
41232: A collection of short stories by Anzia Yezierska about Jewish immigrant women on New York's Lower East Side and their struggles with poverty, love and assimilation. Vivid, poignant and sharply observed.
41257: A study by the Italian writer Alfredo Panzini of the poet Giosue Carducci and how his work changed over time. Clear and scholarly, it suits readers of Italian poetry.
41342: A collection of short stories by Alfredo Panzini, whose title, Little Stories of the Big World, promises brief and humorous glimpses of life. Gentle and observant, the pieces show his affectionate, ironic style.
41382: A German historical novel by Georg Engel about Klaus Stortebeker, the legendary sea pirate of the late medieval North Sea and Baltic. Adventurous and heroic, it retells a famous seafaring legend.
41473: An Italian novel by Matilde Serao from the late nineteenth century, about the life and adventures of its central character in Naples. Vivid, realistic and full of Neapolitan local colour.
41481: An issue of Astounding Stories of Super-Science, an American pulp science fiction magazine from January 1930. It contains short stories of adventure, invention and imagined futures from the early days of the genre.
41486: Jules Michelet's study of witchcraft in medieval Europe, which treats the witch as a figure of popular rebellion and folk belief. Passionate, poetic and controversial, it is a classic and provocative work of history.
41575: Early writings and light prose by the Argentine writer Miguel Cane, showing his youthful wit and his sketches of Argentine social life. Charming and lively, the pieces offer an insight into late nineteenth-century Buenos Aires.
41746: A novel by Vicente Blasco Ibanez, set in the Valencia region of Spain and written in his vivid, dramatic realist style. Its title, May Flower, suggests a bright story of passion and rural life, and it was later adapted into a 1959 Mexican film.
41769: A simple introduction to Pierre Corneille's plays, written for young readers by the French critic Emile Faguet. It explains the great dramatist's tragedies in clear, accessible language.
41785: A speculative study by Harold Bayley of England's prehistoric stone monuments, reading megaliths and earthworks as the remains of a lost ancient language of symbols. Idiosyncratic and learned, it suits readers curious about archaeology and old mysteries.
41818: A short, autobiographical work by Hermann Hesse, presented as the papers of a young writer, with sketches, reflections and memories. Introspective and lyrical, it shows the sensitive self-searching of Hesse's early years.
42065: The official record of the 1896 trial of the Filipino nationalist writer Jose Rizal, who was tried for sedition in Manila. A dry, factual historical document, it shows the case that became a national symbol.
421: The young David Balfour is kidnapped and taken to sea, and then escapes into the Scottish Highlands with a Jacobite rebel. Stevenson's adventure is lively, witty and full of chases and rugged landscapes.
4217: Stephen Dedalus grows up in Dublin, wrestling with religion, desire and the pull of art. Joyce's semi-autobiographical novel is intimate, lyrical and a classic of modernist fiction.
42188: A short Conan the Barbarian story by Robert E. Howard, a fast, action-packed sword and sorcery tale of the imagined Hyborian Age. Violent and atmospheric, it sends Conan into a night of danger and mystery.
42196: A Conan story by Robert E. Howard set in the desert city of Zamboula and taking place over the course of a single night. Dark, violent and fast-paced, it is classic pulp sword and sorcery.
42213: A short biographical essay by Hermann Hesse on the fourteenth-century Italian writer Giovanni Boccaccio, author of The Decameron. Warm, literary and appreciative, it suits readers interested in Boccaccio and Italian literature.
42237: A collection of short stories by Matilde Serao, the Italian writer known for portraying Neapolitan life. The tales are emotional and vivid, focused on the inner lives of women and ordinary people.
42243: A Conan novel by Robert E. Howard, also published as Conan the Conqueror. Conan faces sorcery, warfare and intrigue in a fast-paced sword and sorcery epic of power and fate.
42253: A drama by the Italian playwright Camillo Antona-Traversi, whose title, Dance of Death, suggests a dark, fatalistic stage work with a sombre mood.
42256: Joseph Bedier's retelling of the medieval legend of Tristan and Iseult, the doomed lovers of Arthurian romance. Lyrical and tragic, it is one of the most celebrated versions of this story of passion and fate.
42259: A Conan novella by Robert E. Howard, in which the sword and sorcery hero battles a sinister secret cult in an exotic eastern land. Brutal, fast and full of pulp adventure.
42271: A novel of the First World War by Alfredo Panzini, set in wartime Italy. It portrays the lives and emotions of ordinary people during the conflict, with an ironic and humane tone.
42316: An Italian novel by Matilde Serao, first published in 1885, about the political and social life of Rome in the late nineteenth century, with its ambitions and love affairs. Vivid and realistic, it looks at politics and manners in the Italian capital.
42338: A short novella by Hermann Hesse, written in 1919, about a painter named Klingsor in his last summer. Expressionist, dreamlike and autobiographical, it explores art, love and the approach of old age.
42347: A novel by Alfredo Panzini about a journey taken by a poor man of letters, told with humour and affection. Gentle, wry and observant of Italian life.
42373: A novel by Alfredo Panzini, whose title, The Naive Ones, points to a story of simple, trusting characters. Ironic and affectionate in tone.
42376: A collection of literary portraits and sketches by Armando Palacio Valdes, offering affectionate and sharp pen-pictures of Spanish writers and their lives. Lively and personal, it suits readers of Spanish literature.
42389: Walter Scott's novel set on the Shetland Islands and at sea, with pirates, shipwreck and romance. Adventurous and sweeping, it is one of the Waverley novels and a good choice for lovers of sea stories.
42406: An erotic novel attributed to the French writer Mirabeau, about the sexual education of a young woman, Laura. Frank and explicit, it belongs to the libertine literature of eighteenth-century France and is for adult readers.
42411: An Italian novel by Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi, whose title, Destiny, suggests a story of fate and human suffering. Written in the dramatic, patriotic style of the Risorgimento period.
42416: A collection of stories by Matilde Serao about children and young people, the little souls of the title. Tender, observant and emotional, the stories show the Neapolitan writer's compassion.
42418: Short stories by Alfredo Panzini about women, mothers and children, seen through his ironic and affectionate eye for Italian life. Tender and humorous by turns.
42424: One of Ramon del Valle-Inclan's Modernist Sonatas, the memoirs of the Marquis de Bradomin, a charming and roguish aristocrat in the tradition of Don Juan. Sensual, witty and stylised, it is a classic of Spanish Modernist fiction.
42436: A collection of stories and writings by Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi, the Italian Romantic novelist, including the piece Amelia Calani. Dramatic, emotional and typical of the Italian Romantic period.
42440: One of Ramon del Valle-Inclan's four Modernist Sonatas, the memoirs of the Marquis de Bradomin. This charming aristocratic seducer recounts his romances in a witty, decadent style.
42448: An Italian comedy in three acts by Sabatino Lopez, whose title, The Distance, suggests the gap between people. Light, witty and sharply observed.
42474: A reference book by Edward Sylvester Ellis, a short dictionary of gods, heroes and mythological figures from many cultures, written for schools. Useful and informative for students and curious readers.
42486: Henry James's two novellas in one volume. The Turn of the Screw is a chilling ghost story about a governess at a country house, ambiguous and unsettling, and Covering End is a gentler tale of courtship.
42503: The second volume of Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi's historical novel Paolo Pelliccioni, set in the past and full of Italian political drama. A dramatic and patriotic story in the Romantic manner.
42505: Short stories by Luigi Capuana, the Sicilian writer and critic associated with verismo. The title tale, Fausto Bragia, leads a collection of realist tales of Sicilian and Italian life.
42513: An 1895 novel by Gabriele D'Annunzio, written under the influence of Nietzsche, that explores heroic and aesthetic ideals. Lush, decadent and philosophical, it is a key work of D'Annunzio's aesthetic period.
42524: Cervantes's masterpiece in French translation. A country gentleman reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out as a knight-errant, with his squire Sancho Panza. Funny, moving and endlessly inventive, it is one of the great novels of world literature.
42577: A critical study by the Italian poet Giovanni Pascoli of the moral structure of Dante's Divine Comedy. Scholarly and passionate, it offers a reading of Dante for those interested in Italian literature.
42588: An Italian novel by Gerolamo Rovetta, whose title, The Young Lady, suggests a story of a young woman and her world. A late nineteenth-century work in the sentimental style of its time.
42608: New sketches and stories by Luigi Capuana, the Sicilian writer, portraying peasant life and the people of the Sicilian countryside. Realist and observant, they show the harsh and human character of rural life.
42643: A novel by Luigi Capuana, whose title, The Enemy Is Within Us, suggests an inner struggle and a psychological drama. Realist and introspective.
42648: Swift's satirical masterpiece, in French translation. Lemuel Gulliver's voyages take him to the tiny Lilliputians, the giants of Brobdingnag, the floating island of Laputa and the land of the Houyhnhnms. Witty, savage and fantastical, it satirises politics, science and human pride.
42649: A collection of comic anecdotes and funny events from eighteenth-century Sicily, gathered from an anonymous Sicilian and published by the folklorist Giuseppe Pitre. Humorous and vivid, it reflects Sicilian popular wit and custom.
42673: A 1910 novel by Gabriele D'Annunzio, passionate and sensual, drawing on the author's own romantic life. Its title, Maybe Yes, Maybe No, hints at love's uncertainties and at the cult of modern daring.
42681: A romance of the French Revolution and the Terror by Alexandre Dumas, with royalist plots and a love story at its heart. Thrilling, romantic and full of dramatic set pieces.
42684: A short Italian tale by Gerolamo Rovetta, whose title, Underwater, suggests a hidden or submerged feeling. Restrained and psychological, it is typical of the late nineteenth-century Italian short story.
42698: A collection of short stories by Luigi Capuana, whose title, Ah! Life, suggests reflections on everyday existence. Realist, wry and observant of Sicilian and Italian characters.
42704: Oscar Wilde's one-act tragedy based on the biblical Salome and the prophet John the Baptist. Lush, decadent and intense, it is a sensual and disturbing play of desire, power and obsession.
42711: A collection of traditional French songs and nursery rhymes for young children, with piano accompaniments by the composer Charles-Marie Widor. Charming, simple and musical, it is a classic for family singing.
42743: The first part of a five-volume French retelling of the Arthurian romances of the Round Table, put into modern language. Full of knights, quests and courtly love, it is a good introduction to Arthurian legend.

42765: The third book of George Sand's autobiography, continuing her account of her life, her friendships and her writing. Candid and reflective, it gives a vivid picture of nineteenth-century Paris and its writers.
42776: The second volume of Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi's novel Il secolo che muore, a dramatic and patriotic story of a turbulent era. Romantic and political, it suits readers of Italian historical fiction.
42777: The third volume of Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi's novel Il secolo che muore, continuing its dramatic story of a turbulent era. Romantic and political, it suits readers of Italian historical fiction.
42778: The fourth volume of Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi's novel Il secolo che muore, continuing its dramatic and patriotic story. It has the grand manner of the Italian Romantic historical novel.
42881: The first volume of Walter Scott's Gothic romance of the Scottish borders, the story of a young woman promised in marriage to a man she does not love, amid family feuds. Dark and romantic, it inspired Donizetti's opera Lucia di Lammermoor.
42882: The second volume of Walter Scott's Gothic romance of the Scottish borders, in which the tangled loves and family feuds of the story deepen. Dark and romantic in mood.
42883: The third volume of Walter Scott's Gothic romance of the Scottish borders. Tense, emotional and dark, it brings the Lammermoor story to its climax.
42900: The classic French fairy tales of Charles Perrault in German translation, under the title Goose-Mother's Tales. Including Cinderella, Puss in Boots and Sleeping Beauty, these short moral tales are ideal for young readers.
42928: A one-act Italian comedy by Roberto Bracco, whose title, One of the Honest Men, suggests a light moral satire on respectability.
42929: A three-act Italian drama by Roberto Bracco, whose title, Lost in the Dark, suggests lives lost in hardship and despair. Realist and intense, it was filmed more than once.

4300: Leopold Bloom wanders through Dublin on an ordinary day in June 1904, and his encounters and thoughts shape a vast, inventive portrait of the city. Joyce's modernist novel is dense, funny and famously challenging.
43017: A novel by Pio Baroja, the Spanish writer of the Generation of '98, set in a harsh Spanish city. Its title, Weeds, reflects a bleak, realist view of life, and it forms part of the trilogy The Struggle for Life.
43030: A novel by Vicente Blasco Ibanez about the son of a blacksmith who becomes a famous painter, and his romances with the women in his life, in Rome, Paris and Madrid. Sensual and dramatic, it draws on the life of the painter Goya.
43033: Mala hierba, the middle part of Pio Baroja's trilogy The Struggle for Life, a gritty series of novels of Spanish city life inspired by the Darwinian idea of struggle for survival. Naturalistic and bleak, it suits readers of Spanish realism.
43063: A detective and murder mystery novel by Oliver Onions, a British writer of the early twentieth century, set in England. Clever, puzzling and atmospheric, it suits fans of classic whodunits.
43098: A selection of writings by the American anarchist and feminist Voltairine de Cleyre, including essays, poems and speeches on freedom, labour and women's rights. Passionate, radical and articulate.
43115: An Italian novel by Annie Vivanti, whose title invokes the scandalous Messalina of ancient Rome. Provocative and dramatic, it explores women and power in a bold, sensual manner.
43217: A collection of short stories by the Italian writer known as the Marchesa Colombi, with tales of everyday life, women and social customs in Italy. Witty and observant, the pieces are typical of late nineteenth-century Italian fiction.
43226: A novel by Grazia Deledda, the Sardinian writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Set in a Sardinian village, it follows a woman's life after divorce, in a stark and passionate portrait of island society.
43285: A three-act Italian drama by Roberto Bracco, whose title, The Unripe Fruit, suggests a premature passion or a young love. Realist and psychological, in the playwright's serious style.
43332: A moral children's story by Christoph von Schmid, the German writer of didactic tales for young readers, about honesty, family and a little lamb. Simple, gentle and instructive, it reflects nineteenth-century children's literature.
43333: A German novel by Bernhard Kellermann set around the German revolution of November 1918, when the monarchy fell. Political and dramatic, it portrays the upheaval and the people caught up in it.
43335: A novella by Heinrich Mann about an ambitious woman whose drive for success shapes her life. Sharp and psychologically precise, it shows the author's ironic eye for social climbing and vanity.
43356: A four-act Italian drama by Roberto Bracco, whose title, The Little Spring, suggests purity, renewal or a hidden source. Realist and emotional in the playwright's manner.
43360: A set of short Italian plays by Roberto Bracco, including Photograph Without..., Snowy Night and The Chatterbox. Brief and varied, they show the playwright's range from light comedy to intense drama.
43441: A history of the French Symbolist and Decadent literary movements by the poet and critic Gustave Kahn. An insider's account, valuable for readers of late nineteenth-century French poetry.
43458: The first volume of Walter Scott's Old Mortality, a novel of the Scottish Covenanters and religious zeal set against royal power. Gripping and historical, it was the basis of Bellini's opera I Puritani.
43459: The second volume of Walter Scott's Old Mortality, a novel of the Scottish Covenanters, rising tensions and the struggle between religious zeal and royal power. Gripping and historical.
43460: The third volume of Walter Scott's Old Mortality, which builds to the Battle of Bothwell Bridge in 1679. Gripping and historical, it was the basis of Bellini's opera I Puritani.
43511: A four-act Italian drama by Roberto Bracco, whose title, The Ghosts, suggests a play about the past and psychological haunting. Dark and intense, in the playwright's realist manner.
43535: The second volume of Moliere's complete works, comic plays of the great French dramatist. Sharp and sparkling satires of manners, vanity and hypocrisy.
4367: Ulysses S. Grant's memoir recounts his military career in the Mexican War and the American Civil War, written with clarity and modesty. The book is candid, dignified and a classic of military autobiography.
43787: A novel by Rene Bazin set in Brittany, the French coastal region. Its setting gives it a regional and traditional flavour, with a warm sense of local life.
43822: A bibliographical essay on the works of Pietro Aretino, the sixteenth-century Italian satirist whose erotic writings made him notorious. Scholarly and frank, it is for specialists in Renaissance literature and book history.
43851: The second volume of Balzac's vast cycle of novels and stories, a panoramic portrait of French society from the Restoration to the July Monarchy. Vivid and sharp, it shows money, power and ambition in Paris and the provinces.
43861: A selection of thoughts and sayings taken from the works of the Cuban writer and patriot Jose Marti. Short, inspiring and often moral, the pieces are good for dipping into.
43901: A selection of letters by Madame de Sevigne, the seventeenth-century French marquise whose correspondence chronicles court life, gossip and family affairs. Witty, intimate and vivid, the letters are classics of French prose.
44238: Oscar Wilde's novel about a beautiful young man whose portrait ages while he keeps his youth, a story of vanity, decadence and moral corruption. Witty, gothic and provocative, it is among the most famous novels of its era.
44272: A collection of short grotesque stories by the German writer Mynona, the pen name of Salomo Friedlaender. Bizarre, witty and absurd, the pieces play with the strange side of everyday life.
44355: The third volume of Ferdinando Petruccelli della Gattina's historical novel Il re dei re, set in the eleventh century during the struggle between popes and emperors. Dramatic and political, it is a sweeping story of medieval power.
44358: A novel by Miguel de Unamuno about Tula, a single woman who longs to be a mother and gives her life to others within her family. Psychological and thoughtful, it explores love, duty and identity in the Spanish provinces.
44403: The third volume of the Roman de la Rose, the thirteenth-century French allegorical poem of courtly love set in a dream garden. Symbolic, witty and long, it shaped European love poetry.
44512: A novel by Miguel de Unamuno, a modern retelling of the story of Cain and Abel, in which two men who were friends since childhood are destroyed by envy. Psychological and intense.
44529: A Spanish novel by Concha Espina, a popular early twentieth-century writer of sentimental and regional fiction. Its title, Sweet Name, suggests a tender, romantic story.
44537: Romain Rolland's biography of the Russian novelist Leo Tolstoy, a sympathetic study of his life, faith and writing. Thoughtful, admiring and personal, it suits readers of Tolstoy and of biography.
44549: A medieval Italian encyclopedia of knowledge, arranged as questions and answers between a wise man and a king, on nature, science and morality. A window onto medieval beliefs and learning.
44598: A German utopian novel by Richard Michaelis, written as a reply to Edward Bellamy's utopian Looking Backward. It imagines a future shaped by the social reform and political ideas of the late nineteenth century.
44610: A collection of grotesque, satirical sketches by the German humorist Hans Reimann. Short, absurd and sharply comic, the pieces mock everyday German life of the early twentieth century.
44713: The fourth volume of the Roman de la Rose, the thirteenth-century French allegorical poem of courtly love in a dream garden. Symbolic and witty, it shaped European love poetry.
44714: The travels of Marco Polo, the Venetian who described China, Persia and Asia to European readers in the late thirteenth century. Full of wonders and marvels, it remains one of the great travel books of world literature.
44763: Anecdotes about the animals of the First World War by the Italian writer Giulio Caprin. Horses, dogs and other animals played their part in the war, and this book tells their stories in a touching, anecdotal style.
44797: An Italian historical novel by Massimo d'Azeglio about the Challenge of Barletta, a 1503 combat between Italian and French knights. Patriotic, chivalrous and heroic, it is a key text of the Risorgimento.
44802: A comic introduction to English grammar by Percival Leigh, written in a mock-serious style. Witty and playful, it turns the rules of grammar into jokes and light satire.
44877: A famous seventeenth-century French erotic dialogue, L'Escole des filles, reprinted from an original text. Explicit and frank, it is a historical example of the erotic literature of its time and is for adult readers only.
4488: A nineteenth-century English novel by George Meredith about marriage, love and social conventions. It is witty, romantic and full of lively conversation.
44931: A travel book by the French artist and writer Albert Robida, illustrating the old towns of Flanders and northern France with his own drawings. Detailed, visual and nostalgic, it is a fine guide to historic Flemish towns.
44956: Tolstoy's realist masterpiece, in the first volume of a German edition. Anna, a married woman in St Petersburg society, begins a passionate affair with the dashing officer Vronsky. 44957: The second volume of the German edition of Tolstoy's great novel, continuing the stories of Anna, caught in a passionate affair in high society, and Levin, a landowner seeking meaning in country life. Emotionally intense and psychologically deep, with vivid portraits of Russian society.
4499: The short fiction of the Victorian novelist George Meredith, with sharp wit, romance and observations of social manners. These pieces are a good introduction to his style.

4501: A German fairy tale by Clemens Brentano, a playful story of talking birds and a magical kingdom, written for children. It is whimsical and light.
45058: A light-hearted adventure novel by Jules Verne about Kin-Fo, a rich Chinese man who is bored with life and, after a business setback, takes a drastic decision. The tale moves briskly across China with plenty of comedy, travel and colourful incident, in Verne's lively, inventive style.
45091: A sharp, satirical play by Frank Wedekind, first written in 1891, about teenagers coming of age as puberty and sexual curiosity collide with the intolerance and hypocrisy of the adults around them. Its mood is frank, bitter and confrontational, and it is a landmark of German drama.
45119: A volume from the complete works of Guy de Maupassant, the French master of the short story. His realistic tales of ordinary people, from Norman peasants to Parisian society, are concise, observant and often ironic, with a keen eye for human weakness.
45123: A seduction novel by Heinrich Mann, begun in 1905 and published in 1907. A young singer, Lola Gabriel, is drawn between a reserved German admirer and a charming, reckless Florentine count. 4517: A bleak New England farm, a crushing winter and a secret love triangle form the setting of Wharton's short, intense novella. It is emotional, austere and full of quiet tension.
45334: A classic Italian historical novel by Alessandro Manzoni, set in seventeenth-century Lombardy under Spanish rule. 45438: The Spanish translation of Robert Louis Stevenson's adventure classic. A boy, Jim Hawkins, comes into possession of a treasure map and sets sail for a hidden island with a crew that includes the charming, one-legged cook Long John Silver. Swashbuckling, atmospheric and full of tension.
45451: A romance by Harry Johnston, an older-style novel whose title, The Man Who Did the Right Thing, points to a story about a moral choice. Its characters and setting are not described here, so it will suit readers who enjoy classic Victorian-era romantic fiction.
4548: Three men fly a balloon across central Africa in an adventurous scientific expedition full of mishaps and discoveries. Verne's early adventure is light, exciting and full of geography.
45524: A collection of short stories by Stephen Crane, including the title tale, based on his own experience of surviving a shipwreck off Florida. Four men are cast adrift in a small boat, struggling to reach the shore. The stories are spare, vivid and full of tension and quiet loyalty.
45565: A historical study by Alberto Guglielmotti of piracy in the Mediterranean and the papal navy from 1500 to 1560. Volume 1 is a detailed, serious work for readers interested in naval history and the Italian past, rather than a narrative story.
45566: The second volume of Alberto Guglielmotti's historical study of the war against Mediterranean pirates and the papal navy, covering the years 1500 to 1560. A detailed, scholarly work for readers of naval and Italian history rather than a novel.
45594: An essay by the poet Giovanni Pascoli offering a general interpretation of Dante's Divine Comedy, focusing on the poem's hidden allegorical meaning. It is a scholarly and literary work, best suited to readers who already know Dante and want deeper reflection on his poem.
45595: An Italian prose work by Enrico Panzacchi, a late nineteenth-century writer, titled Women and Poets. Its title suggests essays on literature and on the women who have inspired poets. A short, reflective book for readers of Italian literary culture.
45600: A short tragedy in eight scenes by Heinrich Heine, published and staged in 1823. Written in the Romantic style of its day, it is a brief, dramatic work by one of Germany's most celebrated poets, full of irony and emotional intensity.
45634: Myths and sacred stories of the Cherokee people, recorded by the ethnologist James Mooney in the late nineteenth century and published by the Bureau of American Ethnology. 45647: A collection of short sketches by Edmondo De Amicis, the author of Cuore, about life in the Italian army. Lively, observant and warm, the pieces show ordinary soldiers and their daily routines, with humour and a sense of camaraderie.
45653: An Italian prose work by Enrico Panzacchi, a writer of the late nineteenth century, titled The Dead and the Living. Its title suggests reflections on death, memory and those left behind. A short, reflective book for readers of Italian literature.
45670: The memoir of Count Felix von Luckner, the German naval officer whose raider Seeadler cruised the Pacific in the First World War, becoming a legend for daring. The book recounts adventures at sea, bold exploits and narrow escapes, told with the energy of a seafaring adventure story.
45692: A short biography by Madame de La Fayette, author of The Princess of Cleves, of Henrietta of England, who became Duchess of Orléans at the glittering court of Louis XIV. Elegant and psychologically sharp, it mixes court intrigue with a personal portrait of a princess.
45698: An Italian novel titled Beyond, by Alfredo Oriani, a writer and social critic of the late nineteenth century. Oriani's ideas on nation and history were later claimed by Fascism, so the book is also of interest to readers studying Italian political thought.
45798: A German novella by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, first published in 1842, about the unsolved murder of a Jewish man in a village in the Westphalian hills, based on a real case. Told in a quiet, realistic manner, it is a dark, atmospheric study of suspicion, guilt and village life.
45803: A collection of historical and moral short stories by Cesare Cantù, a nineteenth-century Italian historian and writer. The tales aim to teach as well as entertain, with a didactic tone and an interest in the past and in moral conduct.
45829: Volume 1 of Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's long Spanish novel La araña negra, known in English as The Black Spider, published in nine parts. The author is known for sweeping, dramatic storytelling, and this part opens a large, melodramatic narrative.
45830: Volume 2 of Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's long Spanish novel La araña negra, published in nine parts. The author's sweeping, dramatic storytelling continues, building a large, melodramatic narrative that suits readers who enjoy long, plot-driven novels.
45833: Volume 5 of Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's nine-part Spanish novel La araña negra. The author's sweeping, dramatic storytelling is at its most absorbing here, in a long, melodramatic narrative that rewards readers who like plot-driven, large-scale fiction.
45835: Volume 7 of Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's nine-part Spanish novel La araña negra. Written in the author's sweeping, dramatic style, this part continues a long, melodramatic story suited to readers who enjoy large, plot-driven fiction.
45837: The final volume, number 9, of Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's Spanish novel La araña negra. The author's sweeping, dramatic storytelling reaches a close in this part of a long, melodramatic narrative, best read in sequence from the first volume.
45970: The first volume of L'Âme enchantée, Romain Rolland's long novel sequence, titled Annette and Sylvie. A French psychological novel about the inner lives and friendships of its characters, written with the warmth and idealism typical of Rolland.
4599: A modest country family in Barsetshire is caught up in romance, rivalry and the choices of the heart. Trollope's novel is gentle, witty and full of social detail.

46000: A collection of short stories by the Spanish writer Felipe Trigo, published in the early twentieth century and titled Innocent Tales. Short, direct narratives of ordinary people and everyday situations, suited to readers who want brief, straightforward fiction.
46021: A collection of letters Goethe wrote to his friends in Leipzig, where he studied as a young man. The letters give an intimate and witty glimpse of the poet's early years, his friendships and his developing ideas.
46031: Unpublished passages and drafts from Alessandro Manzoni's novel I promessi sposi, gathered for readers who want to see how the masterpiece was written. Of most interest to students of Italian literature and of the novel's making.
46082: A study by the poet Giovanni Pascoli, presented as an outline of the story behind Dante's Divine Comedy. It is a scholarly, literary essay for readers who already know the poem and want to explore its structure and meaning.
46111: The sequel to From the Earth to the Moon. Jules Verne's three adventurers, now shot in a projectile around the Moon, see its far side at close range. A fast-paced, scientific adventure full of imaginative engineering and lively banter.
46164: A five-act Italian play by Roberto Bracco, a leading dramatist of late nineteenth-century Naples. Written in a realistic, emotional style, it is a serious stage drama for readers interested in Italian theatre of the period.
46182: The first two parts of Ramón del Valle-Inclán's Sonatas, the memoirs of the Marquis de Bradomín, a witty, lyrical aristocrat and self-styled Don Juan. Written in ornate, poetic prose, they recall his romantic and sensual adventures in a mood of elegant melancholy.
46184: A witty German novel by Theodor Fontane, published in 1892 and set in Berlin society. It satirises the pretensions of Jenny Treibel, a wealthy, status-conscious widow whose family plans clash with a young couple's hopes. Light, ironic and observant of social life.
46196: The first series of a Spanish selection of stories by Edgar Allan Poe, the master of eerie atmosphere, mystery and suspense. Sharp, economical tales of dread and ingenuity, translated into Spanish for readers of the Spanish-speaking world.
46201: The first volume of the Spanish translation of Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, a chivalric epic and continuation of Boiardo's Orlando innamorato. Full of knights, enchanted places, love and war, it mixes high adventure with irony and wit.
46211: An Italian novel titled Shadows of Sunset by Alfredo Oriani, a writer and social critic of the late nineteenth century. The title suggests a melancholy, reflective mood, suited to readers of Italian fiction of the period.
46213: A drama in three acts and an epilogue by Roberto Bracco, a playwright known for emotional, socially aware theatre in late nineteenth-century Italy. A serious stage play for readers interested in Italian drama of the period.
46225: An Italian work of fiction titled Quartet by Alfredo Oriani, a writer and social critic of the late nineteenth century. Its title suggests a piece built around four voices or characters, for readers of Italian literature of the period.
46268: A German translation of Paul Claudel's ode The Muses, a formal lyric poem by the French poet and diplomat. Its elevated, rhythmic verse addresses the Muses and the spirit of art, for readers of modern French poetry.
46276: A Western adventure romance by the French writer Gustave Aimard, set on the frontier of California. Full of danger, rivalries and a search for hidden riches, it is a fast-moving tale in the style of nineteenth-century frontier fiction.
46279: A Spanish translation of a Gustave Aimard frontier adventure set on the wild borderlands of the American West. Fast action, danger and rivalry between trappers, settlers and raiders make it a lively read for lovers of Western adventure.
46295: A comedy by the nineteenth-century Italian playwright Valentino Carrera, titled Capital and Labour. From his collected comedies, it is likely to deal with the tensions between employers and workers, for readers of Italian social drama.
46296: A comedy by the Italian playwright Valentino Carrera, titled Dedication, Scribble, from his collected comedies. A short piece of nineteenth-century Italian theatre for readers interested in the drama of the period.
46297: A comedy by the Italian playwright Valentino Carrera, titled Nanni's Quaternion, from his collected comedies. A nineteenth-century piece of Italian stage writing, for readers interested in Italian theatre of the period.
46351: A comedy by the Italian playwright Valentino Carrera, titled A Lawyer of the Future, from his collected comedies. A satirical nineteenth-century piece of Italian theatre, for readers interested in the stage and social manners of the period.
46352: A comedy by the Italian playwright Valentino Carrera, titled The Last Days of Goldoni, from his collected comedies. It takes as its subject the great Venetian playwright Goldoni, for readers interested in Italian theatre and its history.
46387: A volume from the complete works of Guy de Maupassant, the French master of the short story. Its realistic tales of ordinary lives and social manners are concise, observant and often ironic, with a sharp eye for human weakness.
46411: Wilhelm Raabe's first novel, published in 1857 under a pseudonym and presented as a chronicle of a small street and its residents. Told in twenty-one diary-like entries, it is gentle, humorous and full of quiet observations on everyday life.
46440: The log of the first Portuguese voyage to India, led by Vasco da Gama in 1497 to 1499, translated by E. G. Ravenstein. It is a firsthand naval account of the first sea route between Europe and India, full of navigation, encounters and hardship.
46463: The second volume of Manzoni's unpublished passages and drafts from I promessi sposi, gathered for readers who want to see how the novel took shape. Of most interest to students of Italian literature.
46466: An Italian novel titled Arrigo the Wise by Anton Giulio Barrili, a popular nineteenth-century Genoese novelist. Written in the storytelling manner of its period, it suits readers who enjoy traditional Italian fiction.
46496: The second series of a Spanish selection of classic American stories, including tales by Washington Irving and Edward Everett Hale. Their tales of folklore, humour and character are short, accessible and rooted in early American storytelling.
4650: Follows a naive young man through a string of disasters and absurd adventures as he searches for his beloved Cunégonde, while his tutor insists that everything is for the best. Voltaire's satire is witty, sharp and a classic of Enlightenment fiction.
46613: An Italian novel titled Saint Cecilia by Anton Giulio Barrili, a popular nineteenth-century Genoese novelist. Written in the traditional storytelling manner of its period, it suits readers who enjoy classic Italian fiction.
46683: A volume from Champagnac's collection of the most tragic real-life events, recounting true crimes and the cases of innocent people caught up in them. Dramatic and grim, it is a nineteenth-century French chronicle of crime and injustice.
46717: A short Italian work by Giuseppe Regaldi, a nineteenth-century poet and writer, titled La Dora. The title is all that is known here, so it is best approached as a period Italian text for readers of its literature.
46723: Part one of La plebe, a social novel by Vittorio Bersezio about the lives of ordinary working people in nineteenth-century Italy. Its realistic portrayal of everyday struggles and community life makes it a valuable window onto the period.
46724: Part two of La plebe, Vittorio Bersezio's social novel about the lives of ordinary working people in nineteenth-century Italy. Its realistic portrait of everyday struggles and community life continues here.
46725: Part three of La plebe, Vittorio Bersezio's social novel about the lives of ordinary working people in nineteenth-century Italy. The realistic portrait of everyday struggles and community life reaches its conclusion in this final part.
46748: The first volume of I Barbarò by Gerolamo Rovetta, a popular Italian novelist of the late nineteenth century. Its title, The Tears of Others, points to a family-centred story of feeling and social life, for readers of period Italian fiction.

46847: An Italian work titled The Duke of Athens by Niccolò Tommaseo, a writer and lexicographer known for his dictionary of the Italian language. The title suggests a historical story of medieval Italy, for readers interested in the period.
46870: A French account by the philosopher C.-F. Volney, written after his travels in America, describing the climate, soil and conditions of the United States and Florida. It also includes observations on French colonial settlements and on the Native peoples he encountered.
46874: A 1920 Italian novel by Annie Vivanti, set in London, about two sheltered sisters from the provinces who are drawn into the luxurious household of a self-styled noblewoman. As their trust gives way to unease, the story becomes a sharp, dark tale of manipulation.
46875: A collection of short stories by the Italian writer Enrico Castelnuovo, including The Broken Mirror and The Stopped Clock. Lean, observant and centred on ordinary people, these late nineteenth-century tales show a careful eye for everyday life.
46898: A collection of Florentine folk tales and short stories, taken down from the spoken voices of ordinary people by the nineteenth-century scholar Vittorio Imbriani. Lively, simple and rooted in the oral storytelling tradition of Tuscany.
46900: A collection of short stories and novellas by Antonio Ghislanzoni, a nineteenth-century Italian writer who was also the librettist of Verdi's Aida. The tales show his range as a storyteller in the Italian literary culture of his day.
46914: An Italian literary work built around Cervantes' Don Quixote, by the journalist and critic Edoardo Scarfoglio. It offers his own reflections on the classic novel, for readers who already know the book and enjoy literary criticism.
4693: A collection of biographical sketches of famous couples and loves in history, retold with a romantic and admiring tone. It is light reading for those interested in notable lives.
46931: The first volume of Gérard de Nerval's Voyage en Orient, an account of his travels in Egypt and Lebanon in 1842. It mixes vivid observations of Cairo's women and of the Druze and Maronite communities with dreamy, lyrical prose.
46932: The second volume of Gérard de Nerval's Voyage en Orient. It includes his Nights of Ramadan in Cairo, retellings of Oriental tales such as the story of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and a lyrical, dreamlike mix of travel and imagination.
46939: A German work titled The World in a Hundred Years, a speculative look at how society and civilisation might develop over the next century. Its imagined future reflects the hopes and anxieties of its own time, for readers interested in early visions of the future.
46957: An Italian historical novel by Massimo d'Azeglio, first published in 1841, set in sixteenth-century Florence. It explores the bitter rivalry between the Palleschi and the Piagnoni, two political factions, and the wider struggle for the city's future.
46999: A novel by the Neapolitan writer Matilde Serao, titled Sister Giovanna of the Cross. The title points to a story centred on a nun and on the inner life of a woman within a religious community, for readers of Italian fiction.

47041: A collection of short stories by Alfredo Panzini, an Italian writer of the early twentieth century, titled Triumphs of Woman. Its tales centre on women and their lives, told in the accessible, observant style of its period.
47058: A book about Italian political exiles living in London in the nineteenth century, by the journalist and writer Ferdinando Petruccelli della Gattina. Its title, The Nights of the Emigrants in London, suggests a reflective, atmospheric portrait of exile.
47074: A 1916 Italian romantic novel by Guido da Verona, a bestseller of its day. Its tender, sentimental love story and melodramatic mood made it hugely popular, and it was later filmed in 1976, starring Monica Vitti.
47102: A satirical Italian work by Antonio Ghislanzoni, the librettist of Verdi's Aida, titled The Art of Getting into Debt. Its wry title suggests a light, comic look at money and social pretensions in nineteenth-century Italy.
47103: A Spanish novel by Pío Baroja, one of the leading novelists of the Generation of '98, titled The Apprentice Conspirator. Its title points to a young man drawn into political plotting, told in Baroja's restless, realistic style.
4712: A romance in which a wandering man on foot becomes involved in a fight against political corruption over a town's water supply. Holman Day's novel is brisk, romantic and full of rural American colour.
47138: An Italian work titled The Secret Book by Antonio Ghislanzoni, a nineteenth-century writer and librettist. The title suggests a story built around a hidden document or secret, for readers interested in Italian fiction of the period.
