47184: An anthology of Puerto Rican prose and verse, collected by the writer and journalist Manuel Fernández Juncos. It gathers writing from the island's literary tradition, offering a varied introduction to the literature of Puerto Rico.
47221: The first volume of Ernst Eckstein's Quintus Claudius, a historical romance of Imperial Rome. Set in the ancient city's public and private life, it blends historical detail with romantic adventure, in the tradition of nineteenth-century German historical fiction.
47287: The first volume of the Spanish version of the Arabian Nights, the famous collection of tales framed by Scheherazade, who tells stories night after night. Full of magic, genies, lovers and clever tricks, it is a classic of world storytelling.
47294: The first volume of Il Nemico, an Italian novel titled The Enemy by Alfredo Oriani, a writer and social critic of the late nineteenth century. A serious work of period Italian fiction, for readers interested in the literature and ideas of its time.
47295: The second volume of Il Nemico, an Italian novel titled The Enemy by Alfredo Oriani, a writer and social critic of the late nineteenth century. A serious work of period Italian fiction, for readers interested in its literature and ideas.
47341: A Heimat novel by Ludwig Ganghofer, the popular Bavarian writer, set in the forests and mountains of southern Germany. Its title, The Silence in the Forest, suggests a romantic, sentimental tale of rural life close to nature.
47345: A fable-like novel by Judith Gautier, narrated in the voice of a white elephant, offering an imaginative and exotic view of an Asian court. Its lyrical, storytelling style suits readers who enjoy inventive, old-fashioned fiction.
47461: An Italian translation of selected Canterbury Tales by Geoffrey Chaucer. A group of pilgrims on the road to Canterbury tell stories to pass the time, and the tales are witty, earthy and full of colourful characters, from knights to a miller and a cook.
47479: A polemical French work by Han Ryner, offering critical studies of about two hundred contemporary women writers in a sharp, satirical tone. It is a document of early twentieth-century literary quarrels, for readers interested in French literary debate.
47530: The second volume of Charles Dickens's Oliver Twist. The orphan boy, raised in a harsh workhouse, is drawn into London's criminal underworld under Fagin and the Artful Dodger. Dark, vivid and sharply comic in places, it is a classic of Victorian city life.
47565: The second volume of Giovanni Boccaccio's commentary on Dante's Divine Comedy, written as lectures in Florence. It offers detailed explanations of the poem's text, for readers who want to study Dante in depth.
47566: The third volume of Giovanni Boccaccio's commentary on Dante's Divine Comedy, written as lectures in Florence. It offers detailed explanations of the poem's text and of Dante's world, for serious readers of medieval Italian literature.
47584: José Rizal's novel, first published in 1887 and set in Spanish colonial Manila. Crisóstomo Ibarra returns home from Europe and confronts corruption, prejudice and the power of the Spanish friars. Its critique of colonial injustice made it a landmark of Philippine literature.
47631: The second volume of the Spanish version of the Arabian Nights, the famous collection of tales framed by Scheherazade, who keeps telling stories night after night. Full of magic, lovers, genies and clever tricks, it is a classic of world storytelling.
47642: A February 1904 issue of The Strand Magazine, the popular British monthly famous for publishing Sherlock Holmes stories. Its mix of short fiction, illustrated articles and features offers a lively snapshot of Edwardian popular reading.
47711: A German translation of August Vermeylen's novel that explores the legend of the Wandering Jew, a figure from Christian folklore condemned to wander the world. Its mood is melancholy and reflective, for readers of older European fiction.
47715: Volume 7 of the nine-volume Cambridge Edition of Shakespeare's complete works, a scholarly edition of the plays and poems by the English playwright. Designed for careful study, with textual notes, rather than as a single story.
47720: A special edition for young readers of Tolstoy's Childhood, an autobiographical novel following a boy growing up in a Russian aristocratic family. Gentle, perceptive and close to everyday feelings, it shows the early life of a sensitive young mind.
47786: An Italian novel by Sibilla Aleramo, published in 1906 and one of the first openly feminist Italian novels. Drawing on the author's own life, it follows an unnamed woman's struggle for self-determination in a society that denied women freedom. Intimate and direct.
47798: Luigi Barzini's account of the 1907 Peking to Paris motor race, a gruelling journey of thousands of miles across deserts, mountains and rough tracks in the early days of motoring. Lively, dramatic reportage full of breakdowns, bad roads and sheer determination.
47804: Friedrich Schiller's early, fiery play about Karl Moor, an idealistic young nobleman who, after a bitter family quarrel, turns to outlawry and leads a band of robbers in the forests. Passionate and rebellious, it is a landmark of the Sturm und Drang movement.
47818: A collection of short stories by Hermann Hesse, published in 1907 and titled This Side. Reflective and lyrical, the tales follow ordinary people, artists and wanderers in their search for meaning, showing Hesse's early voice.
4785: Set among Breton fishermen who sail to the cold Icelandic waters to catch cod, this French novel is melancholy and lyrical, full of the sea and its hardships. Pierre Loti's story is evocative and moving.
47888: A drama by Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi, the Livornese writer and patriot, whose title, The Whites and the Blacks, refers to the bitter factions of medieval Florence. A stage work of Italian Risorgimento-era passion for liberty and history.
4791: A German professor and his nephew follow a coded message into a volcano in Iceland and descend into the Earth's interior. Verne's adventure is full of wonder, geology and underground marvels.
47978: An Italian work by Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi, the Livornese writer and political activist, titled A Father's Revenge. Its title suggests a dark, dramatic story of vengeance, for readers of Italian Romantic fiction.
48064: A German story for young girls, written in the nineteenth century, about the joys and sorrows of a teenage girl growing up. A gentle, sentimental coming-of-age tale of the kind once popular in German family reading.
48070: A collection of seafaring language and proverbs by Emanuele Celesia, a Genoese scholar of dialect and folklore. Useful to readers of Italian dialect and maritime culture rather than a story, it offers a window onto the speech of sailors.
48093: A realist novel by Benito Pérez Galdós about León Roch, an idealistic engineer, and the tensions in his marriage and family life. Psychologically observant and set in nineteenth-century Spain, it suits readers who enjoy close studies of character and society.
48135: The six plays of Hrotsvitha, a tenth-century canoness of Gandersheim, in Latin with a French translation. Written as Christian alternatives to the comedies of the Roman writer Terence, they are early examples of drama in the Latin West, mainly of interest to students of medieval literature.
48155: A two-volume scholarly history of ancient Greek, Etruscan and Roman pottery, illustrated with many vases and careful analysis of their shapes, decoration and makers. Non-fiction for readers of ancient art and archaeology.
48296: A romance titled Linnet by Grant Allen, the prolific Victorian writer of popular fiction and science. A late-Victorian romantic novel for readers who enjoy the gentle, sentimental fiction of its era.
48320: Arthur Conan Doyle's twelve stories featuring the consulting detective Sherlock Holmes and his friend Dr Watson, first published in The Strand Magazine in 1891 and 1892. Quick, clever mysteries in London, with Holmes's sharp deductions and dry wit. This illustrated edition adds vivid pictures.
48359: Flaubert's realist novel about Emma Bovary, a doctor's wife in a Normandy town who longs for passion and a more glamorous life than her marriage allows. Its precise, ironic style and sharp portrait of provincial society make it a classic, though its mood is often bleak.
48361: An Italian novel by Adolfo Albertazzi, a writer of the early twentieth century, titled Facing Fate. The title suggests a story of struggle against circumstance, for readers of period Italian fiction.
48383: Edgar Allan Poe's tales, translated and gathered into French by Charles Baudelaire in 1864. Murder, mystery, horror and ironic humour run through these grotesque and serious stories, dark and atmospheric in the classic Poe manner.
48400: The first novel of Federico De Roberto's Uzeda cycle, set among the Sicilian aristocracy. It follows Teresa Uzeda through her early life and adult disappointments, in a psychologically probing and melancholy portrait of disillusion in love and society.
48445: A historical novel by Guerrazzi about the siege of Florence in 1529 and 1530, when the last Florentine republic resisted imperial and papal forces. Patriotic and dramatic, it reflects the nineteenth-century Italian admiration for heroic resistance.
48490: A historical novel by Guerrazzi about Pasquale Paoli, the Corsican leader who fought for his island's independence, and the defeat at Ponte Nuovo in 1769. Patriotic and tragic in tone, it suits readers interested in island history and Risorgimento-era fiction.
48527: A German translation of Dostoevsky's novella The Double, about Golyadkin, a minor St Petersburg civil servant who is confronted by a physical double who seems to take his place. Psychological, disturbing and half-comic, it is a study of identity and anxiety.
48529: The first volume of Montaigne's Essays, in a private edition by Michaud. Montaigne's personal reflections on life, death, friendship, custom and self are written with candid, casual wisdom. A Renaissance classic, serious but very readable.
48530: A collection of Italian proverbs and sayings by John Florio, the English writer and teacher of Italian, from the late sixteenth century. Titled The Garden of Recreation, it is a witty, colourful anthology for readers of language and Renaissance culture.
48542: An Italian work by Antonio Fiacchi, titled Èl Sgner Pirein, whose dialect title points to a local, colloquial voice rather than standard Italian. Dialect writing like this gives a lively sense of a regional community.
48557: The first volume of the memoirs of Adam Oehlenschläger, the Danish Romantic poet and playwright. Written in later life, they recall his early years, his literary friendships and the Romantic culture of his time.
48576: A collection of political short stories by Antonio Ghislanzoni, the nineteenth-century Italian writer and librettist of Verdi's Aida, reflecting the political concerns of the Risorgimento era.
48590: A volume of Pierre Corneille's complete works, the French dramatist of tragedies such as Le Cid and Cinna. Heroic, rhetorical theatre about honour, duty and passion, in a formal classical style.
48654: A novel titled Incest by Eduardo Zamacois, a prolific Spanish writer of sensational fiction in the early twentieth century. It treats a difficult, controversial subject in a provocative way, and is not suited to younger or sensitive readers.
48670: A collection of plays by Eduardo Zamacois, titled Gallant Theatre. Its title suggests light courtship and social comedy from the early twentieth-century Spanish stage, for readers who enjoy theatre of manners.
48779: A collection of humorous short stories by Adolfo Albertazzi, an Italian writer of the early twentieth century. The tales are light, witty and comic in tone, suited to readers who want an easy, amusing read.
48783: A Spanish novel by Pío Baroja, one of the Generation of '98 writers, titled The Brigand's Squadron. Its title points to a band of outlaws, told in Baroja's restless, realistic style.
48801: A short Italian work by Aldo Palazzeschi, the playful and irreverent writer, titled The Handsome King. Its fairy-tale title and witty, satirical style suggest a light, mocking story for readers of early twentieth-century Italian literature.
48820: A comedy in three acts by Gerolamo Rovetta, the popular Italian playwright of the late nineteenth century. First staged in 1889, it was later adapted for an Italian silent film in 1917, and suits readers of period Italian theatre.
48850: A futurist novel by Aldo Palazzeschi, first published in 1911, about Perelà, a man made of smoke who drifts into a world of ordinary people. A playful, satirical fable that mocks social conventions and the powers that govern them.
48878: A songbook of traditional French songs for children, with piano accompaniments by Jean-Baptiste Weckerlin and charming illustrations by Maurice Boutet de Monvel. A nostalgic collection for young readers and musicians.
48881: Flaubert's historical novel set in ancient Carthage, following the revolt of mercenary soldiers and the priestess Salammbô, daughter of the Carthaginian general Hamilcar. Richly researched, lush and violent, it contrasts sharply with his realist novels.
48888: The Nibelungenlied, the great medieval German epic of heroes, love, betrayal and revenge, rooted in the legends of Siegfried and the Burgundian court. Written in rhymed verse, it is a foundational work of German literature.
48893: Théophile Gautier's daring 1835 novel about the beautiful and mysterious Mademoiselle de Maupin, whose charm entangles two admirers. Lush, witty and provocative, it is known for its preface championing art for art's sake. Volume 1 of 2.
48903: The third volume of the Spanish version of the Arabian Nights, the famous collection of tales framed by Scheherazade, who keeps telling stories to hold back the dawn. Full of magic, lovers, genies and clever tricks, it is a classic of world storytelling.
48913: Eleven lectures on wine given in Italy in the winter of 1880, covering its production, history and enjoyment. A cultural non-fiction work for readers interested in wine and Italian food traditions.
48919: A collection of Goethe's letters, mostly from his youth, which shed light on the emotions and experiences behind his novel The Sorrows of Young Werther. An intimate look at the young poet and his passions.
48943: A sensational Italian novel by the Futurist writers F. T. Marinetti and Bruno Corra, subtitled an erotic-social novel. Its bold, provocative experiments reflect the Futurist appetite for shock and modernity, and some readers may find it explicit.
48944: The first part of Galdós's novel Gloria, about religious intolerance in a provincial Spanish town. The love between Gloria, a devout Catholic, and Daniel, a young man of Jewish background, runs up against fierce fanaticism. A passionate, thoughtful social novel.
48945: The second part of Galdós's novel Gloria, in which the clash between religious fanaticism and personal love in a provincial Spanish town grows more intense. Passionate, thoughtful and dramatic social fiction.
48946: Galdós's complete novel Gloria, about religious intolerance in a provincial Spanish town, where the love between Gloria, a devout Catholic, and Daniel, a young man of Jewish background, comes up against fierce fanaticism. Passionate, thoughtful and dramatic.
48954: A Spanish novel by Concha Espina, a popular early twentieth-century novelist, titled Awakening to Die. Its title suggests a dramatic, emotional story of inner awakening, for readers of period Spanish fiction.
49008: The eighth volume of the nine-volume Cambridge Edition of Shakespeare's complete works, a scholarly edition of the plays and poems by the English playwright. Designed for careful study, with textual notes.
49013: A comic verse play by Pedro Muñoz Seca, premiered in Madrid in 1918, that parodies the exaggerated honour dramas of the Spanish Golden Age. Its many verse forms and comic excess make it one of the most performed plays in Spain.
49024: A collection of letters Goethe wrote to Countess Auguste zu Stolberg, a close friend and correspondent. Personal and warm, they offer insight into his thoughts, friendships and daily life.
49105: A travel book by Edmondo De Amicis, offering vivid sketches of Italian cities, regions and the people who live in them. Warm, observant and affectionate, it is a rewarding read for anyone curious about Italy.
49133: A three-act Italian drama by Annie Vivanti, titled The Useless Mouths. Its title suggests a story of hardship and the cost of scarcity, in the serious theatrical style of an author popular in the early twentieth century.
49149: A satirical novel by Miguel de Unamuno, published in 1902, about Avito Carrascal, a self-important intellectual who believes he can turn a child into a genius through rigid theory. A sharp comedy about pedantry and the follies of education.
49168: The second volume of Montaigne's Essays, in a private edition by Michaud. Montaigne's personal reflections on life, death, friendship and custom are written with candid, casual wisdom, a Renaissance classic that rewards slow reading.
4918: A sentimental Scottish love story by S. R. Crockett, set in the countryside, full of gentle romance and rural life. It is a light and warm read.
49184: A collection of short stories by Enrico Castelnuovo, titled At the Window. Quiet, precise scenes of everyday life are observed from a window's vantage point, in the careful realist style of late nineteenth-century Italian fiction.
49210: The fourth and final volume of letters to Ludwig Tieck, the Romantic poet and critic, from his many correspondents. A window onto the literary circles of German Romanticism, for readers interested in its personalities and debates.
49219: A novel by Antonio Ranieri, the friend of the poet Giacomo Leopardi, about Ginevra, an orphan raised in the Annunziata foundling home in Florence. Sentimental and reflective, it dwells on the sorrows of foundlings and the charity that sheltered them.
49223: A collection by Alfredo Oriani titled Campfire Embers, whose title suggests reflective writings and sketches from the open air. Oriani was a social critic of the late nineteenth century whose writing is serious and intense.
4923: An early romance by Upton Sinclair that takes its title from the legend of King Midas and the golden touch. It is a short, inventive story of wealth and its dangers.
49280: A Spanish novel by Pío Baroja, from the Generation of '98, titled The Roads of the World. Its title suggests a restless journey through life, told in Baroja's realistic, wandering style.
49297: A volume of the nine-volume Cambridge Edition of Shakespeare's complete works, a scholarly edition of the plays and poems by the English playwright. Designed for careful study, with textual notes.
49365: Lectures given in Florence in 1891 on everyday life in fourteenth-century Italy, covering its customs, arts, cities and society. A non-fiction cultural history for readers interested in the medieval Italian world.
49388: A regional novel by José María de Pereda, set among the humble seafaring families of Santander in the mid-nineteenth century. Pereda captures the everyday life of the port in vivid detail, with a warm, affectionate eye for its characters.
49413: A Spanish Romantic historical novel by Enrique Gil y Carrasco, published in 1844 and set in medieval León, with the Knights Templar at its heart. A story of nobility, love and conflict, it is an early model of the Spanish historical novel.
49417: Las máscaras, a two-part drama by Ramón Pérez de Ayala, the early twentieth-century Spanish novelist and critic. Its title points to disguise and appearance, in thoughtful, intellectual theatre for readers of Spanish drama.
49420: A collection of verse by Olindo Guerrini, the Italian poet and satirist, titled Scraps. Guerrini was known for sharp, witty poems, so the book suits readers of lively Italian poetry.
49424: The German edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island. A boy, Jim Hawkins, gets hold of a treasure map and sets sail for a hidden island with a crew that includes the charming, one-legged cook Long John Silver. Swashbuckling and full of tension.
49433: The sixth novel of Galdós's Episodios nacionales, narrated by Gabriel de Araceli. It recounts the second siege of Zaragoza during the Peninsular War in 1809, in vivid, patriotic historical fiction full of street fighting and ordinary heroism.
49441: An account by the missionary R. P. Duchaussois of life among Indigenous peoples and Inuit in the polar regions of Canada. A non-fiction travel and missionary narrative, with ethnographic observations of its period.
49463: A collection of stories for young readers by Pietro Thouar, a Florentine writer of the mid-nineteenth century. Moral tales written for children, gentle in tone and typical of Italian writing for the young of its era.
49485: A collection of short stories by Enrico Castelnuovo, led by the title tale Natalia. Written in his careful, observant style, the stories portray ordinary lives in late nineteenth-century Italy.
49510: A collection of short stories by Caterina Percoto, a writer from Friuli who portrayed peasant and rural life with realism and compassion. Simple, humane tales for readers interested in regional Italian fiction.
49582: A German translation of a work by René Arcos, a French writer, titled The Common Thing. Judging by its title, it is a reflective work about shared human life, for readers of French literature in translation.
49599: The collected published and posthumous writings of Carlo Bini, a Livornese writer of the early nineteenth century. A varied set of essays and pieces that offers a window onto the literary and political climate of Tuscany.
49626: A novel by Sibilla Aleramo, the author of Una donna, titled The Passage. Written in her introspective and direct style, it continues her exploration of women's inner lives in early twentieth-century Italy.
49660: A collection of Arab legends set in the Alhambra palace in Granada, retold by the Spanish novelist Manuel Fernández y González. Romantic tales of love, magic and the Moorish past, with the palace's atmosphere as their backdrop.
49712: Marcel Schwob's collection of twenty-two short imaginary biographies of real and legendary figures. Learned, inventive and ironic, the sketches play with the idea of biography, for readers who enjoy short, inventive prose.
49738: Fifteen cheerful tales by Josephine Siebe about children in the village of Oberheudorf, full of everyday mischief and warmth. Written for young readers in German.
49756: A novel by Emilia Pardo Bazán, the Galician writer and critic, titled The Chimera. Its title suggests an unattainable dream, and it is a psychological novel of the early twentieth century for readers of Spanish fiction.
49759: A short work by Luigi Capuana, the Sicilian writer, that examines spiritualism and claims of spirit communication with a sceptical, questioning eye. It reflects the late nineteenth-century fascination with psychic phenomena.
49773: Flaubert's novel of Frédéric Moreau, a young man who arrives in Paris full of romantic hopes and becomes infatuated with an older married woman. A subtle, ironic portrait of disappointed ambition through the turbulent 1840s.
49807: A collection of short stories by Federico De Roberto, first published in 1887 and titled The Lot. Psychologically sharp and unsentimental, the tales show his clear, precise eye for character.
49836: A 'nivola', or novel-in-the-making, by Miguel de Unamuno, first published in 1914. Augusto Pérez, a rich, idle young man, questions his own existence, and the author appears in the story itself. A witty, philosophical novel about fiction and identity.
49837: An Italian work by Antonio Beltramelli titled Ah, Giacometta, Your Little Garland! Its warm, folksy title suggests a romantic and lightly sentimental story, for readers of early twentieth-century Italian fiction.
49887: A collection of aphoristic reflections by the American-born writer Natalie Clifford Barney, who lived in Paris and wrote about love, women and freedom from convention. Short, witty and frank, it is a notable document of Parisian literary life.
49908: A novel by Hermann Hesse, partly drawn from his own schooling, about a gifted boy under pressure from a rigid school system and his own high expectations. Earnest, sensitive and critical of education, it is a classic of school fiction.
49977: The French libretto of Richard Wagner's Ring cycle, four music dramas drawn from Germanic and Norse myth. Gods, giants, dwarves and heroes contend over a cursed gold ring, in epic and mythic scale.
49987: A historical romance by G. P. R. James, one of the most popular novelists of the Victorian period, set in the medieval past. Full of forest adventure, knights and chivalric drama, it is a classic of old-fashioned historical fiction.
500: A wooden puppet named Pinocchio comes to life and longs to become a real boy, getting into trouble along the way. Collodi's children's classic is playful, moral and full of mischief and surprises.
50027: A witty three-act comedy by Leandro Fernández de Moratín, first staged in Madrid in 1806. It is about young women, family pressure and arranged marriage, and was once banned by the Inquisition. Sharp, sensible and lively.
50126: A Spanish novel by Pío Baroja, from the Generation of '98, titled The Resources of Cunning. Its title points to a clever, roguish story, told in Baroja's restless and realistic style.
50133: H. P. Lovecraft's cosmic horror story, set in the fictional rural town of Dunwich in Massachusetts. Strange events and a sinister family build slowly to a terrifying climax. A classic of weird fiction, atmospheric and unsettling.
50136: Cheerful stories of the Oberheudorf boys and girls in the town, by Josephine Siebe. Light, amusing tales of childhood, with warmth and everyday comedy, written for young readers in German.
50154: A collection of short stories by Alphonse Daudet, first published in 1873, drawn from the Franco-Prussian War and the troubled Paris of its aftermath. Realistic and tender, with a melancholy tone that captures ordinary people's hardship.
50173: Volume 3 of Molière's complete works, bringing together comedies by France's greatest comic playwright. Sharp, witty satires of manners, hypocrites and pretension, in classic French verse and prose.
50277: Stories of boys and girls growing up in a small town, by Josephine Siebe. Light and warm in tone, these tales of childhood are written for young readers in German.
50285: A German crime novel by Norbert Jacques, the book behind Fritz Lang's film. Its master criminal, Dr Mabuse, a brilliant gambler and master of disguise, manipulates people and events from the shadows. Fast, sensational and full of suspense.
50290: A science fiction story by Frank Belknap Long, a writer associated with H. P. Lovecraft and the early American pulp magazines. Titled Space Station 1, it suits readers who enjoy classic, imaginative futuristic fiction.
50291: A novel in dialogue form, published in Venice in 1528 and probably written by the Spanish cleric Francisco Delicado. It follows Lozana, a lively Andalusian woman in the seedy underworld of Rome, in a frank, bawdy and vivid style.
503: A rich collection of fairy tales from many lands, gathered by Andrew Lang for children. The stories are colourful and fun, a classic introduction to traditional folklore.
50306: Unpublished fragments of Ariosto's poem Rinaldo ardito, drawn from the original manuscript. Of interest to students of Ariosto and Italian Renaissance epic, with the bold knight Rinaldo at the centre.
50398: Tall tales by Baron Münchausen, the fictional nobleman who recounts impossible adventures, from riding a cannonball to escaping monsters, all delivered with a straight face. Witty and playful, a classic of comic exaggeration.
50442: A romantic comedy in three acts by Alessandro de Stefani, titled Tristan and the Shadow. Light and theatrical in tone, it suits readers of Italian stage comedy.
50444: A historical novella by Wilhelm Raabe, set in 1673 in the town of Höxter, where an angry mob threatens the local Jewish community. Based on real events, it blends history with moral courage and humane storytelling.
50445: A novella by Wilhelm Raabe, written in 1874 and set against the symbolic background of the river Innerste in the Harz mountains. It follows a wild young man returning from the Seven Years' War, in a reflective and humane story of change.
50492: The first volume of Le Sage's picaresque novel, following Gil Blas, a witty young man who moves from one master and one scrape to another across Spain. Comic, episodic and full of colourful characters and satire.
50528: Pitt und Fox, a novel by Friedrich Huch, first published in 1909, about the love affairs of the Sintrup brothers in a German setting. Lighthearted and warm, with a focus on character and the paths love takes in young lives.
50603: A collection of very short detective puzzles, each presenting a crime in a few lines for the reader to solve. Quick, playful and brain-teasing, suited to anyone who enjoys mysteries in small doses.
50605: The letters of the French philosopher Denis Diderot to Sophie Volland, his devoted companion, written over many years. Intimate, witty and wide-ranging, they mix personal news with thoughts on art, life and ideas.
50616: Gustav Freytag's classic guide to the structure of drama, which analyses how plays from the Greeks to Shakespeare and his own time are built. Non-fiction for writers and readers of theatre, and the source of the well-known Freytag's pyramid.
50657: An English prose translation, with notes, of the Roman satirists Juvenal, Persius, Sulpicia and Lucilius. Juvenal's biting poems attack corruption, greed and the excesses of Roman life, dense with allusion but sharp and often very funny.
50674: A travel account by Tommaso Alberti of his journeys to Constantinople between 1609 and 1621, offering a view of the Ottoman capital in the early seventeenth century. Of interest to readers of travel writing and the Mediterranean world.
50681: A volume from an anthology of German humorous writing, featuring comic tales by E. T. A. Hoffmann and Bettina von Arnim. Witty, imaginative and often eccentric, these stories show the lighter side of German Romanticism.
50697: A collection of very short Futurist plays by F. T. Marinetti and Bruno Corra, written as synthetic theatre that compresses action into a few brief, bold and often absurd scenes. Experimental and provocative, it reflects the Futurist revolt against tradition.
50718: A scholarly study by the French Celticist Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville of Irish mythology, especially the Mythological Cycle and its gods, the Tuatha Dé Danann. Non-fiction for readers of Celtic myth and early literature.
50726: A Spanish novel by Pío Baroja, titled The Adventurer's Route. Its title suggests a restless, wandering story, told in Baroja's realistic and direct style, for readers of Spanish fiction of the early twentieth century.
50742: A prose translation of the Old English epic Beowulf, in which a hero comes to the aid of a Danish king by battling the monster Grendel and then Grendel's mother. Vivid, heroic and full of ancient northern drama.
50887: A German collection of Edgar Allan Poe's short stories, including the title tale Ligeia, along with seven of his poems. Gothic, haunting and atmospheric, these tales of obsession and the uncanny are classics of the genre.
50954: The complete poetic and dramatic works of Robert Browning in the Cambridge Edition. Browning's dramatic monologues probe the minds of their speakers with irony, dark humour and psychological depth, and this large volume gathers them all.
50965: Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales in a German edition, illustrated with dark, haunting drawings by the Austrian artist Alfred Kubin. Familiar tales of the moving and the uncanny take on a strange, dreamlike mood.
5097: Three shipwrecked men are taken prisoner aboard the Nautilus, a submarine far ahead of its age, by the mysterious Captain Nemo. Verne's undersea voyage is inventive, detailed and full of marine wonder, in the original French.
50974: A nineteenth-century French study by Charles Desmaze of crime, vice and divorce in Paris, written as a sensational and moralising chronicle. A non-fiction work for readers of Parisian social history.
51: Anne Shirley leaves her beloved Avonlea to study at a college in Nova Scotia, where she meets new friends and faces the choices of growing up. The third Anne book is lighter and more reflective, with a cosy, bookish mood.
51019: The first volume of George Borrow's account of his travels in Spain as an agent for the Bible Society, distributing Bibles and meeting Romani people, priests, bandits and officials. Adventurous, vivid and often humorous, it reads like a novel.
51020: The second volume of George Borrow's account of his travels in Spain as an agent for the Bible Society. Adventurous, vivid and often humorous, it follows his encounters with a wide range of Spanish people and places.
51029: Volume eight of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of essays and literary criticism by the leader of Spanish-language modernismo. Thoughtful and stylish, for readers of Spanish poetry and literary theory.
51130: A sixteenth-century Spanish tragicomedy in the manner of La Celestina, the famous play about love and go-betweens. Its title, which calls it a third Celestina, shows how closely it follows that model, for readers of Spanish Renaissance drama.
512: A collection of short stories and sketches by Nathaniel Hawthorne, set in an old manse in New England. The tales are reflective, gently ironic and full of quiet symbolism.
5131: A disillusioned young nobleman travels across Europe, reflecting on history, nature, art and his own restless heart. Byron's long poem is romantic, melancholy and full of vivid landscapes.
51338: Cyrano de Bergerac's comic, satirical voyage to the Moon and the Sun, in which the narrator meets strange inhabitants and their absurd customs. Witty, inventive and daring, it is one of the earliest works of science fiction.
51356: Nietzsche's early work arguing that Greek tragedy arose from the tension between Apollonian order and Dionysian intoxication. Philosophical and passionate, it is a key text for readers of philosophy and classical culture.
514: The four March sisters grow up during the American Civil War, facing poverty, ambition and love. Alcott's warm, classic novel is tender, funny and full of family life and the joys of growing up.
51428: A novel titled That Which Hath Wings by Richard Dehan, the pen name of the Irish novelist Clotilde Graves. A popular late-Victorian and Edwardian novel of its day, its title suggests a story of freedom and escape.
51450: A novel by Emilia Pardo Bazán, the Galician writer and critic, titled The Black Mermaid. Its title points to a story of the sea and of the strange and alluring, and a 1947 Spanish film was based on it.
51465: A sixteenth-century Spanish comedy, titled Selvagia or Serafina, from the Renaissance theatre. For readers of early Spanish drama and its traditions, with a title that promises love, wit and the theatre of the period.
51476: A Gothic novel by Gustav Meyrink, inspired by the Golem legend and set in the old Jewish quarter of Prague. Following a gem cutter whose strange dreams and sense of identity begin to unravel, it is mystical, dreamlike and eerie.
51582: A cheerful German tale by Josephine Siebe about a group of boys who arrive in the big city. Light, funny and lively, it was written for young readers.
51587: A short story by Sibilla Aleramo titled Transfiguration. Its title suggests a moment of spiritual change, and it is written in her intimate and direct style.
51604: Volume ten of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of his critical opinions on literature and the arts. Thoughtful and sharply written, for readers of Spanish-language modernismo.
51624: A book by Massimo Bontempelli titled From the Stelvio to the Sea, which suggests a journey from the high Alpine pass down to the Adriatic. A travel and landscape work by the Italian writer.
51627: Volume fourteen of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of his short stories and chronicles. Lively, observant pieces for readers of the Spanish-language modernismo movement.
51649: The final volume of G. W. M. Reynolds's sprawling Victorian serial, which follows the crime, poverty and vice of London's underworld in lurid, melodramatic detail. Sensational and social, it was hugely popular in its day.
51689: The third volume of George Borrow's account of his travels in Spain as an agent for the Bible Society, meeting Romani people, priests, bandits and officials. Adventurous and vivid, with a wry and humorous tone.
51721: A collection of stories by Eduardo Zamacois titled Of Flesh and Bone. Realist tales of human passions and frailty in early twentieth-century Spain, for readers of Spanish short fiction.
51722: A German novel by Paul Keller set in the Spreewald, the wetland region of Brandenburg with its canals, villages and rural traditions. Warm and regional, in the German Heimat tradition.
51775: The second volume of Richard Burton's unexpurgated English translation of the Arabian Nights, with the frame story of Scheherazade and many tales. Frank, lush and full of adventure, it is a famous Victorian translation with extensive notes.
51802: A volume from C. A. Walckenaer's study of the life and letters of Madame de Sévigné, the witty seventeenth-century letter writer. The volume throws light on court and family life in the age of Louis XIV.
51826: A French novel titled Aymeris by the painter and writer Jacques-Émile Blanche, who moved in the artistic and literary circles of Paris. It offers a view of the artistic and social life of its time.
51876: A satirical study of literary manners by Fernand Kolney, centred on the salon of a Parisian hostess. Witty and gossipy, it is a window onto the literary world of early twentieth-century Paris.
51977: Théophile Gautier's critical portrait of Victor Hugo, written by a fellow Romantic who knew him well. Admiring and vivid, it offers a personal view of Hugo's work and reputation.
5200: A travelling salesman wakes one morning to find himself transformed into a giant insect, and his family must come to terms with the change. Kafka's novella is strange, bleak and darkly comic.
52006: Choderlos de Laclos's epistolary novel of 1782, told entirely through letters. Two aristocratic libertines, Valmont and Merteuil, plot seductions and manipulations in pre-revolutionary France. Witty, cynical and psychologically sharp, it is one of the great French novels.
52050: Volume fifteen of Rubén Darío's complete works, his autobiography. A personal account of his life, poetry and career by the leader of Spanish-language modernismo.
52083: A collection of humorous stories about school life by Ernst Eckstein, the nineteenth-century German writer. Light, comic and nostalgic, it shows the everyday comedy of pupils and teachers.
52093: The first volume of a novel by Juan Valera, the Spanish writer and diplomat, which reworks the Faust legend in a Spanish setting. It explores the illusions and idealism of its title character in Valera's witty and urbane style.
521: A shipwrecked sailor is stranded on a remote tropical island, where he builds a life through ingenuity, faith and hard work. Defoe's classic adventure is practical, detailed and full of survival lessons.
52185: A non-fiction survey of German caricature in the nineteenth century by the writer Georg Hermann, with its satirical drawings and cartoons. For readers of art history and social satire.
52218: Gerhart Hauptmann's naturalist social drama of 1889, which exposes the harsh conditions of a family trapped by poverty and social inequality. A young intellectual is drawn into their troubles. Powerful, raw and critical of society.
5225: Encolpius and his companions wander through the decadent Rome of Nero, in a sequence of comic episodes including a famous extravagant feast. Petronius's satire is bawdy, witty and fragmentary.
52262: Washington Irving's sketches and tales of the Alhambra palace in Granada, full of legends of Moors, Spaniards and local characters. Romantic, nostalgic and lyrical, it is a classic travel book about Spain.
52282: The fourth volume of C. A. Walckenaer's study of the life and letters of Madame de Sévigné, the witty seventeenth-century letter writer. It throws light on court and family life in the age of Louis XIV.
52299: A non-fiction collection of caricatures and cartoons from the First World War, with commentary on how artists used satire during the conflict. For readers of war history and visual culture.
5230: A scientist discovers how to make himself invisible and becomes a menace to the quiet village where he takes refuge. Wells's novel is eerie, witty and full of Victorian suspense.
52330: Gustav Freytag's bestselling realist novel of 1855, following a young clerk, Anton Wohlfart, through the world of merchants and business. A portrait of middle-class ambition, honesty and social change, once one of the most read novels in Germany. Volume 1 of 2.
52353: A travel account by J. Hirschberg of a journey around the world, with descriptions of distant lands, peoples and cities. A non-fiction voyage narrative in the style of late nineteenth-century travel writing.
52392: A bleak realist novel by Benito Pérez Galdós, set in Madrid and centred on a lower-middle-class family struggling with poverty and pride. Its main character, a former civil servant, clings to his dignity as hardship closes in. Satirical, sad and sharply observed.
524: Ann Veronica Stanley, a young woman in Edwardian London, rebels against her strict father to pursue an education and independence. Wells's novel is a lively, witty look at the New Woman and the constraints of the era.
52404: A romantic novel titled The Girl Philippa by Robert W. Chambers, the American writer of popular early twentieth-century fiction. Light romantic fiction for readers of its era.
52428: The fifth volume of C. A. Walckenaer's study of the life and letters of Madame de Sévigné, the witty seventeenth-century letter writer. It gives a close view of the court and society of her time.
52484: A children's fantasy by Carlo Collodi about a wooden marionette, Pinocchio, whose mischief leads him into many perils and temptations. Along the way he meets odd and memorable characters who teach him lessons about life. Playful, moral and full of wonder.
5250: Nana, a beautiful former courtesan, rises through the ranks of Parisian society, and her charms bring ruin to the men who pursue her. Zola's novel is vivid, naturalistic and full of Second Empire excess.
52511: Essays by the French critic Jacques Rivière on writers, composers and painters, from Baudelaire and Claudel to Debussy, Cézanne and Gauguin. Thoughtful criticism for readers interested in French literature, music and art.
52597: Two short psychological love stories by Emilia Pardo Bazán, both published in 1889. Morriña is a quiet, domestic tale about a mother, her son and a new servant, with sharp and detailed analysis of feeling.
52611: An eighteenth-century occult romance by Jacques Cazotte, about a young officer pursued by a devil in the guise of a beautiful woman. Eerie, witty and sensual, it helped establish the French taste for the supernatural.
52643: A novel by Rabindranath Tagore, translated into German, about love, marriage and politics in early twentieth-century Bengal. A wife is drawn toward a fiery nationalist while her husband seeks a gentler path. Thoughtful and emotionally intense.
52744: A short Italian collection by Lucio D'Ambra, the early twentieth-century writer, containing three dialogues and two stories. Light, reflective and witty, with a modern feel.
52831: The seventh volume of Balzac's Human Comedy, containing the third part of his Scenes of Provincial Life. Balzac's vast, interlinked novels portray French society through ambition, money and love.
52857: Volume three of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of his travel writing and reflections on Europe, titled Sunlands. Lyrical, observant and cosmopolitan, for readers of Spanish-language modernismo.
52892: A naturalist drama by Arno Holz and Johannes Schlaf, first staged in Berlin in 1890, showing a poor family in the city's lower middle class. Stark, unsentimental and realistic, it was a landmark of German naturalism.
52927: The French translation of Homer's Odyssey, the ancient Greek epic of Odysseus and his long voyage home after the Trojan War. Full of monsters, goddesses and cunning, with the faithful Penelope waiting at home.
52929: The final volume of C. A. Walckenaer's study of the life and letters of Madame de Sévigné, the witty seventeenth-century letter writer. It gathers her world of court, family and gossip in the age of Louis XIV.
52985: The first volume of a German anthology of humorous writing, featuring tales by Peter Rosegger and Wilhelm Raabe. Warm, comic and folksy sketches of German life.
52986: Volumes four and five of a German anthology of humorous writing, a mix of comic stories and sketches by various authors. Lighthearted reading for anyone who enjoys nineteenth-century German humour.
53110: A scholarly treatise on the archaeology and art history of Italic, Etruscan and Roman art, with illustrations and careful analysis of ancient artefacts. A reference work for readers of classical art and Italian antiquity.
5314: A treasury of German fairy tales collected by the Brothers Grimm, in an English translation for children. The stories are folkloric, bold and full of magic and moral lessons.
53154: A novel by Philippe Aubert de Gaspé, the French-Canadian writer, titled Cameron of Lochiel after a Highland Scottish clan chief. Its title suggests a tale of Highland honour and clan loyalty, for readers of early Canadian fiction.
53184: A collection of short stories by Gabriele D'Annunzio, set in and around his native Pescara on the Adriatic coast. Vivid and sensual, the tales capture the land, the sea and the lives of local people, linked into a whole.
53207: The first volume of a Spanish translation of Shakespeare's plays by the scholar Marcelino Menéndez y Pelayo. A formal, scholarly rendering for readers who want Shakespeare in Spanish.
5322: A soldier named Woyzeck is pushed to the edge by poverty, humiliation and strange experiments, and his mental state begins to crack. Büchner's unfinished play is stark, haunting and remarkably modern.
53223: A study of the poet Giacomo Leopardi by Federico De Roberto, the Sicilian novelist. A critical and biographical essay for readers interested in the Italian poet and his place in literature.
5323: Effi Briest, a young woman married to an older official in Prussia, longs for excitement and freedom, and her choices bring consequences. Fontane's realist novel is measured, moving and sharply observant of society.
53292: A collection of folk legends and sagas from the Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge) on the Saxon-Bohemian border, gathered by the folklorist Johann August Ernst Köhler. Traditional tales of spirits, mines and village life for readers of German folklore.
53294: José Zorrilla's memoirs of his youth and of the literary life of Romantic Spain, full of colourful portraits of the writers and society of his day. A warm, anecdotal book for readers of Spanish Romanticism.
53303: An Italian novel by Lucio D'Ambra, a writer of the early twentieth century, titled The Mirage. Its title suggests dreams, illusions and hopes that stay just out of reach.
53330: A Spanish version of the pastoral romance Daphnis and Chloe by the ancient Greek writer Longus, together with fragments of legends from the ancient East. Idyllic, sensual and charming.
53416: A romantic novel by Charles Garvice, one of the most popular writers of sentimental love stories in the late Victorian and Edwardian period. Light, emotional and comforting.
53419: An anthology of twenty-five ghost stories from various writers. Short, eerie tales of the supernatural for readers who enjoy chilling and atmospheric fiction.
53436: The second volume of a novel by Juan Valera, the Spanish writer and diplomat, which reworks the Faust legend in a Spanish setting. It continues to explore the illusions and idealism of its title character in Valera's witty style.
53439: Jules Verne's survey of nineteenth-century travel and exploration, describing the great voyages, explorers and discoveries of his time. Non-fiction written with Verne's enthusiasm for science and geography.
53457: A nature book by Hermann Löns, told as an animal story about a hare and its life in the countryside of northern Germany. Gentle, observant and rooted in the landscape.
53517: A Spanish historical novel by Pío Baroja about the political strongmen of the 1830s, told in his restless and realistic style. For readers interested in nineteenth-century Spanish history and fiction.
53536: A children's walk through the Paris Exposition, in which two children stroll through the Champ-de-Mars and the Esplanade des Invalides. A lively, informative non-fiction piece for young readers of the period.
53552: A selection of the works of Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer, the Romantic poet whose intimate, melancholy rhymes and legends are loved across the Spanish-speaking world. Short, lyrical and evocative.
53587: The first volume of a Romantic chivalric novel by Mariano José de Larra, set in fifteenth-century Castile under the sickly King Henry III. Full of knights, intrigue and passion, it is a historical romance by Spain's great satirical journalist.
53628: Theodor Fontane's last novel, set in a Brandenburg village and centred on Dubslav von Stechlin, a genial and ageing aristocrat. Its gentle, witty portrait of village life, friendships and changing times is full of Fontane's humour and reflection.
537: Doyle's collection of twelve stories blends eerie tales of terror with clever tales of mystery. The stories are atmospheric, varied and well suited to readers who enjoy a shiver with their detective puzzles.
53743: A Spanish novel by Eduardo Zamacois titled The Mystery of a Little Man. Its title suggests a puzzling, character-driven story in the sensational style of its author.
53779: The second part of Stendhal's unfinished autobiography, in which he writes about his love affairs, aspirations, childhood and schooling in Grenoble. Candid, witty and self-examining, it is a rewarding read for Stendhal's admirers.
53798: A collection of short stories by Javier de Viana, the Uruguayan writer, about rural life and customs in the countryside, with the gaucho world at its centre. Authentic, colourful and close to the land.
53801: An Italian work by Gerolamo Rovetta, the popular late nineteenth-century writer, titled His Excellency's Wife. Its title points to a story of status and marriage among the powerful, for readers of period Italian fiction.
53837: An anthology of Spanish prose writers, gathering passages from the great authors of Castilian literature. A varied introduction to Spanish prose across the centuries.
53856: An anthology of German poetry and prose, arranged in thirteen books and compiled by the writer Wilhelm Schäfer. A collection of German writing from many periods, of interest to readers of German literature.
53874: A historical romance by James Grant, a prolific Victorian writer of adventure novels, titled Under the Red Dragon. Its title suggests the history of Wales or the border wars, for readers who enjoy old-fashioned historical adventure.
53930: Volume five of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of his chronicles and writings on Paris. Stylish and observant, for readers of Spanish-language modernismo.
53946: A non-fiction account by a German naval officer of a warship's voyage in the South Seas, with descriptions of islands, peoples and naval life in the late nineteenth century. For readers of travel and naval history.
53947: A comic farce in three acts by Carlos Arniches, the popular Spanish playwright, about a respectable family and the comic chaos that follows. Affectionately satirical and very funny.
541: In 1870s New York high society, a lawyer is engaged to a sweet young woman until he meets her unconventional cousin, who has returned from Europe. Wharton's novel is elegant and ironic, a subtle study of manners, duty and longing.
54112: Volume eighteen of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of his journalism and writing, titled Everything on the Wing. Lively, quick and stylish, for readers of Spanish-language modernismo.
54167: A sixteenth-century catalogue of the remarkable and monstrous curiosities of Italy, by Ortensio Landi. A strange, entertaining collection of wonders and oddities, for readers interested in Renaissance curiosities.
54178: A novel by Massimo Bontempelli, published in 1921, set in Milan just after the First World War. Its adventures and strange episodes capture the restless, uncertain mood of postwar Italy, with a playful and modern style.
54183: Kipling's stories of Mowgli, a boy raised by wolves in the Indian jungle, and of his animal friends and enemies. Adventurous, moral and beautifully told, in this French translation.
54202: The first part of Goethe's Faust in French translation. The scholar Faust makes a pact with Mephistopheles and falls in love with Gretchen. A dramatic, philosophical tragedy about knowledge, desire and guilt, and one of the great works of German literature.
54219: A short book of literary essays and portraits of English writers by the American poet and essayist Louise Imogen Guiney. Gentle, appreciative and well read, it suits readers who enjoy English literature and its personalities.
54228: A collection of sketches by José María de Pereda about the life of a confirmed bachelor, told with his gentle, ironic eye for provincial Spanish society. Witty, affectionate and full of small-town character.
5423: Gwynplaine, a travelling performer with a face scarred into a permanent grin, is caught up in the politics of early eighteenth-century England. Hugo's novel is melodramatic, philosophical and full of street theatre and Gothic grandeur.
54231: A one-act French drama in prose by Oscar Méténier, a writer of gritty, naturalistic plays about working-class and low-life Paris. Short, dark and realistic, with a sharp sense of the stage.
54285: A Spanish novel by Pío Baroja, titled The Taste of Revenge. Its title points to a story of grudges and retribution, told in Baroja's restless and realistic style.
54393: A collection of essays by André Gide on literature, morality and the freedom of the artist, written in his thoughtful, questioning style. For readers who enjoy literary criticism and the debates of the early twentieth century.
54423: A drama of love, marriage and what is real versus what only seems so, adapted by Galdós from his own novel of 1889 and staged in 1892. Its mood is intense and psychological, suited to readers of Spanish realist theatre.
54430: A Spanish translation of a Gustave Aimard adventure, titled The Mexican Nights. Full of fast action, danger and rivalry in the wild frontier settings typical of nineteenth-century adventure fiction.
54436: Volume one of a four-volume selection of plays by Pedro Calderón de la Barca, the great Spanish dramatist of the Golden Age. Religious dramas, honour plays and comedies, rich in verse and wit.
54521: A novel by Benito Pérez Galdós, published in 1889, that tells the same story as his play Realidad from a different viewpoint. Its title, The Unknown Woman, points to a mystery at its centre, told with shifting perspectives.
54528: Octave Mirbeau's book about a motor-car journey through Europe, named after the car's registration number. Part travelogue and part cultural criticism, it also includes a chapter on Balzac, and its mood is witty, restless and opinionated.
54690: Volume one of a German collection of comic tales about Nasreddin Hodja, the wise and witty trickster figure of Turkish, Arab and Balkan folklore. Short, humorous anecdotes with a sly moral point.
54691: Volume two of a German collection of comic tales about Nasreddin Hodja, the wise and witty trickster of Turkish, Arab and Balkan folklore. Short, sly anecdotes that are easy to dip into.
54787: The Italian translation of Maria Cummins's sentimental American bestseller The Lamplighter, about an orphaned girl and the kindly lamplighter who looks after her. Warm, moral and emotional, it was a huge bestseller in its day.
54791: A novel by Emilia Pardo Bazán titled Gastón's Treasure. Its title suggests a story built around a prized possession or an inheritance, told in her realist and psychologically observant style.
54819: A collection of comic and bawdy tales by Bonaventure des Périers, the sixteenth-century French writer. Full of jokes, wit and satire on clergy and society, these lively and earthy tales are a classic of Renaissance storytelling.
54831: An Italian novella by Anton Giulio Barrili titled From the Cliff. Its title suggests a dramatic coastal setting, in the traditional storytelling manner of nineteenth-century Italian fiction.
54972: Volume one of J. J. Grandville's richly illustrated book of animated flowers, in which plants take on human forms and personalities in witty, satirical scenes. A classic of French caricature for readers who love illustration.
54983: A French book of nature stories told from the viewpoint of small creatures, following the adventures of a red ant and the memoirs of a pierrot. Gentle, lighthearted animal storytelling in the French tradition.
55: Dorothy, a Kansas farm girl, is swept by a cyclone to the magical Land of Oz, where she sets off on the yellow brick road with a scarecrow, a tin woodman and a cowardly lion. Baum's classic is bright, whimsical and cheerful.
550: Silas Marner, a lonely linen weaver in a country village, has been wronged and lives only for his gold. Eliot's short novel is gentle and realistic, with a warm, humane view of village life and the power of human kindness.
55058: A regional novel by José María de Pereda, the Cantabrian writer, set in the everyday world of his native northern Spain. Warm, realistic and observant of local character, in the style of late nineteenth-century Spanish fiction.
551: Survivors of a sunken submarine find themselves on an island where prehistoric creatures still roam. Burroughs's lost-world adventure is fast-paced and pulpy, full of dinosaurs, danger and jungle action.
55139: The third novel of Galdós's Torquemada series, following Torquemada, a greedy and ageing moneylender in Madrid, as he pursues wealth and status for his family. Sharp, satirical and psychologically observant.
55167: A volume from the complete works of Guy de Maupassant, another group of his realist short stories and novellas. He observes the lives and desires of the French middle and lower classes with a sharp and often pessimistic eye.
55171: A picaresque classic set during the Thirty Years' War, following Simplicius, a foundling raised in the forest, who is swept into the horrors of war. Earthy, satirical and full of vivid episodes.
55179: A Victorian adventure novel by James Grant, centred on the Charge of the Light Brigade in the Crimean War and one of the six hundred cavalrymen who rode into the guns. Military, patriotic and dramatic.
55201: Plato's dialogue, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, in which Socrates and his companions discuss justice and the ideal city-state. Famous for the allegory of the cave and the philosopher-king, it is a foundation of Western political philosophy.
55206: A collection of Spanish fables in verse by Félix María Samaniego, the eighteenth-century writer who adapted Aesop and La Fontaine. Short, witty animal stories with a moral point, classic for children and adults alike.
55215: Nathaniel Hawthorne's retellings of Greek myths for children, in a Spanish translation. Gentle and imaginative versions of tales such as Midas and Perseus, full of wonder and quiet humour.
553: The third novel of Burroughs's Caspak trilogy continues the story of a lost island full of prehistoric monsters and dangerous rivals. It is a fast, colourful pulp adventure for readers who enjoy escapes and battles.
55321: A German collection of short stories by Hermann Hesse, titled Neighbours. Reflective and lyrical, the tales explore ordinary people in their everyday worlds, with the early Hesse's sensitivity.
55367: A French song by the cabaret writer Jules Jouy, in which toys sing of their lives. A light, playful and witty piece for readers of French popular song.
55448: A short prose piece by Ramón del Valle-Inclán, titled Midnight: A Starry Vision of a Moment of War. Lyrical and dreamlike, it is a brief poetic meditation on war and the night sky.
55456: Lewis Carroll's classic nonsense tale in Henri Bué's French translation. Alice follows a White Rabbit down a hole into a world of riddling creatures, shifting sizes and absurd logic. Playful, witty and timeless.
55480: A long Oriental poem by José Zorrilla, set in Granada and its Moorish past, preceded by the legend of al-Hamar. Romantic, lush and full of legend, it reflects the Spanish Romantic fascination with the Alhambra.
55487: The fifth volume of Gogol's complete works in German, containing his plays. Their satire of provincial officials and of marriage in Russia is sharp, absurd and very funny.
55514: A collection of love stories by Emilia Pardo Bazán, exploring desire, affection and disappointment with her sharp, psychologically precise style.
55554: A volume gathering three works by Gérard de Nerval: The Dream and Life, a dreamlike autobiographical account; Daughters of Fire, a set of nostalgic novellas; and Bohemian Gallantries. Dreamy, lyrical and intimate.
55563: A novel by Galdós in which the gentle, bookish Manso, an idealistic man of Madrid, becomes entangled in the lives of the people around him. Psychologically sharp, witty and reflective.
55565: A novel by Clara Viebig, first published in 1899, set in a village in the Eifel hills of western Germany, where the lives and struggles of the women take centre stage. A successful work of German regional fiction.
55616: Volume twenty of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of his scattered prose pieces. Varied, stylish and observant, for readers of Spanish-language modernismo.
558: An ordinary man in London is drawn into a spy conspiracy after a murder, and he must flee across Scotland with secrets he does not understand. Buchan's thriller is brisk, suspenseful and a classic of the early spy genre.
55812: A collection of stories by Emilia Pardo Bazán, grouped as Christmas and Epiphany tales, tales of the homeland and ancient tales. Warm, varied and rooted in Spanish tradition.
55822: Malinowski's classic ethnography of the Kula ring, a system of ceremonial exchange among the Trobriand Islanders of Melanesia. Based on years of fieldwork, it is a foundational study of anthropology, rich in detail and insight.
55860: The first part of the Paris scenes of Balzac's Human Comedy, portraying the ambition, money, love and social climbing of the French capital. Vast, vivid and richly observed.
55869: Jules Verne's account of the great navigators of the eighteenth century, including explorers such as Cook and La Pérouse. Non-fiction written with Verne's enthusiasm for science, geography and the age of discovery.
55882: A collection of short novels by Emilia Pardo Bazán set in Marineda, a literary version of A Coruña. The title story follows two sisters, Dolores and Concha, as they face life in very different ways. Observant and realist.
55914: The eighth and final volume of a German anthology of humorous writing, featuring pieces by Otto Julius Bierbaum and Gorch Fock. Lighthearted and comic, for readers who enjoy a good laugh.
55916: Three short novels by Miguel de Unamuno with a prologue, including the celebrated San Manuel Bueno, mártir, about a village priest who keeps his doubts hidden from his flock. Philosophical, moving and sharply humane.
55917: Volume two of a four-volume selection of plays by Pedro Calderón de la Barca, the great Spanish dramatist of the Golden Age. Religious dramas, honour plays and comedies, rich in verse and wit.
560: Richard Hannay returns in another First World War spy adventure, with intrigue, disguises and daring escapes. Buchan's novel is a lively, patriotic thriller with plenty of tension.
56044: A novel by Emilia Pardo Bazán titled Sweet Master. Its title hints at a story of a dominating figure and the emotions around it, told in her realist and psychologically observant style.
56047: Volume twenty-two of Rubén Darío's complete works, a collection of his portraits of thinkers, artists and politicians of his time. Vivid and perceptive, for readers of Spanish-language modernismo.
56054: Dumas's swashbuckling classic. The young Gascon d'Artagnan arrives in Paris and falls in with three musketeers, Athos, Porthos and Aramis, in a world of duels, intrigue and friendship. Witty, dramatic and full of adventure. Volume 1 of 2.
5610: A light, witty romance by Henry Harland set among English-speaking visitors in Italy, full of charm and social observation.
56149: Huysmans's novel about Des Esseintes, a reclusive and ailing aesthete who retreats from bourgeois society into art, luxury and private obsession. Richly written and strange, it is a key text of the decadent movement.
56156: A novella by Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, first published in 1870, about a man who becomes obsessed with a woman in furs and enters a strange relationship of power and submission. Sensual, philosophical and provocative, it gave its name to masochism.
56265: A collection of legends and myths of the Rhine by X.-B. Saintine, the French writer. Tales of river spirits, castles and ancient heroes, rooted in the landscape of the German Rhine.
56327: La Fontaine's fables in French, witty and wise animal stories drawn from Aesop and from Eastern and Western sources. Each short fable carries a moral, and the book is a classic of French literature.
564: In a cathedral town, a choirmaster's secret obsessions hide a sinister mystery surrounding his nephew's disappearance. Dickens's final novel is dark and atmospheric, and it was left unfinished when he died.
56451: Volume one of Leopoldo Lugones's El Payador, a celebration of the payador, the improvising singer-poet of the Argentine pampas. Lyrical and patriotic, it praises gaucho culture and the open plains.
56463: Francis Bacon's Essays, short reflective pieces on subjects such as truth, ambition and friendship, together with his Wisdom of the Ancients, which reads Greek myths as hidden moral lessons. Concise, shrewd and still widely read.
56498: Three works by Machiavelli: The Mandrake, a sharp and cynical comedy; Clizia, a comedy after Plautus; and Belfagor, a satirical tale of a devil sent to earth to find a wife. Witty and worldly, showing Machiavelli's wit beyond politics.
56641: A selection of poems by Eduard Mörike, the German lyric poet whose songs and reflective verses on nature, love and inner life are among the best loved in German.
56682: A novel by Enrico Castelnuovo titled The Moncalvos, about a family in nineteenth-century Italy. Realist and reflective, in the style of the period's Italian family novels.
56857: A biographical study of Carlo Porta, the Milanese dialect poet, and of the city of Milan in his day. Non-fiction for readers interested in Milanese culture and dialect poetry.
5700: A romantic novel by Charlotte Yonge set in eighteenth-century costume, with love, manners and family duty at its heart. It is gentle, old-fashioned and full of period charm.
57333: A Project Gutenberg compilation of short stories by Anton Chekhov, gathering many of his tales of ordinary Russians, doctors, clerks and lovers. Subtle, humane and often wry, these stories are masterpieces of the form.
57336: A scholarly history by T. Rice Holmes of ancient Britain and Julius Caesar's invasions, drawing on classical sources. Non-fiction for readers of Roman and British history.
57426: A children's fantasy from 1893 by Ingersoll Lockwood, in which a young hero makes a marvellous journey underground. Playful and imaginative, it was little known for more than a century after its first publication.
57448: José Ortega y Gasset's short essay on Don Quixote, first published in 1914, in which he develops his idea that 'I am myself and my circumstance'. A philosophical reflection for readers of Cervantes and Spanish thought.
575: Francis Bacon's short, sharp essays cover ambition, friendship, marriage, study and public life in pithy, quotable language. They are ideal for dipping into and for thoughtful reflection on everyday wisdom.
57550: A study of Filipino folklore by the scholar Isabelo de los Reyes, gathering the beliefs, legends, superstitions and customs of the Philippines. Non-fiction for readers of Filipino culture and tradition.
57565: Alessandro Manzoni's tragedies, sacred hymns and odes, a collection of his verse for the stage and for the church. Dignified, moral and lyrical, for readers of Italian poetry.
57641: The second part of a romance of Sussex by Alfred Ollivant, a warm novel of English country life. Romantic and rural, in the tradition of the English countryside novel.
57648: A selection of traditional Spanish ballads about El Cid, the medieval hero of Castile. Short, rhythmic narrative verse about his battles, his honour and his exile.
57654: Homer's Iliad in Luis Segalá's Spanish translation, the epic of the Trojan War, centred on Achilles' wrath and the disasters it brings to the Greeks. Epic and tragic, full of gods, heroes and battle.
57669: A short detective story by Jacques Futrelle, featuring the brilliant scientist and detective Professor Van Dusen, known as The Thinking Machine. A classic puzzle built around a locked cell, with the reader invited to work out the solution.
57741: A Russian Symbolist novel by Fyodor Sologub, in which Peredonov, a provincial schoolteacher, slides into paranoia and petty malice as his world turns grotesque. Dark, satirical and claustrophobic.
57763: A romance set in Japan by Onoto Watanna, the pen name of the Anglo-Canadian writer Winnifred Eaton, who wrote popular fiction about Japan in the early twentieth century. Romantic, exotic and melodramatic, for readers of its era.
57780: Ariosto's letters, with a historical and critical introduction, documents and notes. Of interest to readers of the Italian Renaissance, the letters reveal the poet's public and private life.
5781: A schoolboy named Augustin Meaulnes stumbles on a mysterious party in the countryside and spends years searching for the girl he met there. Alain-Fournier's novel is dreamy, nostalgic and full of youthful longing.
57850: A novella by Stefan Zweig about an extreme obsession, told with psychological intensity and touches of Freudian insight. A tense, dark study of how passion can overwhelm reason.
57872: A German novel by Max Dreyer about settlers who work to cultivate the bleak Hohenmoor moorland. Its subtitle, A book of wrath and confidence, points to struggle and hope in a harsh landscape.
57883: A collection of short stories by Francesco Dall'Ongaro, the nineteenth-century poet and patriot, reflecting the literary and social interests of the Risorgimento era.
57964: Defoe's castaway adventure in the French translation: Robinson Crusoe, shipwrecked on an island, makes a life for himself with his own hands for many years. Resourceful, practical and reflective.
580: Mr Pickwick and his friends form a club to study the world, and their travels across England bring comic misadventures. Dickens's first novel is a bright, episodic and warmly funny read.
58211: The second volume of Dumas's swashbuckling musketeer novel. The musketeers and d'Artagnan are drawn into further intrigue, political danger and the schemes of the Cardinal's allies. Witty, dramatic and full of adventure.
58221: Homer's Odyssey in Luis Segalá's Spanish translation, the epic of Odysseus's long and perilous journey home after the Trojan War, facing monsters, sirens and the sea, while the faithful Penelope waits at home.
58238: The first two volumes of Dostoevsky's collected works in German, containing Crime and Punishment. A poor former student in St Petersburg plans and commits a murder and then wrestles with guilt, conscience and the desire to confess. A psychological masterpiece.
583: A drawing master is drawn into a mystery when he meets a mysterious woman dressed in white, and a conspiracy threatens an heiress. Collins's sensation novel is gripping, clever and an early model of the detective story.
58425: A non-fiction record of the myths, superstitions and folk survivals of Bolivia, collected by the Bolivian folklorist M. Rigoberto Paredes. For readers of Andean folk culture and traditional beliefs.
58706: Volume four of Montaigne's Essays, in a private edition by Michaud. Montaigne's personal reflections on life, death, friendship and custom are written with candid, casual wisdom. A Renaissance classic.
58801: Volume three of Montaigne's Essays, in a private edition by Michaud. Montaigne's personal reflections on life, death, friendship and custom are written with candid, casual wisdom. A Renaissance classic.
58820: Dorothy L. Sayers's first Lord Peter Wimsey mystery. The aristocratic amateur detective investigates a dead man found naked in a bath, a case that puzzles the police. Witty, polished and classically structured.
58866: Agatha Christie's second Hercule Poirot novel, set on the golf links of northern France, where Poirot and his friend Captain Hastings are drawn into a murder. Clever, witty and full of clues for the reader to follow.
589: David Balfour, now a young man, travels from Edinburgh to London and Holland, facing danger and intrigue in the aftermath of the Jacobite rising. This sequel to Kidnapped is lively and full of Scottish adventure.
59112: Karel Čapek's 1920 play, which introduced the word robot to the world. In a factory producing artificial workers for humanity, the robots come to matter in ways their makers never expected. A prophetic, thoughtful science fiction drama about labour, power and humanity.
5921: The first part of Cervantes's classic follows Alonso Quijano, who reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out as a knight-errant with his squire Sancho Panza. This Ormsby translation is witty, warm and full of comic adventures.
59222: A short German work by Bernhard Kellermann titled Schwedenklee's Experience. Its title suggests a story about a single, personal incident, for readers of early twentieth-century German fiction.
5946: The second part of Cervantes's classic continues the adventures of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, now famous across the land and meeting people who have read about them. Ormsby's translation is witty, reflective and full of comedy.
59464: A historical novel by Lion Feuchtwanger, first published in 1923, about Margarete Maultasch, the so-called ugly duchess of fourteenth-century Tyrol, whose reputation was shaped by slander and legend. Vivid, ironic and political.
59492: Spain's great Romantic drama by the Duke of Rivas, first staged in Madrid in 1836. The fiery Don Álvaro and the noblewoman Leonor are caught in a web of fate and family opposition. Passionate, stormy and dramatic.
598: The sagas of the kings of Norway, from the legendary beginnings to the twelfth century, told in vivid prose. Snorri Sturluson's history is rich in battles, feuds, rulers and Norse myth.
59827: The first volume of Frank Harris's notorious autobiography, a frank and boastful account of his sexual adventures and his life as a writer and editor. Explicit in places, it is a frank period document, not suited to younger readers.
59828: A Victorian penny dreadful serial that introduced the murderous barber Sweeney Todd, who preys on his customers in Fleet Street. Lurid, gruesome and melodramatic, in the sensational style of its day.
59892: A collection of Irish short stories by Donn Byrne, the title story Changeling drawing on the folk traditions of Ireland. Romantic, mysterious and lyrical, for readers who enjoy tales of old Ireland.
599: Becky Sharp, a clever and ambitious orphan, climbs the ranks of society while her friend Amelia struggles with a more gentle fate. Thackeray's satirical novel is witty, sweeping and sharply observant of social vanity.
59931: A romance novel by Gilbert Frankau, first published in 1922. Emotional and romantic, it is typical of the popular fiction of its time, for readers who enjoy sentimental love stories.
60: In 1790s Revolutionary France, a daring English gentleman secretly rescues aristocrats from the guillotine while hiding behind a mysterious alias. Baroness Orczy's adventure novel is a fast-paced, romantic thriller full of disguises and suspense.
600: A bitter, self-conscious narrator living alone in St Petersburg rants and reflects on his life, his pride and his place in the world. Dostoevsky's short novel is intense, philosophical and psychologically sharp.
60032: Volume two of Arturo Graf's study of the myths, legends and superstitions of the Middle Ages. Scholarly and wide-ranging, it is for readers interested in medieval culture and folk belief.
601: A devout Madrid monk, admired by all, slowly gives in to temptation and sets off a chain of terrifying events. Lewis's Gothic novel is lurid, dramatic and full of ghostly and sinister scenes.
60198: Lope de Vega's Golden Age play about a village that rises against its tyrannical lord, based on a real revolt in 1476. Dramatic and rousing, it is a classic of Spanish theatre about justice and communal courage.
60201: A scholarly work of lectures on Vedic mythology by Angelo De Gubernatis, the Italian Indologist. Non-fiction for readers interested in ancient Indian myth and religion.
60316: A Persian romance in William Ouseley's English translation, following Prince Bakhtyar through a collection of tales rich in magic, lovers and moral lessons. A window onto classical Persian storytelling.
60340: Dostoevsky's novel of Prince Myshkin, a gentle and innocent man who returns to St Petersburg and is drawn into passion and rivalry with the proud Nastasya Filippovna. Intense, moving and psychologically profound.
60344: The German edition of Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, the adventures of a shipwrecked sailor who makes a life for himself on a desert island. Resourceful, practical and reflective, a classic of castaway fiction.
60353: Two novellas by the Russian writer Mikhail Artsybashev, Millions and The Death of Ivan Lande. Their titles point to money and death, and their tone is sombre and realist, reflecting the disillusion of early twentieth-century Russia.
60464: A novel by Pío Baroja about a young doctor, Andrés Hurtado, who struggles with the gap between scientific belief and the disappointments of life in turn-of-the-century Spain. Autobiographical in feeling, sceptical and reflective.
60586: Oscar Wilde's comic ghost story of an American family who move into an English country house haunted by an old ghost. Witty, playful and mocking of both the supernatural and national pride. This Italian edition also includes Lord Savile's Crime.
