60656: H. G. Wells's classic science fiction novel, first published in 1898, imagines an invasion of England by hostile Martians. It is told by an unnamed narrator who witnesses the panic and destruction across the countryside around London, and it remains a gripping early tale of alien war.
60720: The fifth part of Proust's great novel sequence, set in Paris, follows the narrator's jealous and obsessive love for Albertine, whom he keeps under close watch in his apartment. It is a slow, introspective book about desire, suspicion and the restless workings of memory.
60746: Gautier's 1863 adventure novel is set in seventeenth-century France and follows a penniless young nobleman who joins a troupe of traveling actors. It is a lively, colourful story of swordplay, theatre life and romance, full of picturesque scenes.
6087: A mysterious aristocrat arrives in London society and begins to prey on the people around him, while a young man follows him across Europe. Polidori's short Gothic tale is eerie and elegant, a forerunner of the vampire story.
60882: Stendhal's 1822 treatise is a reflective study of romantic love and how the mind idealises the person we desire. Drawing on his own unrequited passion, it is a witty, observant essay that suits readers who enjoy psychology and French thought.
60884: A satirical continuation of Don Quixote, written in 1614 by a rival author under a pseudonym, it follows the old knight and his squire on new adventures. It is a playful, sometimes mocking sequel that offers a glimpse of how Cervantes's hero was read by his contemporaries.
60976: Washington Irving's short story from 1819 is a fable of the Catskill Mountains, set in colonial New York. An easygoing villager named Rip Van Winkle wanders into the hills, meets strange companions and falls into a long sleep, leaving a warm, wry and atmospheric tale.
61091: The notorious eighteenth-century English novel is narrated by a young woman who, in London, makes her way through the world of brothels. It is a frank and sensual classic of erotic fiction, with a comic, worldly tone and a strong sense of its period.
61168: Agatha Christie's 1924 mystery follows Anne Beddingfeld, a bold young woman who witnesses a man die at a London tube station. Her search for the truth takes her from the city to South Africa, in a brisk, glamorous puzzle full of travel and intrigue.
61179: Swift's satirical masterpiece follows Lemuel Gulliver through a series of fantastical voyages to strange lands, including a land of tiny people and a land of giants. It is a witty, biting satire of human pride, politics and the travellers' tales of its age.
61202: A collection of short novels by Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote, published in 1613. These tales of love, adventure and social life in Spain are lively and varied, and show the author's gift for storytelling.
61244: A set of Spanish sketches by Pedro Antonio de Alarcón, portraying the customs and everyday life of nineteenth-century Madrid. The pieces are light, observant and full of local colour, suited to readers who enjoy social portraits.
61262: A collection of short detective stories by Agatha Christie, in which the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot solves a variety of puzzles. The cases involve greed, jealousy and revenge, and are neatly clever in the classic English mystery style.
61266: Hesse's 1910 novel follows a composer and the woman he loves, set against the world of music and opera. It is a quiet, reflective story of art, desire and the difficulties of two people who cannot quite reach each other.
61270: A short work by Jean Lorrain about Paris and its literary and intellectual life at the turn of the twentieth century, drawn partly from correspondence. It will appeal to readers interested in fin-de-siecle France, its writers and its cultural circles.
6130: The Greek warriors and the Trojans clash during the tenth year of the Trojan War, and the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon drives the story. Pope's version of Homer is polished, grand and full of heroic speeches.
61304: The first volume of the chronicle of Salimbene de Adam, a Franciscan friar of Parma writing in thirteenth-century Italy. It is a lively, gossipy account of popes, emperors and the events and people he met, full of personal anecdotes.
61305: The second volume of the chronicle of Salimbene de Adam, a Franciscan friar writing in thirteenth-century Italy. It continues his vivid, opinionated and often humorous record of medieval politics, religion and daily life.
6133: The gentleman thief Arsène Lupin uses wit, disguise and daring to outwit the police and the rich in a series of stories. Leblanc's collection is light, clever and full of Parisian style.
61541: Arturo Graf's cultural history, in two volumes, explores how medieval people remembered and imagined ancient Rome. It is a scholarly but engaging study of legends, legends of ruins, and the city's shifting place in the medieval mind.
61542: The second volume of Arturo Graf's study of how the Middle Ages remembered and imagined ancient Rome. It follows legends, ruins and literary visions of the city, for readers curious about the history of ideas and of Rome itself.
6157: A poor cobbler in Russia takes in a stranger who turns out to be an angel, sent down to learn what it is that people live by. Tolstoy's parable is simple, moral and warm.
61751: Sir Richard Burton's study of the sword, written in the late nineteenth century, surveys weapons and swordsmanship across many cultures and periods. It is a learned, sometimes eccentric book, full of anecdote and the author's restless curiosity.
61851: Dostoyevsky's novel is set in the poor, gloomy streets of Saint Petersburg, where a destitute former student plans and commits a murder. It is a dark psychological thriller about guilt, pride and the mind under strain, with a tense, feverish atmosphere.
61885: A collection of memories by Edmondo De Amicis, recalling childhood and school days, with related sketches of small everyday lives. Warm, gentle and nostalgic, it gives a vivid picture of nineteenth-century Italian life.
61887: Dickens's historical novel is set in London and Paris during the French Revolution, and tells of love, loyalty and sacrifice in a time of terror. It is a dramatic, emotional story of two cities in turmoil, with memorable characters and vivid crowd scenes.
61906: Dostoyevsky's political novel, in German translation, is set in a provincial Russian town where a group of revolutionaries and nihilists gather around a charismatic and dangerous figure. It is a dark, sharply satirical story of ideas and their violent consequences.
61921: An Italian version of Swift's satire, following Lemuel Gulliver on his voyages to strange and imaginary lands. Witty, bitter and inventive, it mocks human vanity, politics and the travel literature of its time.
61963: Zamyatin's dystopian novel is set in a totalitarian future state of glass buildings and enforced order, where citizens are known by numbers. It follows D-503, a loyal engineer whose growing doubts lead him toward rebellion, in a stark and striking vision of conformity.
62: A Confederate veteran is transported to Mars, where he finds himself strong and agile in a strange land of green men, sword fights and lost cities. Burroughs's pulp adventure is fast, colourful and full of heroic action.
62201: Dickens's novel follows a young orphan who falls in with a gang of pickpockets in the dark streets of London. It is a vivid, moving story of crime, poverty and kindness, full of memorable characters and the grim and colourful life of the city.
62215: Gaston Leroux's novel, set in the Paris Opera House, follows a young singer who becomes entangled with a mysterious figure who haunts the building. Half mystery and half gothic romance, it is atmospheric, theatrical and full of suspense.
6235: A historical romance by Gilbert Parker set during the Anglo-French wars, with a plot centred on the Channel Islands. It is adventurous and patriotic, full of intrigue and romance.
62359: Enrique Gaspar's novel, first published in 1887, tells of a machine that lets its inventor travel through time. Written with social satire and gentle humour, it is an early Spanish science fiction story and includes a separate tale set in China.
62361: A collection of short stories by the Spanish writer Leopoldo Alas, written in the late nineteenth century. The tales are subtle, ironic and sharply observed, offering a portrait of provincial Spanish life.
62400: A collection of short stories by Edmondo De Amicis, set in nineteenth-century Italy. The tales are warm, simple and humane, with a strong sense of everyday people and their concerns.
62404: Mary Shelley's Gothic novel, in French translation, is told largely through letters and recounts a young scientist who creates a living being from dead matter. It is a haunting story about ambition, rejection and responsibility, with a chilling and tragic mood.
62477: A collection of folk tales from Pomigliano d'Arco in southern Italy, gathered by Vittorio Imbriani and set down in local dialect with variants from other towns. Lively and earthy, it preserves the spoken storytelling of ordinary people.
62615: Ruskin's study of Amiens Cathedral, in its French translation by Marcel Proust, is a meditation on Gothic architecture, sculpture and faith. It is a reflective, richly written work for readers interested in art, religion and the beauty of medieval buildings.
62627: Stevenson's gothic novella follows a London lawyer who investigates the strange bond between his old friend, a respected doctor, and a sinister, unpleasant man. It is a dark, tense mystery about hidden identity, respectability and the divided self.
62691: Gracian's allegorical novel from the seventeenth century follows two travellers, Critilo and Andrenio, on a long journey through a world of human vices and follies. It is a witty, philosophical and satirical book about the art of living wisely.
62813: A collection of literary essays by Arturo Graf on Italian writers of the Romantic and modern periods, including Foscolo, Manzoni and Leopardi. Scholarly and thoughtful, it suits readers interested in Italian literature and its critics.
63100: A German novel of the twentieth century by Kasimir Edschmid, set in a world of artistic and emotional restlessness. It is a modern work for readers interested in German fiction of the period.
63179: A novel by the Goncourt brothers, set in the art world of nineteenth-century Paris, where painters, critics and dealers pursue fame. It is a sharp, detailed portrait of studios, ambition and the cost of artistic success.
6318: Harpagon, a miser obsessed with his hoard of money, creates chaos in his household as he plans to marry off his children for profit. Molière's comedy is sharp, funny and a classic of French theatre.
63194: Walter Scott's historical romance is set in twelfth-century England, in the time of King Richard the Lionheart and the rivalry between Saxons and Normans. It is a colourful tale of knights, tournaments, love and loyalty, full of pageantry and adventure.
63328: A volume of plays by the seventeenth-century Spanish dramatist Pedro Calderon de la Barca. These works show the drama of the Spanish Golden Age, with its honour, love, religion and dazzling theatrical plotting.
6341: E. T. A. Hoffmann's collection of eight eerie tales, including the famous story of the Sandman, explores madness, obsession and the uncanny. The stories are dark, dreamy and full of Gothic atmosphere.
63412: Galdos's novel, published in 1884, is set in Madrid during the late reign of Alfonso XII, when speculation and money dominated the city. It follows a family drawn into financial dealings, offering a sharp view of a society obsessed with wealth.
63424: A collection of folk tales from Chile, gathered by the scholar Ramon A. Laval. The stories are lively and rooted in local tradition, offering a window into the oral culture of the country.
63464: A school reading book by W. Jaime Molins about the Pampa, the grassland region of Argentina. It describes the land, its people and its way of life in a simple, informative style for young readers.
63465: A collection of German fairy tales gathered by Ludwig Bechstein and illustrated with woodcuts after Ludwig Richter. It is a classic, charming book of folk stories, suited to children and to readers who love fairy tales.
63469: A 1951 exposé by two American journalists, Jack Lait and Lee Mortimer, about the social life, gossip and hidden scandals of Washington, D.C. Fast-moving and sensational, it is a snapshot of postwar Washington's society and politics.
63509: A Spanish translation of three plays by Sophocles: Oedipus the King, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone. These tragedies of fate, guilt and loyalty are among the most celebrated works of ancient Greek drama.
63754: Ida Tarbell's autobiography recounts her life as one of America's pioneering investigative journalists, from her early years to her work exposing corporate abuses. It is a candid and lively account of a writer's career and the changing world of the press.
63816: Blasco Ibanez's travel book, the second volume of his account of a round-the-world cruise, takes the reader across America, Asia and Africa in the 1920s. Written with vivid description and personal opinion, it is a lively record of the interwar world.
64: John Carter returns to Barsoom, the red planet also called Mars, to rescue his wife Dejah Thoris from a hostile city of temple priests. This second Mars adventure is breathless, full of sword fights and exotic worlds.
64058: A selection of verse fables in Spanish, in the tradition of animal stories that teach moral lessons. The short, witty poems are a classic example of the fable form, suited to readers of all ages.
64317: F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel is set in the summer of 1922 on Long Island, where a mysterious millionaire throws lavish parties. It follows his obsession with a former love, told through the eyes of a young narrator, in a glittering and melancholy portrait of the Jazz Age.
64414: A highland novel set in the mountains of Bavaria, by Ludwig Ganghofer, first published in 1883. It is a romantic and vivid story of alpine life, centred on a hunter and the wild country around him.
64465: A collection of novellas by the seventeenth-century Spanish writer Maria de Zayas, dealing with love, honour and the fate of women. These stories are dramatic and often dark, with intricate plots and sharp social commentary.
64466: Hesse's short novel follows an artist whose marriage and family life are falling apart. It is a quiet, introspective story about creativity, restlessness and the tensions between art and ordinary life.
64482: Mark Twain's classic novel, in German translation, follows a boy who escapes his drunken father and sets out down the Mississippi River with a runaway slave named Jim. It is a funny, bittersweet story of friendship, freedom and the moral questions of American life.
64522: A collection of fairy tales and short stories by Hermann Hesse, many of them dreamy and symbolic. The tales are poetic and reflective, offering an introduction to Hesse's imaginative world.
64589: A collection of short stories by the Spanish writer Leopoldo Alas, with ironic and observant tales of provincial life. The stories are subtle and witty, with a sharp eye for human foibles.
64830: An erotic memoir, published in French, told in the first person by a woman recounting her experiences in a frank and direct way. It is explicit and sensational, meant for adult readers interested in the erotic literature of the period.
64836: James Grant's historical romance is set in sixteenth-century Scotland, during the reign of James V, and follows the intrigues of court and the fortunes of a young lawyer. It is an adventurous tale of Scottish history, loyalty and romance.
6498: In a German court, a young nobleman falls in love with a musician's daughter, and their romance is threatened by intrigue and class prejudice. Schiller's bourgeois tragedy is passionate, dramatic and full of political tension.
6518: Soldiers in the camp of the general Wallenstein talk, argue and drink, showing the mood of an army in the Thirty Years' War. Schiller's lively play opens his trilogy with humour and vivid characters.
65238: Agatha Christie's mystery is set at a country house, Chimneys, where a weekend party gathers and a crime soon follows. Light and witty in tone, it introduces Superintendent Battle and a playful, fast-moving cast of aristocrats and schemers.
65391: Dumas's adventure novel, written with Auguste Maquet, follows Edmond Dantes, a young sailor falsely imprisoned in a fortress off Marseille. It is a gripping story of injustice, patience, disguise and revenge, set in nineteenth-century France and Italy.
65434: Rousseau's unfinished late work is a series of reflective walks, written as he looks back on his troubled life. Meditative and lyrical, it dwells on nature, solitude, happiness and the sense of being persecuted by the world.
65444: Alfred Doblin's story, first published in 1924, is based on a real Berlin poisoning case of 1923. It traces the life of a lively young woman, her violent marriage and the friendship that leads her toward crime, in a gritty, documentary-style portrait of the city.
65661: Thomas Mann's great novel, first volume, follows a young man who visits his cousin at a Swiss sanatorium high in the Alps. Reflective and ironic, it explores illness, time, philosophy and the strange world of the mountain hospital.
65662: The second volume of Thomas Mann's novel of life in a Swiss sanatorium in the Alps. The patients and their philosophical debates deepen, in a leisurely, ironic and intellectually rich story about illness and the meaning of time.
65689: Leopoldo Lugones's collection of stories, published in 1906, mixes fantasy with early science fiction, drawing on scientific ideas and the strange in everyday life. Inventive and eerie, it is a landmark of Argentine speculative fiction.
65736: Jules Verne's adventure novel follows the English gentleman Phileas Fogg and his French valet Passepartout as they race around the world in a wager. Full of journeys, close calls and changing scenery, it is a brisk, cheerful and inventive story of travel.
65738: A collection of parables written in 1335 by the Castilian prince Juan Manuel. In each tale, the wise counsellor Patronio answers the questions of Count Lucanor with a story, drawn from Aesop and Arabic sources, that teaches a moral lesson.
65903: Jung's study, first published in 1912, explores the unconscious through myth, fantasy and symbol, using a famous series of dreams and visions. It is a challenging and richly imaginative work for readers interested in psychology, mythology and religion.
6593: The warm-hearted foundling Tom Jones is raised in a country household and leaves home for London, falling into scrapes and romance. Fielding's comic novel is lively, bawdy and full of memorable characters.
65999: A volume of satirical dream visions by the Spanish writer Francisco de Quevedo, written in the early seventeenth century. Sharp, witty and fantastical, these sketches mock vice and corruption in Spanish society.
66023: A Spanish translation of the tragedies of Aeschylus, the great Greek dramatist of myth and fate. These plays of gods, ancient curses and moral struggle are powerful and dramatic, and essential reading for lovers of classical tragedy.
66262: The second volume of Francisco de Quevedo's satirical dream visions, written in the early seventeenth century. Witty, savage and imaginative, these sketches expose the follies and corruption of Spanish life.
66337: A Spanish translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses, the classic collection of myths in which gods and mortals are transformed into new forms. Full of vivid storytelling, love, violence and wonder, it is a foundation of Western myth.
6635: A Kentucky tale of rural life and small-town charm, full of local colour and warm human comedy. It is gentle, sentimental and easy to read.
6638: A German almanac of fairy tales by Wilhelm Hauff and other writers from the early nineteenth century, full of magic, wit and folk-inspired stories.
6640: Another German almanac of fairy tales by Wilhelm Hauff and other writers from the early nineteenth century, with magic, wit and folk-inspired stories.
66446: A short Agatha Christie story in which Hercule Poirot investigates a crime connected with a train journey. It is a brisk, neatly plotted mystery, suited to readers who enjoy short detective fiction.
6645: A selection of the writings of Heinrich von Kleist, the sharp and intense German writer, with stories set in Germany, Italy and the West Indies. The works are dramatic, tense and full of extreme emotion.
66452: A short novella by the young Austrian writer Hans Kaltneker, who died in 1919 at the age of twenty-four. Lyrical and intense, it explores love and the feelings of a young man in a time of uncertainty.
6647: A corrupt village judge tries to hide his own guilt while investigating a burglary, and a broken jug holds the clues. Kleist's play in blank verse is witty, clever and a German classic.
6651: Reinhard recalls a childhood love and the girl he once knew by a quiet lake in northern Germany. Storm's novella is wistful, tender and full of melancholy memory.
66583: George Kunz's book surveys the folklore of gems and charms, looking at the magical powers that people have attributed to jewels, amulets and talismans. It is an illustrated, curious and learned book for readers interested in folk belief and precious stones.
66591: Apuleius's comic novel tells of a young man who is accidentally turned into a donkey and suffers a string of bizarre and bawdy adventures. It is a lively, witty and sometimes earthy story of magic, mystery and religious transformation.
66626: A short story by the Portuguese writer Eca de Queiros, in which the familiar Biblical story of Adam and Eve is retold with irony and humour. It is a playful, satirical tale that looks at the first couple with a modern, amused eye.
66897: An illustrated French book by Olivier Diraison-Seylor on ideas of beauty and personal care, with pictures of women and reflections on aesthetics. It is a decorative, period piece for readers interested in the art and culture of beauty.
67098: A. A. Milne's children's classic, illustrated by E. H. Shepard, is a collection of stories about a bear called Winnie-the-Pooh and his friends in the Hundred Acre Wood. Gentle, funny and full of charm, it is a warm book for children and for adults alike.
67138: Hemingway's first novel follows a group of American and British expatriates who travel from Paris to the fiesta of San Fermin in Pamplona, to watch the bulls and the bullfights. Spare, restrained and sharply observed, it is a classic portrait of postwar disillusionment.
67160: A short Agatha Christie story in which Hercule Poirot takes on a murder case. Clever and compact, it suits readers who enjoy quick, well-crafted detective puzzles.
67173: A short Agatha Christie story in which Hercule Poirot investigates a dispute over an inheritance. It is a neat, tightly plotted puzzle, good for readers who like short classic mysteries.
67189: The third novel of Galdos's Episodios nacionales series, set during the French occupation of Spain in 1808 and the uprising in Madrid. Following the adventures of Gabriel de Araceli, it blends history with a lively, dramatic plot.
67217: A girls' school novel by Agnes Sapper, written for readers aged thirteen to sixteen, following a young student through her last school year. It is a gentle, warm story of friendship, growing up and the life of a German girls' school.
67248: A short detective tale by Pedro Antonio de Alarcon, based on a real crime that was reported in the Spanish press. Often considered the first crime story in Spanish literature, it is a tense, compact mystery.
67261: A study of folk beliefs, customs and traditions in the Erzgebirge mountains of Saxony, written in the nineteenth century. It is an absorbing record of superstition and rural life for readers interested in folklore.
6737: Crisóstomo Ibarra returns to his Philippine hometown after years abroad and finds himself challenged by the abuses of the Spanish colonial system. Rizal's novel is political, passionate and deeply patriotic.
674: Plutarch's Parallel Lives pairs the biographies of famous Greeks and Romans, such as Alexander and Caesar, to draw out their characters. These classic portraits are lively, moral and full of anecdote.
67541: Dostoyevsky's last novel, in German translation, follows a father and his sons in a Russian family, whose quarrels over money, love and faith lead to a murder. It is a powerful, philosophical story of guilt, doubt and brotherhood.
67595: Arturo Graf's collection of essays on the Italian literature of the sixteenth century, including writers such as Aretino and Veronica Franco. It is a scholarly, thoughtful study of the period's poetry, love lyrics and social life.
6761: A villainous and charming dandy cheats, swindles and seduces his way through eighteenth-century Europe. Smollett's picaresque novel is witty, dark and full of rogues.
67676: A volume of essays by the satirical Spanish writer Mariano Jose de Larra, sketching the life, manners and politics of Madrid in the 1830s. Sharp and witty, these pieces mock fashion, bureaucracy and public life.
6768: A collection of early comic stories by P. G. Wodehouse, with light, fast-moving English humour and eccentric characters. The stories are bright, silly and delightful.
67799: Castiglione's Renaissance dialogue, set at the court of Urbino, discusses the qualities of the ideal courtier, gentleman and lady. Elegant and witty, it is one of the most influential books on manners and conduct in European history.
67804: Archibald Clavering Gunter's historical novel is set during the Eighty Years' War in the Netherlands in the late sixteenth century. It is a romantic adventure of war, loyalty and love, in a colourful, old-fashioned style.
67961: Ovid's witty didactic poem, in Spanish translation, offers advice on the art of seduction in ancient Rome. Playful, cynical and sophisticated, it is one of the most famous love poems of the classical world.
67979: L. M. Montgomery's novel is set in a small Ontario town in the early 1900s, where a young woman who has long been controlled by her family begins to chart a life of her own. It is a warm, romantic and hopeful story of self-discovery.

68283: Lovecraft's cosmic horror story, written in 1926, follows a narrator who pieces together clues from the notes and papers of a dead relative. It is an eerie, unsettling tale of ancient, unnameable beings and the limits of human knowledge.
68355: A volume of Voltaire's history of the reign of Louis XIV, the French king whose court and wars shaped Europe. Elegant and opinionated, it offers a sweeping view of French politics, culture and society in the seventeenth century.
6838: A condemned man awaits his execution in a prison and tells, in his own voice, the thoughts and fears of his final day. Hugo's short novel is intense, lyrical and a powerful plea against capital punishment.
68443: A Spanish translation of three comedies by Aristophanes: The Acharnians, The Knights and The Clouds. These sharp, bawdy and political plays satirise Athenian politics, war and intellectual life with great comic energy.
68566: Goethe's great drama in Spanish translation, Part One, follows the scholar Faust, who makes a bargain with the devil Mephistopheles and falls in love with the young Gretchen. It is a dark, poetic and philosophical work about knowledge, desire and guilt.
68663: A study of the Colosseum in Rome, tracing its history over twenty centuries, from its construction to its later life. Scholarly and vivid, it looks at its architecture, inscriptions and the plants that grew among its ruins.
68957: The first issue of the American pulp magazine Weird Tales, from March 1923, featuring fantasy, horror and adventure stories. It is a classic of early weird fiction, full of strange and eerie tales from the golden age of pulp.
69087: Agatha Christie's mystery novel is narrated by a country doctor in a village where a wealthy man has been found dead. Clever, cunning and famously surprising, it is one of the most celebrated detective novels of the twentieth century, with the detective Hercule Poirot at its centre.
69294: Guido da Verona's Italian novel from the early twentieth century is a romantic story of love and social scandal, written in the popular, passionate style of its time. It suits readers who enjoy melodrama and the emotional conflicts of Italian society.
69327: Kafka's unfinished novel, published after his death in 1925, follows a man who is arrested one morning and told he is accused, though no one will say of what. It is a disturbing, darkly comic allegory of bureaucracy, guilt and helplessness, and one of the most influential books of the twentieth century.
69552: Kipling's collection of animal stories is set in the Indian jungle and follows a boy raised among wolves, along with the beasts who share his world. Vivid, adventurous and full of fables, these tales are a classic for readers of all ages.
69566: The Egyptian Book of the Dead is a collection of ancient spells and hymns, written on papyrus, meant to guide the dead through the underworld. It is a fascinating window into ancient Egyptian religion, magic and belief in the afterlife.
696: A nobleman's son is killed in a strange accident in a medieval castle, and the household is gripped by an ancient prophecy. Walpole's novel is the first Gothic novel, full of supernatural twists and dramatic atmosphere.
69608: The June 1923 issue of the pulp magazine Weird Tales, an early outlet for American fantasy, horror and adventure stories. It is a snapshot of the fast-growing world of the early weird fiction magazines.
69700: The final collection of Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories, first published in the Strand Magazine in the 1920s. Twelve tales of crime and deduction, featuring the famous detective and Dr Watson, show Holmes at work in London.
69799: The second of three volumes in Spanish of the comedies of Aristophanes, featuring The Wasps, Peace, The Birds and Lysistrata. These bawdy, satirical plays mock Athenian politics, war and society with inventive comic energy.
69873: A collection of Spanish short stories by Nilo Maria Fabra, published in the nineteenth century, with a political edge. The tales offer a sharp, observant view of Spanish society of the period.
69917: The Golden Legend is a medieval collection of saints' lives compiled by Jacobus de Voragine in the thirteenth century. Full of miracles, martyrdoms and legend, it was one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages and a rich source for art and culture.
69944: Lion Feuchtwanger's 1925 historical novel is based on the life of Joseph Suss Oppenheimer, a court financier in eighteenth-century Germany. It is a dramatic story of power, prejudice and intrigue at a German princely court.
6996: The tragedy of two young lovers from feuding families in Verona, told with passion, poetry and the swift pace of youth. Schlegel's German translation of Shakespeare's play is lyrical and moving.
700: Little Nell and her grandfather lose their home, and they travel through a grim England of hardship and strange characters. Dickens's novel is sentimental and emotional, with a vivid cast of eccentric figures.
70008: Dorothy L. Sayers's 1927 mystery introduces her aristocratic sleuth Lord Peter Wimsey, who investigates a death in England. Witty and clever, it is a classic country-house puzzle for lovers of the Golden Age detective novel.

70114: Agatha Christie's 1927 mystery finds the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot, with his friend Hastings and Inspector Japp, facing a secret international criminal organization. It is an energetic, globe-trotting puzzle of disguise, danger and clever detection.
70175: G. K. Chesterton's collection of detective stories features Father Brown, a small, unassuming Catholic priest who solves crimes through his understanding of human nature. The tales are witty, humane and full of paradox, a delight for readers who enjoy clever puzzles.
70200: A two-volume collection of biographical sketches of English women writers, each written by the writer herself or by others. It offers a personal, varied picture of literary women and their lives.
70542: The third of three volumes in Spanish of the comedies of Aristophanes, including The Frogs and Plutus. Satirical, playful and sharply political, these plays show the wit of ancient Athenian comedy.
70652: Lovecraft's cosmic horror novella follows an Antarctic scientific expedition that uncovers strange and terrifying ruins deep in the ice. It is a chilling, atmospheric story of the unknown, told with a vast sense of ancient, inhuman time.
708: Young Princess Irene discovers that a clever old great-grandmother, living high in the house above her, is protecting her from goblins that live beneath the mountain. MacDonald's fantasy is charming, gentle and full of wonder.
70845: Bunyan's Christian allegory, in German translation, follows Christian on his journey from the City of Destruction toward the Celestial City. Full of temptations, trials and vivid characters, it is one of the most famous allegories in English and Christian writing.
70854: Philip Sidney's long prose romance is a pastoral world of shepherds, princes in disguise, love and adventure. It is an elaborate, poetic book full of songs, debates and twists of fortune, typical of Elizabethan literature.
70891: Victor Hugo's novel is set in fifteenth-century Paris, centred on the great cathedral of Notre-Dame. It tells of a deformed bellringer, a beautiful street dancer and a priest consumed by desire, in a richly detailed picture of medieval life.
70954: A French novel of the early twentieth century by Pierre Mille, whose title, Three Women, points to the stories of three women at its heart. It is a period piece of French fiction, suited to readers of the Belle Epoque.
70993: Emilio Salgari's adventure novel is set in Brazil, where a fearless hero fights to protect a native people from ruthless enemies. Action-packed and colourful, it is a classic of Italian adventure fiction for younger readers.
70995: Jean Giraudoux's novel, published in 1917, is a personal narrative of the First World War, written in the aftermath of the conflict. It is a reflective, elegant book about memory, loss and the shadow of the war on French life.
70997: Salvatore Farina's Italian novel of the nineteenth century is a romance of love, jealousy and the rivalries of the heart. Written in a warm, sentimental style, it suits readers who enjoy classic Italian fiction.

7109: Voltaire's satire follows a naive young man through a string of disasters and absurd adventures as he searches for happiness, while his tutor insists that everything is for the best. The book is witty, sharp and a classic of Enlightenment fiction.
71218: Dante's Vita Nuova, published around 1294, mixes prose and poems to tell of his lifelong love for Beatrice. It is a lyrical, intimate work of courtly love, and an early landmark of Italian poetry.
71399: A collection of Tuscan folk tales by Pietro Thouar, gathered in the nineteenth century. The stories are simple, lively and rooted in popular oral tradition, offering a window into the storytelling of ordinary Italians.
71490: Jack London's short adventure novel follows Buck, a large domestic dog stolen from his home in California and taken to the frozen Klondike to work as a sled dog. It is a vivid, powerful story of survival, instinct and the wild.
71733: The second volume of Menendez y Pelayo's history of the Spanish novel. It continues his detailed survey of fiction in Spain, for readers who want a learned account of its literary development.
7178: Proust's first volume recalls the narrator's childhood in the village of Combray, where a taste of tea-soaked cake brings back a flood of memories. The book is lyrical, reflective and rich in sensory detail.
7184: A Canadian novel whose subtitle alludes to the damage done by careless speech. It is a moral and sentimental story from the period, with a clear message.
71841: Jack London's novel follows a wolfdog born in the wild of the Canadian north, who is caught between the harsh life of the wilderness and the company of humans. It is a powerful, brutal and moving story of a dog's struggle to find where he belongs.
71865: Virginia Woolf's novel follows Clarissa Dalloway as she prepares for a party on a single June day in post-war London. Moving between many minds, it is a subtle, lyrical portrait of memory, time and ordinary life.

72036: Georges Polti's study proposes that all dramatic plots can be reduced to thirty-six basic situations, from revenge and rivalry to sacrifice. It is a practical, theoretical book for readers interested in storytelling and how plots are built.
7205: The prophet Zarathustra descends from the mountains to preach a new vision of humanity in Nietzsche's poetic prose. The book is bold, aphoristic and provocative.
7206: Nietzsche's early essay on Greek tragedy explores the balance of the Apollonian and the Dionysian in art and culture. It is ambitious, passionate and a key text of modern philosophy.
72139: Jack London's novel, published in 1908, is a political science fiction story set in the United States, where a rising oligarchy crushes a socialist movement. It is an early dystopian work, told through a long manuscript from the future, and a gripping political thriller.
7256: A poor young couple struggle to buy each other a Christmas present with very little money, and their sacrifices reveal their love. O. Henry's story is short, warm and sentimental.
72824: Agatha Christie's 1928 mystery is set on the luxurious Blue Train from the Riviera to Calais, where a valuable jewel goes missing. Hercule Poirot is drawn in as glamorous passengers and their secrets are revealed, in a neat, stylish puzzle.
73: Young Henry Fleming, a private in the Union army, runs from his first battle and then struggles with shame as he longs to prove his courage. Crane's short, vivid war novel is intense and psychological, capturing the confusion of combat.
730: An orphan boy raised in a harsh workhouse escapes to London, where he falls among a gang of pickpockets. Dickens's novel is grim but compassionate, full of vivid Victorian street life and memorable villains.
73144: D. H. Lawrence's final novel, first published in 1928, follows Constance Chatterley, trapped in an unhappy marriage to a wealthy, war-wounded husband. Her growing relationship with the gamekeeper on the estate is a frank, sensual and passionate story of class and desire.
73255: The first volume of Julio Cejador's history of Spanish language and literature, tracing the subject from its origins to the reign of Charles V. Scholarly and detailed, it suits readers who want a wide survey of Spanish letters.
73257: The second volume of Julio Cejador's history of Spanish language and literature, covering the age of Charles V. It continues his broad, scholarly survey of Spanish writing and culture.
7326: A farmer in Staffordshire is drawn into the Jacobite rising of 1745, and his loyalties and adventures test him. George Gough's novel is a straightforward and lively adventure story.
73486: Edmondo De Amicis's classic children's book, written in the form of a school diary, follows a young Italian boy through a year at school in Turin. Warm, moving and full of small heroic and sad moments, it has been loved by generations of readers.
73500: The first of three volumes in Spanish of the tragedies of Euripides, the Athenian dramatist. These plays of passion, family conflict and the gods are among the most powerful works of ancient Greek drama.
73533: A translation of the Poetic Edda, a collection of Old Norse poems about the gods, heroes and myths of the Viking world. Dramatic, terse and full of fate and violence, these poems are foundational to Norse literature.

74008: Theodor Storm's novella tells of Hauke Haien, a gifted and determined dike-reeve on the North Sea coast of Schleswig-Holstein, whose mind is set on protecting the land from the sea. It is a powerful, atmospheric story of ambition, superstition and the forces of nature.
74029: Alexandre Dumas fils's novel, first published in 1848, tells of a young Parisian who falls in love with Marguerite Gautier, a celebrated courtesan. It is a passionate, tragic romance set in fashionable Paris, paired with a Corsican tale of family honour.
74041: A volume of the Arabian Nights, the classic collection of tales in which a storyteller spins stories through the night. Full of magic, romance, cunning and adventure, it is a rich and endlessly entertaining treasury of folk tales.
74222: Hermann Hesse's novel, first published in 1919 under a pseudonym, follows a boy in a German town who struggles to find his true self. Introspective and symbolic, it explores the search for identity, doubt and the pull of a mysterious friend.
74228: Champollion's illustrated guide, based on the ancient Egyptian monuments, presents the gods and mythological figures of ancient Egypt. It is a scholarly yet visual book, a window into the world of the pharaohs and their deities.
7439: Forty-one English fairy tales retold by Flora Annie Steel, with wonderful illustrations by Arthur Rackham. The tales are magical, varied and charming.
74704: The second of three volumes in Spanish of the tragedies of Euripides. These plays of myth, passion and human suffering show the sharp and questioning vision of one of ancient Greece's greatest dramatists.
74723: Antonio Pigafetta's account of Magellan's expedition, translated into English, is the record of the first voyage around the world. Written by a participant, it describes storms, strange lands and the crew's perilous journey, a gripping first-hand adventure.
74908: A selection of short stories by Guy de Maupassant in Spanish translation. These tales of French life are sharp, economical and often ironic, and show why he is a master of the short story.
7500: Heidi, the orphan girl who grew up in the Swiss mountains with her grandfather, leaves the mountain hut to learn and see more of the world. Spyri's sequel is warm, moral and full of alpine landscapes.
75004: A Spanish novel of the early twentieth century by Eduardo Zamacois, set in a society where opinion and reputation weigh heavily. It is a social novel for readers interested in Spanish life of the period.
75011: Erich Maria Remarque's novel of the First World War follows a group of German schoolboys who enlist and are sent to the front. It is a harrowing, honest account of trench warfare, friendship and the lost generation's disillusionment.
75126: Gertrudis Gomez de Avellaneda's novel is set on a sugar plantation in Cuba, where a gentle enslaved man falls in love with a woman of the planter's family. It is an emotional, humane anti-slavery romance, and an early important work of Cuban fiction.
75201: Hemingway's novel, set during the Italian campaign of the First World War, follows an American lieutenant who serves as an ambulance driver and falls in love with an English nurse. Spare and intensely felt, it is a moving story of love, war and loss.
75288: Agatha Christie's 1929 mystery begins with a practical joke among a group of young people, which ends in a death. Superintendent Battle investigates, in a light, playful puzzle full of English village life and eccentric characters.
75397: Anna Elisabet Weirauch's German novel, the first part of a two-volume story, explores the awakening of a young woman to love and her own identity in the lesbian world of 1920s Berlin. It is a frank, emotional novel of its time.
75472: Miguel de Unamuno's essay on Don Quixote and Sancho Panza is a philosophical reflection on the two characters and their meaning for Spanish life. Thoughtful and passionate, it suits readers interested in Cervantes and Spanish thought.
75613: A collection of short stories by the Argentine writer and journalist Jose S. Alvarez, known as Fray Mocho. The tales describe life in Buenos Aires and the city's streets, people and characters, with humour and vivid local detail.
75643: Edgar Wallace's 1926 crime novel is set in an old Sussex abbey, where the ghost of a monk is said to guard a lost treasure. It is a gripping, spooky thriller, full of secrets, suspicion and mystery.
75679: A short story by the Russian writer Aleksei Remizov, in German translation, from the early twentieth century. It is a stylised, lyrical tale of Russian life, for readers interested in Russian fiction of the period.
75685: The second volume of Anna Elisabet Weirauch's German novel about a young woman's awakening to love and identity in 1920s Berlin. It continues the story with frankness and emotional depth.
75699: A German collection of tales from the Arabian Nights, the classic cycle of stories told by Scheherazade. Magical, sensual and full of clever tricks, these folk tales offer a colourful introduction to Arabic storytelling.
75739: Victor Hugo's epic novel, the first part, follows Jean Valjean, a former convict who tries to build a new life in nineteenth-century France. Through poverty, justice and mercy, it is a vast, moving story of redemption and social conscience.
75790: H. B. Drake's adventure novel is a tale of treasure, romance and danger in England. Full of mystery and old legends, it is a gripping, traditional adventure story.
75802: Hermann Hesse's novel follows Harry Haller, a middle-aged and troubled man who feels estranged from the world around him. Introspective and strange, it explores the divided self, the crisis of modern life and the search for meaning.
75808: Edgar Wallace's 1929 thriller is a crime story set in England, full of criminals, sudden twists and the thrills of the genre. It is a brisk, lively read for fans of the classic British thriller.
75814: A collection of dramatic short stories by the Spanish writer Emilia Pardo Bazan, set in nineteenth-century Spain. The tales are sharp, varied and full of insight into social life, especially the lives of women.
75838: Alfred Doblin's 1924 science fiction novel, experimental in style, follows the development of human society across centuries, from a colony in Greenland into the distant future. It is a sweeping, ambitious book about technology, nature and conflict on a global scale.
75840: Mary Elizabeth Braddon's novel is an early sensation story, set in Yorkshire, in which an orphan plots to gain an aristocratic fortune. Full of intrigue, secrets and a race to prove innocence, it is a gripping Victorian mystery.
75858: Edgar Wallace's 1925 novel is a crime story in which a young woman and a mysterious countess are at the centre of strange events. It is a lively, twisty thriller, with the flavour of the classic British crime novel.
75877: The third volume of M. E. Braddon's Victorian novel, a domestic and psychological story of family life and morality. It offers a rich, absorbing view of Victorian society and its tensions.
75896: Maurice Leblanc's stories follow Arsene Lupin, a gentleman thief and master of disguise who outwits the police. Witty, stylish and full of daring escapes, they are a classic of French detective fiction.
75909: A dime-novel style detective story by Nat Ridley, set partly in Mexico. It is a fast-paced, adventurous tale of crime and pursuit, in the popular style of its period.
75922: Mary Roberts Rinehart's humorous stories follow Letitia Carberry, known as Tish, and her two spinster friends, who get into all sorts of comic trouble. Light, funny and warm, they are a gentle pleasure for readers who enjoy comedy of manners.
75937: A volume of Chambers's Journal, a Victorian periodical that mixed literature, science and art for a general readership. It offers a varied picture of nineteenth-century popular reading.
75948: A Victorian miscellany that gives plain answers to everyday questions about science, technology and curiosities. It is a fascinating compendium for readers who enjoy odd facts and the wonder of the age.
75949: Edgar Wallace's 1927 thriller is set in an old castle, where a mysterious and sinister threat unfolds around the story's characters. Dark and atmospheric, it is a classic crime thriller for lovers of old-fashioned mystery.
75967: Norbert Jacques's novel introduces Dr Mabuse, a criminal mastermind with hypnotic powers who preys on gamblers and the wealthy in Germany. Dark, inventive and full of menace, it is the start of a famous series of crime stories.
75988: Alfred Kubin's dreamlike fantasy novel, first published in 1909, is set in a strange imaginary kingdom reached through nightmares and visions. Eerie, surreal and disturbing, it is a classic of early European fantasy.
75998: Leslie Charteris's 1929 mystery novel, which does not feature his famous hero the Saint, is a story of conspiracy and crime in England. It is a brisk, exciting thriller for readers who enjoy classic detective fiction.
76: Huck Finn escapes his drunken father and flees down the Mississippi River on a raft with Jim, a runaway enslaved man. Twain's picaresque novel is funny, episodic and deeply humane, written in vivid colloquial voice about conscience and freedom.
76049: W. C. Tuttle's western mystery follows the cowboy detective Hashknife Hartley as he investigates bank robberies in the American West. Lively and quick-moving, it is a classic western with a detective twist.
76059: A horror story by Harper Williams in which a country physician confronts a mysterious and dangerous creature in the woods of Pennsylvania. It is a moody, eerie tale of the supernatural for fans of old-fashioned horror.
76072: R. Austin Freeman's detective novel features Dr John Thorndyke, a scientific investigator who solves crimes through careful reasoning and forensic evidence. It is a precise, methodical mystery for readers who enjoy a rational puzzle.
76082: A collection of short stories by Ray Humphreys, blending western and detective themes around the sheriff Shorty McKay. The tales are quick, tough and full of frontier action.
76084: Gertrude Hall Brownell's juvenile novel follows a group of teenage girls on a summer holiday at a lake in the Adirondack Mountains of New York. It is a cheerful, wholesome story of friendship, adventure and a deserted bungalow.
76116: R. Austin Freeman's detective novel features Dr John Thorndyke, a scientist who investigates crimes in London with methodical care. It is a precise, carefully reasoned mystery for readers who enjoy scientific detection.
76131: Jack Williamson's horror story is set in a small village, where an uneasy man finds his life shadowed by something strange. It is a brief, atmospheric tale of the uncanny and fear.
76168: Edgar Wallace's 1924 crime novel introduces J. G. Reeder, a mild-mannered civil servant who turns out to be a brilliant detective. It is a clever, lively mystery set in England, full of unexpected twists.
76178: Ann Bannon's 1959 lesbian pulp novel is set in 1950s New York, following a young woman who finds love and a new community in the city's hidden gay world. It is a frank, emotional story of its time and an early classic of lesbian fiction.
76199: A collection of Italian military short stories by A. Olivieri Sangiacomo, written in the nineteenth century. The tales portray life in the army, with its routine, comradeship and hardship, for readers interested in Italian fiction of the period.
76200: Stuart Martin's crime novel, set in the courts of England, follows a judge and the question of capital punishment. Tense and dramatic, it examines justice and guilt through the eyes of those who must decide who lives and who dies.
76208: W. C. Tuttle's western stories follow a frontier sheriff who must weigh loyalty and justice in the rough world of the American West. Brisk, honest and full of action, they are classic western tales.
76212: Edgar Wallace's 1917 crime novel is a story of detection and crime in England, with a fast-moving plot and a range of suspects. It is a lively example of the early British thriller.
76222: Gilbert Collins's adventure novel mixes science fiction with exploration, following travellers who journey into the mysterious lands of China and Tibet. It is an imaginative, exotic story of hidden valleys and strange discoveries.
76225: Robert Louis Stevenson's classic adventure novel follows the young Jim Hawkins, who sails to a distant island in search of buried pirate treasure. Full of pirates, mutiny and memorable characters such as Long John Silver, it is one of the most beloved adventure stories ever written.
76247: Isobel Wylie Hutchison's verse drama is a fantasy in which characters search for joy in a strange and dreamlike setting. It is a lyrical, imaginative piece for readers who enjoy poetic drama.
76257: Edgar Wallace's 1922 crime novel has Scotland Yard pursuing a secret league of blackmailers known as The Crimson Circle. It is a gripping thriller of extortion, gangs and detection in England.
76261: A collection of horror short stories by Dick Donovan, a Victorian writer of popular crime and mystery fiction. The tales are eerie and sensational, with a strong sense of the Gothic and the uncanny.
76308: Alexander Weicker's novel from Luxembourg, written in German, is the adventurous chronicle of a man who feels he is superfluous in the world. It is a wry, lively story of a restless life and its odd turns.
76309: Batty Weber's German-language novel from Luxembourg tells of a man's road to redemption and self-understanding. Written in a plain, earnest style, it suits readers interested in regional German fiction.
76339: Ellery Queen's 1929 detective novel, the first of the Ellery Queen mysteries, is a New York murder puzzle solved through careful deduction. It is a clever, carefully clued book for readers who love a classic whodunit.
76352: S. Fowler Wright's 1929 science fiction novel imagines a strange future world, and was planned as a trilogy. Original and imaginative, it suits readers who enjoy early British science fiction of the imagination.
76358: Herbert Russell Wakefield's collection of English ghost stories offers a set of eerie tales of the supernatural. Quiet and atmospheric, these stories are a good choice for fans of classic ghost fiction.
76360: E. T. A. Hoffmann's 1815 Gothic novel follows Brother Medardus, a monk who finds a mysterious elixir in his monastery and is drawn into crime, lust and the fear of his own double. It is a feverish, eerie tale of guilt, the devil and the divided self.
76391: Jane G. Austin's children's fantasy follows young travellers through the strange realm of Elf-land, with its fairy courts, magic and wonders. It is a gentle, imaginative book for younger readers who love fairy stories.
76409: Edith Allonby's short fantasy story is a gentle, imaginative tale, written in the early twentieth century. It suits readers who enjoy short, dreamlike fiction of the period.
76411: Dan Totheroh's children's fantasy centres on a dragon and a grandmother who tells stories of adventure. It is a warm, old-fashioned tale of imagination and wonder for young readers.
